title: Leonardo da Vinci
intro: Leonardo da Vinci finished only a handful of paintings, and they are now spread across Europe. He was also an engineer, an inventor, and a tireless note-taker, and he often left a painting half done when something more interesting came along.
This thread follows his working life from a workshop in Florence to the French court. It ends with the theft that made his most famous portrait more famous still.

chapters.heading: Apprentice
chapters.text: Leonardo was born in 1452 near Vinci, a small town in the hills west of Florence. He was the son of a notary and a young local woman who were not married. As a teenager he was sent to Florence to train in the workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio. Verrocchio was a sculptor and painter who made altarpieces, statues, and metalwork for the city’s churches and guilds. Verrocchio’s bronze of Doubting Thomas was made for a niche on the outside of Orsanmichele, a guild church in the center of town. Leonardo helped his master on a painting of the Baptism of Christ, now in the Uffizi gallery, and painted one of the angels in it. Giorgio Vasari, who wrote the first lives of the artists in the 1500s, claimed that Verrocchio was so impressed that he gave up painting.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to meet the young Leonardo.
items: A long podcast episode from the Getty museum looks at his years in Verrocchio’s workshop.
An audio tour of the Uffizi passes Botticelli’s mythologies and an unfinished Leonardo.

chapters.heading: The Last Supper
chapters.text: Around 1482, at about thirty, he moved to Milan. He applied for a job with its ruler, Ludovico Sforza, in a letter that promised portable bridges, cannons, and siege machines, and mentioned painting only near the end. He stayed for seventeen years. For the friars of Santa Maria delle Grazie, a church the Sforza family favored, he painted the Last Supper on the wall of their dining hall. The usual method was to paint quickly into wet plaster. Leonardo wanted to work slowly, so he used an experimental mix of oil and tempera on dry plaster instead. It began to flake within his lifetime. He also painted a hall in the Sforza Castle as a forest, with the branches of trees knotting together across the ceiling. In 1499 a French army took Milan, and Leonardo left.

mediaNote.lead: The Last Supper has more good material than almost any painting, and here are four pieces of it.
items: A short video looks at the job letter, which survives in his notebooks.
Another explains how he painted the Last Supper, and why it started flaking so soon.
A podcast episode visits the castle hall he turned into a forest.
And Ross King’s short book tells how the mural was made while war closed in on Milan.

chapters.heading: Lady with an Ermine
chapters.text: While he was in Milan, he painted Cecilia Gallerani, a well-educated girl of about sixteen who was the duke’s mistress. She holds an ermine, a white stoat, which was one of the duke’s emblems, and the animal turns its head the same way she does. Around 1800 a Polish prince, Adam Czartoryski, bought the painting in Italy for his mother’s collection, and it ended up in Kraków. The Nazis seized it during the Second World War. It was found in Bavaria in 1945 and brought back. It is one of only four portraits of women by Leonardo, and it now hangs in the Czartoryski Museum.

mediaNote.lead: If you go to see it, two things will add to the visit.
items: A short video from Sotheby’s tells the story of the sitter and the painting.
And Vinci, a Polish heist comedy, follows two thieves who plan to swap the painting for a fake.

chapters.heading: The battle with Michelangelo
chapters.text: Leonardo went back to Florence, which had become a republic again. In 1503 its government hired him to paint a huge battle scene on a wall of the new council hall in the Palazzo Vecchio, the town hall. A year later it hired Michelangelo, then twenty-nine and already famous for his statue of David, to paint another battle in the same hall. The two men disliked each other, and the city watched the contest closely. Neither painting was finished. Leonardo again tried an experimental technique, and the paint ran when he heated it to dry it. Michelangelo was called to Rome by the pope before he got past his drawing. Both designs survive only in copies.

items: To go further, there is a podcast episode about the contest, and the long argument over what is left of it.

chapters.heading: A drawing the size of a painting
chapters.text: Around this time he also made a large drawing in charcoal and chalk. It shows the Virgin Mary sitting on the lap of her mother, Saint Anne, with the infants Jesus and John the Baptist. It is a cartoon, a full-size drawing made to plan a painting, but no painting from it is known. For many years it belonged to the Royal Academy in London, at Burlington House, which gives it its name. In 1962 the Academy put it up for sale, and the National Gallery raised the money to keep it in Britain with a public appeal. In 1987 a man shot at it with a shotgun. It was restored, and it now hangs in a dim room of its own to protect it from light.

items: For a closer look, there is a short video about the drawing and its history.

chapters.heading: The Mona Lisa
chapters.text: In about 1503, in Florence, he also began a portrait of Lisa del Giocondo, the wife of a silk merchant. He never handed it over. He kept working on it for years, adding thin layers of paint that soften the edges of her face, and he took it with him when he moved. In 1516 the French king, Francis I, invited him to France and gave him a manor house near the royal castle at Amboise, in the Loire valley. He died there in 1519, and the portrait stayed in the French royal collection. For centuries it was admired but not especially famous. That changed in 1911, when an Italian handyman walked out of the Louvre with it under his coat. It was missing for two years, and the newspaper coverage made it the most famous painting in the world.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways to see past the crowds in front of it.
items: A long video from Great Art Explained covers who she was, how Leonardo painted her, and how the theft made her famous.
A short Witness History episode tells the story of the theft.
And a video from Vox explains how the painting rose to stardom.

image: The Last Supper Leonardo Da Vinci - High Resolution.jpg

title: Michelangelo
intro: Michelangelo Buonarroti thought of himself as a sculptor, but popes kept asking him to paint and to build. He spent his long working life going back and forth between Florence and Rome, and most of what he made is still in those two cities.
This thread follows him between them, from his first great statue to the dome of St. Peter’s. It ends in London, with a famous copy and its fig leaf.

chapters.heading: The Pietà
chapters.text: Michelangelo was born in 1475 in a small town in Tuscany and grew up in Florence, where he studied sculpture in the gardens of the Medici, the family who ran the city. In 1496 he went to Rome. There a French cardinal asked him to carve a Pietà for his tomb: the Virgin Mary holding the body of Christ across her lap after the crucifixion. Michelangelo was in his early twenties. He made Mary young and calm, and he polished the marble until it shone. According to an early biographer, he heard visitors credit it to another sculptor. That night he carved his name on the sash across Mary’s chest. It is the only work he ever signed.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to see it properly.
items: A short video looks at how he carved it, and why it is the only work he signed.
And an audio guide to St. Peter’s Basilica starts in the square and passes the Pietà on its way inside.

chapters.heading: David
chapters.text: His success in Rome brought him home to Florence, which had thrown out the Medici and become a republic. In 1501 the cathedral’s board of works gave him a huge block of marble that two other sculptors had started and then abandoned decades before. Out of it he carved David, the young shepherd from the Bible who killed the giant Goliath. It took him nearly three years, and the statue is more than five meters tall. It was meant to go high up on the cathedral. Instead, a committee of artists that included Leonardo da Vinci placed it at the entrance to the town hall, as a symbol of the small republic standing up to its enemies. It stayed outside until 1873, when it was moved into the Accademia gallery. A copy now stands in its place.

mediaNote.lead: David has more good material than any other statue, and here are four pieces of it.
items: A podcast episode follows the committee that argued over where to put it.
A short Smarthistory video explains what the statue meant to the republic.
Great Art Explained looks at how he carved it, and why the proportions look odd up close.
And The Agony and the Ecstasy, Irving Stone’s enormous novel, is the book that first made many readers care about Michelangelo.

chapters.heading: The tomb
chapters.text: In 1505 a new pope, Julius II, called him back to Rome. Julius was a soldier as much as a priest, and he wanted a tomb for himself on a scale nobody had seen: a freestanding monument with more than forty statues. Michelangelo spent months in the quarries of Carrara choosing marble. Then the pope lost interest and spent his money on rebuilding St. Peter’s instead. The project dragged on for forty years, through quarrels, new contracts, and the death of Julius, and it shrank each time. What finally went up, in 1545, was a wall tomb in the church of San Pietro in Vincoli, with a seated figure of Moses at its center. In 1506, while he was in Rome, an ancient statue of the Trojan priest Laocoön and his sons was dug up in a vineyard. The pope sent him to look at it.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the tomb, and the ancient statue he saw.
items: A short video looks at Moses and the tomb as it was finally built.
A podcast episode tells how the project shrank from more than forty statues to a few.
And another video looks at the Laocoön, which still stands in the Vatican Museums.

chapters.heading: The ceiling
chapters.text: Julius then gave him a job he did not want. In 1508 he asked Michelangelo to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, the pope’s private chapel in the Vatican. Michelangelo said he was a sculptor, not a painter, but the pope insisted. He worked for four years on a scaffold he designed himself. He did not lie on his back, as the legend says. He stood, with his head bent back, and he wrote a comic poem about the pain in his neck. The ceiling shows nine scenes from the book of Genesis, from the creation of the world to the story of Noah, surrounded by prophets and sibyls. Down the corridor, at the same time, the young painter Raphael was decorating the pope’s apartments.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways to prepare for the Sistine Chapel.
items: A short video explains what the ceiling shows and how it is arranged.
A podcast episode tells how a reluctant sculptor became a painter under protest.
Ross King’s short book, Michelangelo and the Pope’s Ceiling, tells the story of the four years and the arguments.
And a video about Raphael’s portrait of Julius II shows the pope who hired them both.

chapters.heading: Two slaves
chapters.text: Even while he painted, the tomb was still on his mind. Around 1513 he carved two figures of bound captives for it, one twisting against his ropes and the other sinking as if into sleep. When the plan for the tomb was cut down again, there was no room for them. Michelangelo gave them to a friend, a Florentine exile, who passed them on to the king of France. They are now in the Louvre, where they are known as the Dying Slave and the Rebellious Slave.
chapters.image: Dying and Rebellious Slaves by Michelangelo (Louvre).jpg

items: For a closer look, there is a short video about the two figures and why they never reached the tomb.

chapters.heading: The Medici rooms
chapters.text: By 1520 the Medici were back in power in Florence, and one of them was now pope. They hired Michelangelo to design a funeral chapel for the family at their church of San Lorenzo. He designed the room and carved its tombs, with reclining figures of Night, Day, Dawn, and Dusk. Next door he designed a library for the family’s books, with an entrance hall whose staircase seems to pour down into the room. In 1527 the Medici were thrown out again, and Michelangelo helped design the city’s defenses against them. When they returned in 1530, he is thought to have hidden for weeks in a small room under the chapel. In 1975 drawings were found on its walls, and many experts believe they are his.
chapters.image: Tomb of Lorenzo, Duke of Urbino, New Sacristy (Medici Chapel), San Lorenzo, Florence (2) (48768615417).jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three short videos about the Medici rooms.
items: One looks at the chapel, designed as a setting for his sculpture.
Another looks at the library, and the entrance hall that breaks the rules on purpose.
And a third visits the hidden room under the chapel, with its charcoal drawings.

chapters.place: Sistine Chapel and St. Peter’s, Rome
chapters.heading: Judgment and the dome
chapters.text: In 1534 he left Florence for good and settled in Rome. A new pope asked him to paint the Last Judgment on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel, more than twenty years after the ceiling. It is darker and more crowded than the ceiling, with Christ at the center sending the saved up and the damned down. In the empty skin held by one of the saints, many people see a self-portrait. In 1546, in his seventies, he took charge of building St. Peter’s Basilica, and he designed its great dome, which was finished after his death. He also redesigned the square at the top of the Capitoline Hill. He died in Rome in 1564, at 88. Florence wanted him back, and his body was smuggled out of Rome like a bale of goods and buried in the church of Santa Croce.
chapters.image: Dome of St. Peter's Basilica by Michelangelo (7990081751).jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into his last years in Rome.
items: A short video looks at the Last Judgment and the self-portrait some see in it.
An art historian’s audio tour of St. Peter’s includes a climb up his dome.
And an archaeologist’s walk starts at his square on the Capitoline Hill.

chapters.heading: A copy for London
chapters.text: The last stop is a copy. In 1857 the Grand Duke of Tuscany gave Queen Victoria a full-size plaster cast of David. She is said to have been shocked by its nakedness. A plaster fig leaf was made so that it could be hung on the statue when royal ladies visited. The cast now stands in the Cast Courts of the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, two huge halls built in the 1870s for copies of famous sculpture and architecture. The fig leaf is displayed nearby.

items: For a look inside, there is a short video from the museum about the Cast Courts.

title: Caravaggio
intro: Michelangelo Merisi, called Caravaggio after the town his family came from, changed how European painters used light. In about fifteen years in Rome, he painted saints as ordinary people, lit by harsh beams in dark rooms.
He was also violent, and in 1606 he killed a man. This thread follows him from Milan to Rome, then through four years on the run, and ends with where his paintings are now.

chapters.place: Milan and the town of Caravaggio
chapters.heading: Training in Lombardy
chapters.text: Caravaggio was born in Milan in 1571. When he was five, plague broke out in the city, and the family moved to Caravaggio, a small town to the east, but his father died there of the disease. At thirteen he was apprenticed to Simone Peterzano, a Milanese painter who claimed to have studied with Titian, the great Venetian. Painters in Lombardy, the region around Milan, liked plain, closely observed detail, and Caravaggio took that taste with him. You can see it in his Basket of Fruit, painted later in Rome, with its wormholes and wilting leaves. It hangs in Milan, in the Biblioteca Ambrosiana, a library and gallery founded by the cardinal who owned it.

chapters.place: San Luigi dei Francesi and Santa Maria del Popolo, Rome
chapters.heading: Fame in two chapels
chapters.text: Around 1592 he went to Rome, with no money and no name. At first he painted fruit and flowers for other artists. Then a cardinal took him into his household. In 1599 he won his first public commission: two large paintings for the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi, the French church near Piazza Navona. In The Calling of Saint Matthew, Christ walks into a dim tax office, and a beam of light falls across the men counting money at a table. Nothing like it had been seen in a Roman church. Two more paintings followed for the Cerasi Chapel in Santa Maria del Popolo, by the city’s northern gate. In one, Saint Paul lies blinded on the ground under his horse. Both churches are free to enter, and the paintings still hang where he put them.
chapters.image: Paintings by Caravaggio at Contarelli Chapel-3.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways to prepare for a visit to those chapels.
items: A short video explains The Calling of Saint Matthew.
Another looks at The Conversion of Saint Paul, with the horse that fills most of the canvas.
A third looks at The Crucifixion of Saint Peter, which hangs opposite it.
And Andrew Graham-Dixon’s biography, Caravaggio: A Life Sacred and Profane, is the best account of his life.

chapters.heading: A death on the tennis court
chapters.text: Success did not calm him down. Police records show him arrested again and again, for carrying a sword without a permit, for throwing a plate of artichokes at a waiter, and for attacking people at night. On May 28, 1606, a fight broke out near the tennis courts on Via della Pallacorda, close to the Campo Marzio. It may have been about a bet, a debt, or a woman. Caravaggio killed a young man named Ranuccio Tomassoni with his sword, and he was badly wounded himself. He fled the city. He was sentenced to death in his absence, which meant anyone in the papal states could kill him on sight.
chapters.image: Caravaggio - David with the Head of Goliath - Vienna.jpg

items: For the whole story, there is a podcast episode about the brawl that ended his career in Rome.

chapters.heading: Sanctuary in Naples
chapters.text: He went to Naples, a city ruled by Spain and outside the pope’s reach. It was then one of the largest cities in Europe, crowded and poor, and its patrons wanted him at once. For a new charity, the Pio Monte della Misericordia, he painted The Seven Works of Mercy. It crams feeding the hungry, visiting prisoners, burying the dead, and the other good works into one dark street corner, and it still hangs over the altar of the charity’s chapel. He also painted The Flagellation of Christ for a church in the city. It now hangs in the Museo di Capodimonte, the former royal palace on a hill above Naples.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to look at his Naples paintings.
items: A podcast episode tells how he found sanctuary in Naples and painted his masterpiece there.
And a short video looks at The Flagellation of Christ.

chapters.place: Valletta, Syracuse, Messina, Palermo, and Porto Ercole
chapters.heading: On the run
chapters.text: In 1607 he sailed to Malta, an island ruled by the Knights of St. John, a military order of noblemen. He painted for them, including a huge Beheading of Saint John the Baptist for their church in Valletta, the only painting he ever signed. In 1608 they made him a knight. Within weeks he was in prison after another fight. He escaped over the walls and fled to Sicily, and the order threw him out. He moved from Syracuse to Messina to Palermo, painting altarpieces as he went. In 1609 he was back in Naples, where men attacked him outside a tavern and slashed his face. In July 1610 he set out by boat for Rome, hoping for a pardon, and died of a fever at Porto Ercole, on the coast of Tuscany. He was 38.

chapters.heading: Where the paintings went
chapters.text: After his death, collectors carried his paintings out of Italy and north. The Supper at Emmaus, in which a young, beardless Christ is recognized at a table, is in the National Gallery in London. Amor Victorious, a grinning Cupid stepping over symbols of music, war, and learning, is in Berlin. The Death of the Virgin was rejected by the Roman church that ordered it, perhaps because the model for Mary was rumored to be a drowned woman from the streets. The young Peter Paul Rubens advised the Duke of Mantua to buy it, and it is now in the Louvre. The Taking of Christ was lost for two centuries. In 1990 it was found in a Jesuit house in Dublin, where it had been thought to be a copy, and it now hangs in the National Gallery of Ireland.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four of the paintings that went north.
items: A short video looks at The Supper at Emmaus in London.
Great Art Explained tells the story of The Taking of Christ, and how it was found in Dublin.
A podcast episode looks at Amor Victorious, and why it caused talk in Rome.
And another short video looks at The Death of the Virgin, and why the church turned it down.

title: The Dutch Golden Age
intro: In the 1600s the Dutch Republic, a small country that had broken away from Spanish rule, became the richest place in Europe. Its merchants wanted pictures of themselves, their houses, and their dinners, and painters such as Rembrandt, Vermeer, and Frans Hals worked for that market.
This thread starts on an Amsterdam canal and follows the paintings to the museums across Europe where they hang now. It ends with a forger who fooled the experts.

chapters.heading: A city of merchants
chapters.text: The story begins on the canals of Amsterdam. In 1613 the city started digging a ring of new canals to house the merchants who were making it rich. Dutch ships carried grain, spices, and timber around the world, and the Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, was the largest trading company of its time. The traders built tall, narrow brick houses along the Herengracht, the grandest of the new canals, with storerooms in the attic and hooks on the gables for hoisting goods. They filled the rooms with paintings. Pictures were so common that even bakers and tailors owned them, and hundreds of painters made a living.
chapters.image: Gerrit Adriaensz. Berckheyde - The Bend in the Herengracht in Amsterdam - WGA1920.jpg

items: If you want to walk it with company, there is a podcast episode that tours the canals and tells the story of the Golden Age.

chapters.heading: Frans Hals
chapters.text: One of the first great painters of the period worked in Haarlem, a town just west of Amsterdam. Frans Hals painted portraits with quick, loose brushstrokes that you can still see on the canvas. His sitters seem to be caught in the middle of laughing or talking. Two of his best pictures ended up in Berlin, in the Gemäldegalerie, the city’s gallery of old masters. One shows a boy singing and holding a flute. The other is Malle Babbe, a real Haarlem woman of the 1630s, painted with a tankard of beer and an owl on her shoulder.
chapters.image: Frans Hals Malle Babbe about 1640-1646 Gemäldegalerie Berlin 9387.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Both Berlin paintings have short videos worth watching.
items: One looks at Malle Babbe and the speed of Hals’s brushwork.
The other looks at the singing boy, who may stand for the sense of hearing.

chapters.heading: The Night Watch
chapters.text: In Amsterdam, the leading painter was Rembrandt van Rijn, who had come from the university town of Leiden. In 1642 a company of the civic guard, the city’s citizen militia, paid him to paint their group portrait. Most such pictures showed the men lined up in rows. Rembrandt showed them in motion, getting ready to march, with some faces in bright light and others in shadow. The painting got its name, The Night Watch, much later, after its varnish had darkened. In 1715 it was moved to the town hall and cut down on all four sides to fit a wall. It now has its own room in the Rijksmuseum, the national museum.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the Rijksmuseum’s most famous painting.
items: A podcast episode explains who paid for it, why it looks so busy, and what was lost when it was cut down.
A shorter one shows how Rembrandt used light to pull the men out of the dark.
And Peter Greenaway’s film Nightwatching imagines that Rembrandt hid an accusation of murder in it.

chapters.heading: A girl at a window
chapters.text: Rembrandt could also paint something very simple. In 1645 he painted a girl leaning on a stone windowsill, looking straight out at us. The effect was so real that a story grew up that he had set the painting in a real window to fool people walking past. It is now in south London, in the Dulwich Picture Gallery, which opened in 1817 as England’s first public art gallery. The gallery was built to show a collection that had been put together for the king of Poland, who lost his throne before it could be delivered.

items: For a closer look, there is a short video about the painting and the story of the window.

chapters.heading: Bathsheba
chapters.text: His private life was less simple. After his wife, Saskia, died in 1642, he lived with Hendrickje Stoffels, who kept his house, and they had a daughter, but they never married. In 1654 he painted Bathsheba, the woman in the Bible whom King David saw bathing and summoned to him. She sits naked, holding the king’s letter, and the model was probably Hendrickje. That same year, Amsterdam’s Reformed Church called Hendrickje before its council and condemned her for living with Rembrandt outside marriage. The painting is now in the Louvre in Paris.

items: To see what makes it so moving, there is a short video about the painting and the woman who probably posed for it.

chapters.heading: Vermeer’s rooms
chapters.text: In Delft, a quieter town south of The Hague, Johannes Vermeer worked very differently. He painted slowly, and only about 35 of his pictures survive. Most show one or two people in a room, lit by soft daylight from a window on the left. In The Milkmaid, now in the Rijksmuseum, a kitchen maid pours milk into a bowl, and the bread, the jug, and the plaster wall look almost real enough to touch. In The Glass of Wine, now in Berlin, a man waits while a woman finishes her drink, beside a window of stained glass. Very little happens in either picture.

mediaNote.lead: Two videos look closely at these rooms.
items: Great Art Explained looks at The Milkmaid, and how Vermeer made light, bread, and plaster look so real.
A shorter video looks at The Glass of Wine and its quiet courtship.

chapters.heading: Late Rembrandt
chapters.text: Rembrandt, meanwhile, was living beyond his means. He spent heavily on art and curiosities, and in 1656 he went bankrupt. He lost his large house on the Jodenbreestraat, in the Jewish quarter, where he had lived for almost twenty years and made most of his etchings. The house is now a museum, and it still demonstrates how he printed them. His late paintings grew rougher, with the paint laid on thickly, sometimes with a palette knife. One of them, The Jewish Bride, shows a couple in an embrace, his hand on her heart. Two centuries later, Vincent van Gogh said he would give ten years of his life to sit in front of it with only a crust of bread.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into his last years.
items: A short video shows, step by step, how he made his etchings in this house.
A podcast episode looks closely at The Jewish Bride.

chapters.heading: The painting Vermeer kept
chapters.text: Vermeer kept one painting for himself. The Art of Painting shows an artist, seen from behind, painting a young woman dressed as Clio, the muse of history, with a large map of the Netherlands on the wall. When he died in 1675, deep in debt, his widow tried to keep it from his creditors. In 1940 it belonged to an Austrian noble family, and Adolf Hitler bought it for the huge art museum he planned to build in Linz, the city where he grew up. After the war it went to the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, which still has it.

items: For a closer look, there is a short video about the painting and how Hitler came to own it.

chapters.heading: Rachel Ruysch
chapters.text: The Golden Age did not end with Rembrandt and Vermeer. Rachel Ruysch, the daughter of an Amsterdam professor of anatomy, became one of the best-paid painters of her time. She painted flowers and fruit in great detail, often with insects and lizards crawling among them. From 1708 she was court painter to the Elector Palatine, a German prince in Düsseldorf, and her pictures sold for more than Rembrandt’s ever had. One of her paintings of fruit and insects, from 1711, hangs in the Uffizi in Florence.

items: For a closer look, there is a short video about the painting and how highly she was paid.

chapters.heading: The fake Vermeers
chapters.text: Because Vermeer left so few pictures, every new one caused a sensation. In the 1930s and 1940s, several unknown Vermeers appeared on the market, and experts declared them genuine. One was sold to Hermann Göring, the Nazi leader. After the war, Dutch police traced that sale to Han van Meegeren, a painter who lived in a grand house on the Keizersgracht. They arrested him for selling a national treasure to the enemy. To avoid a charge of treason, he confessed that he had painted it himself, along with the other “Vermeers.” Nobody believed him, so he painted another one in front of witnesses. He was convicted of forgery instead, and he died before he could serve his sentence.

items: For the full story, there is a short podcast episode about the forger who fooled the art world.

image: The Night Watch - Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn.png

title: Monet and the Impressionists
intro: In the 1860s, a group of young painters in Paris turned against the official art world. They painted modern life and the open air, with quick, broken brushstrokes that critics called unfinished.
This thread follows them from their first scandal to Monet’s last great paintings, with detours to London and to the sculptor Auguste Rodin.
image: Claude Monet - Reflections of Clouds on the Water-Lily Pond.jpg

chapters.heading: The Salon des Refusés
chapters.text: In 19th-century France, a painter’s career depended on the Salon, a huge official exhibition held in Paris. Its jury favored polished paintings of history, myth, and religion. In 1863 the jury rejected so many works that Emperor Napoleon III ordered a second show for them, the Salon des Refusés. Crowds came to laugh. The biggest scandal was a painting by Édouard Manet, Le Déjeuner sur l’herbe, showing a naked woman picnicking with two clothed men. Two years later, his Olympia, a nude who stares straight back at the viewer, caused an even bigger outcry. Younger painters saw Manet as a leader.
chapters.image: Henri Gervex - A Session of the Painting Jury - Google Art Project.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Manet’s scandals.
items: A short video looks at Le Déjeuner sur l’herbe, the scandal of 1863.
Another, from Vox, explains why Olympia so shocked the art world.
And The Judgment of Paris, by Ross King, tells how the rebels beat the establishment.

chapters.heading: Impression, Sunrise
chapters.text: Tired of the Salon, the younger painters decided to hold their own exhibition. In April 1874, about thirty artists showed their work in the former studio of the photographer Nadar, on the Boulevard des Capucines. They included Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, and Berthe Morisot, one of the few women in the group. Monet showed a hazy picture of the harbor at Le Havre at dawn, called Impression, Sunrise. A critic mocked the whole group as “Impressionists,” and the name stuck. Monet was then living at Argenteuil, a town on the Seine near Paris, painting sailboats and riverbanks.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into the first Impressionist exhibition.
items: A short video looks at one of Monet’s paintings of the river at Argenteuil.
Another looks at The Cradle, which Morisot showed at the first exhibition.
A third looks at La Loge, Renoir’s picture of a night at the theater, also in the 1874 show.
And a podcast episode tells Berthe Morisot’s story.

chapters.heading: A Sunday dance
chapters.text: Renoir loved painting people enjoying themselves. In 1876 he rented a studio on the rue Cortot in Montmartre, then a village of windmills and cheap cafés on a hill above Paris. Nearby, the Moulin de la Galette ran an open-air dance hall on Sunday afternoons. Renoir carried his large canvas there and painted the crowd, many of them his friends. Sunlight falls through the trees in patches of color onto dresses and faces. In the garden of his studio he painted The Swing, with the same dappled light.
chapters.image: Auguste Renoir - Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette - Google Art ProjectFXD.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Renoir’s Montmartre.
items: An episode of Inside the Masterpiece looks closely at the dance at the Moulin de la Galette.
And a short video looks at The Swing, painted in Renoir’s garden.

chapters.heading: Steam and light
chapters.text: Monet, meanwhile, went looking for the most modern subject he could find. In 1877 he got permission to paint inside the Gare Saint-Lazare, the station for trains to Argenteuil and Normandy. He set up his easel among the tracks and painted a dozen views of locomotives under the great glass roof. What interested him was not the trains themselves, but the steam and smoke catching the light. It was the beginning of his habit of painting the same subject again and again.
chapters.image: Claude Monet - The Saint-Lazare Station - Google Art Project.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to look at the station paintings.
items: A short video looks at one of the views in the Musée d’Orsay.
And in another, Jarvis Cocker, the singer of Pulp, narrates a slow look at the version in London’s National Gallery.

chapters.heading: Degas’s dancers
chapters.text: Degas showed with the Impressionists, but he rarely painted outdoors. He preferred the theater, the café, and above all the ballet. For years he went backstage at the Paris Opera, sketching young dancers in rehearsal, stretching, and waiting. Many of them were working-class girls hoping the ballet would lift them out of poverty. In 1881 he showed a wax sculpture of one of them, Marie van Goethem, aged fourteen, wearing a real tutu and a real ribbon in her hair. Critics found it ugly and disturbing.
chapters.image: Edgar Degas - The Dance Foyer at the Opera on the rue Le Peletier.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Degas’s Paris.
items: A podcast episode tells the story of Marie van Goethem, the model for the Little Dancer.
And another looks at Degas’s painting of a circus acrobat hanging by her teeth.

chapters.heading: Rodin
chapters.text: Sculpture had its own rebel. In 1880, Auguste Rodin was commissioned to make a bronze door for a planned museum of decorative arts. He called it The Gates of Hell and worked on it for the rest of his life. At the top sat a figure of the poet Dante, brooding over the scene, which later became The Thinker. Rodin modeled bodies roughly, with the marks of his hands left in the clay. For years he worked closely with the sculptor Camille Claudel, his student and lover, whose own work was long overshadowed by his. In his last years he worked in the Hôtel Biron, a mansion that is now the Musée Rodin.
chapters.image: Le jardin de l'hôtel Biron (musée Rodin) à Paris, 13 juin 2021.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Rodin’s work.
items: Great Art Explained tells how The Thinker began as Dante on The Gates of Hell.
And a short video tours the Musée Rodin and its garden.

chapters.heading: Monet in London
chapters.text: Monet had first come to London in 1870, escaping the Franco-Prussian War. There he saw the paintings of J. M. W. Turner, an English painter of light, fog, and steam. Thirty years later, famous and well off, Monet came back. He took a room on an upper floor of the Savoy Hotel, overlooking the Thames. Over three winters he painted Waterloo Bridge, Charing Cross Bridge, and the Houses of Parliament again and again. He loved London’s fog, thick with coal smoke, because it changed the color of everything from hour to hour.
chapters.image: Waterloo Bridge. Effet de brouillard. Claude Monet. 1903.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Monet’s London.
items: A short video looks at one of the views of Waterloo Bridge, painted from the Savoy.
And another looks at Turner’s Rain, Steam and Speed, which Monet would have known.

chapters.heading: The water lilies
chapters.text: The last stop brings Monet home. From 1883 he lived at Giverny, a village in Normandy, where he made a garden with a pond full of water lilies. In his last years he painted almost nothing else. His eyesight was failing from cataracts, and the colors grew wilder. In 1918, the day after the armistice that ended the First World War, he offered a set of huge water-lily panels to France as a monument to peace. They were installed in two oval rooms at the Orangerie, in the Tuileries Garden, in 1927, a few months after his death.
chapters.image: Detail nympheas musee de lOrangerie Paris.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the water lilies.
items: Great Art Explained looks at the late water lilies and how they were made.
A short biography video tells Monet’s life through them.
And a short video from Rick Steves tours the Orangerie.

title: Van Gogh
intro: Vincent van Gogh painted for only ten years and sold almost nothing in his lifetime. Today he is one of the most famous painters in the world.

He moved often, and each move changed his work. This thread follows him from a lodging house in London to a village inn outside Paris, and ends at the Amsterdam museum that holds most of his paintings.
image: Van Gogh - Starry Night - Google Art Project.jpg

chapters.heading: A young art dealer in London
chapters.text: Before he was a painter, Van Gogh sold paintings. At twenty he was working for Goupil & Co, a large firm of art dealers, and in 1873 they sent him to their London branch near Covent Garden. He rented a room south of the river, at 87 Hackford Road in Stockwell, and walked across the Thames to work each morning. He fell in love with his landlady’s daughter, but she was already engaged and turned him down. A small drawing he made of the house survives. Unhappy and distracted, he did badly at work, and by 1876 the firm had let him go. He turned to religion instead.
chapters.tip: The house is now Van Gogh House, an artists’ residency that opens for events. A blue plaque marks it.

items: If you want more on his London years, a podcast episode asks how the city set him on the road to painting.

chapters.heading: Hours in front of a Rembrandt
chapters.text: His next plan was to become a minister. In 1877 he moved to Amsterdam to study for the university entrance exams in theology, living with an uncle who ran the city’s naval dockyard. Latin and Greek defeated him, and he gave up within a year. Amsterdam mattered to him in another way, though. He came back in 1885, soon after the new Rijksmuseum opened, and sat for hours in front of The Jewish Bride, a late painting by Rembrandt, the great Dutch painter of the 1600s. He wrote that he would give ten years of his life to sit there for two weeks with only a crust of dry bread.

items: To look more closely at The Jewish Bride, there is a podcast episode about the painting he sat in front of for hours.

chapters.place: Nuenen, and the Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam
chapters.heading: His first big painting
chapters.text: After Amsterdam he tried preaching to coal miners in southern Belgium, and failed at that too. In 1880, at 27, he decided to become an artist. He taught himself to draw, and in 1883 he went to live with his parents in Nuenen, a village in the south of the Netherlands where his father was the pastor. There he painted the people he saw every day, weavers at their looms and families working the fields, almost always in dark browns and grays. The Potato Eaters, from 1885, was his first ambitious picture: a family eating supper by lamplight. Even his friends disliked it. It now hangs in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.
chapters.image: The Potato Eaters - Vincent Van Gogh.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to look harder at The Potato Eaters.
items: A longer video explains what Van Gogh wanted the painting to say, and why critics disliked it.
In a shorter one, two art historians look at why he painted farm workers, and how the rough brushwork suits the family’s hard life.

chapters.heading: Paris teaches him color
chapters.text: In early 1886 he turned up in Paris without warning and moved in with his younger brother, Theo, an art dealer who had been sending him money for years. That summer they took a bigger apartment together at 54 rue Lepic, high on the hill of Montmartre. Through Theo he met painters who were trying new things, among them the Impressionist Camille Pissarro and Paul Gauguin. He also began collecting cheap Japanese woodblock prints, with their flat, bright colors. Over two years he painted about two hundred pictures, and his palette moved from muddy browns to strong reds, yellows, and blues.
chapters.image: 54 rue Lepic, Theo and Vincent Van Goghs Paris house 2010.jpg

items: For more on these two years, there is a podcast episode in which two art historians explain how Paris and the Japanese prints changed the way he painted.

chapters.heading: A yellow house in the south
chapters.text: Paris wore him out. In February 1888 he took the train south to Arles, a small town in Provence, hoping to find the light and color he had seen in the Japanese prints. He rented four rooms in a yellow house on the town’s Place Lamartine and painted quickly: orchards in blossom, the café on the square at night, and the stars over the river Rhône. He dreamed of a “studio of the south” where artists would live and work together, and he talked Gauguin into joining him. To decorate Gauguin’s room, he painted a series of sunflowers in a vase. Gauguin arrived in October. One of those sunflower paintings now hangs in the National Gallery in London.
chapters.image: Vincent van Gogh - The yellow house ('The street').jpg

mediaNote.lead: Three things here take you further into that year in Arles.
items: A podcast episode looks at Starry Night over the Rhône, his painting of the stars over the river.
A feature-length documentary follows the sunflower paintings from Arles to museums around the world.
A short video looks at the self-portrait Gauguin sent him that year.

chapters.heading: The night he cut his ear
chapters.text: The two men painted side by side for nine weeks, but they argued constantly. On the night of December 23, 1888, after a bad quarrel, Van Gogh cut off part of his left ear with a razor and gave it to a young woman who worked at a nearby brothel. Gauguin left for Paris within days. Van Gogh was treated at the town hospital, now a cultural center called the Espace Van Gogh, and a few weeks later he painted himself with his head bandaged. More breakdowns followed. In May 1889 he asked to be admitted to an asylum in Saint-Rémy, a nearby town, and it was there that he painted The Starry Night.

mediaNote.lead: There are two ways to stay with this part of the story.
items: A podcast episode takes a slow look at the self-portrait with the bandaged ear, which now hangs in the Courtauld Gallery in London.
A short video argues that his colors and compositions often reflected his state of mind.

chapters.heading: His last seventy days
chapters.text: A year later he felt well enough to leave. In May 1890 he moved to Auvers-sur-Oise, a village an hour north of Paris, where Dr. Paul Gachet, a doctor who knew many artists, had agreed to keep an eye on him. He took a small attic room at the Auberge Ravoux, an inn on the main street, and painted almost every day, about seventy pictures in seventy days. On July 27 he shot himself in the chest, probably in the fields outside the village, and walked back to the inn. Theo came from Paris, and Vincent died two days later with his brother beside him. Tree Roots, a tangle of trunks at the edge of a field, was probably the last painting he worked on.
chapters.image: Vincent van Gogh - Wheatfield with crows - Google Art Project.jpg

mediaNote.lead: If you want to know more about how it ended, there are three places to go.
items: In a podcast episode, two art historians go through his last weeks in Auvers.
A video looks at Tree Roots, and at the recent discovery of the exact spot he painted.
Loving Vincent is a feature film that investigates how he died, and every frame of it is an oil painting.

chapters.heading: Jo, who made him famous
chapters.text: Theo was already ill, and he died six months after his brother. His widow, Johanna van Gogh-Bonger, known as Jo, was left with a baby son, hundreds of Vincent’s paintings, and the hundreds of letters the brothers had written to each other. Almost nobody wanted the paintings. Jo spent the rest of her life changing that. She lent them to exhibitions, sold them carefully, and in 1914 published the letters, which made people care about the man as well as the work. Her son, also named Vincent, later put the family collection into a foundation, and the Van Gogh Museum opened in 1973 to show it.
chapters.tip: Tickets are timed and sell out; book online. The paintings are hung in the order he made them.

mediaNote.lead: Two things here carry the story on.
items: A podcast episode tells how Jo made Van Gogh famous.
Van Gogh: The Life is a long biography, built on his letters.

title: Picasso and Cubism
intro: Pablo Picasso was the most famous artist of the 20th century, and Cubism, the style he invented with his friend Georges Braque, changed how painters showed the world.

This thread follows him from art school in Barcelona to the studios of Paris, where a handful of painters took apart the old rules of picture-making. It ends in Madrid, with the painting he made about the bombing of a small Basque town.

chapters.heading: A teenager in Barcelona
chapters.text: Picasso was born in 1881 in Málaga, in the south of Spain. His father was a painting teacher, and when Pablo was 13 the family moved to Barcelona, where his father had taken a post at the city’s art school, La Llotja. The boy enrolled there too, and he quickly outgrew his teachers. By 15 he was painting large, polished pictures in the traditional style the school taught. You can see them in the Picasso Museum, which fills five medieval palaces on Carrer de Montcada in the old town. Many visitors are surprised at how conventional, and how skilled, the young Picasso was.
chapters.image: 062 Casa Finestres, Museu Picasso, c. Montcada 23 (Barcelona), pati.jpg

items: For a short tour, there is a video about the museum and the student work that shows how fast he learned.

chapters.heading: The Bateau-Lavoir
chapters.text: Barcelona was not enough for him. After several trips to Paris, he settled there in 1904, at 22, in a run-down building of studios on the hill of Montmartre. It was cold in winter and had one water tap for the whole house. His friend the poet Max Jacob nicknamed it the Bateau-Lavoir, after the laundry boats moored on the Seine. Picasso lived there for five years. He painted circus performers in soft pinks, in what is now called his Rose Period, and he met Fernande Olivier, who became his partner. The building burned in 1970 and was rebuilt, but the little square in front of it is much as he knew it.

items: If you want to see it on foot, a walking tour of Montmartre passes the Bateau-Lavoir on its way up the hill to Sacré-Cœur.

chapters.heading: Les Demoiselles d’Avignon
chapters.text: In 1907, in his Bateau-Lavoir studio, he worked for months on a large canvas of five naked women. Their bodies are made of sharp, flat angles, and two of the faces look like masks, influenced by African and ancient Iberian sculpture he had been studying. He named it after Carrer d’Avinyó, a street of brothels in Barcelona’s old town that he had known as a teenager. A friend later gave it the title it has now, Les Demoiselles d’Avignon, the young ladies of Avignon. When Picasso showed it to his friends, most of them were shocked. He kept it in the studio and did not exhibit it until 1916. It is now in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

items: For more on what makes it so strange, there is a video about how its masks and broken-up space opened the way to Cubism.

chapters.heading: Little cubes
chapters.text: One of the friends who saw the painting was Georges Braque, a young French painter. At first he hated it, and then it set him thinking. In the summer of 1908 he went to paint at L’Estaque, a fishing village on the coast just north of Marseille. Paul Cézanne, the painter both men admired most, had worked there years before. Braque reduced the houses, trees, and railway viaduct to simple blocks. When he showed the pictures in Paris that autumn, a critic said they were made of little cubes. The name Cubism stuck. For the next six years, Braque and Picasso worked so closely that their pictures can be hard to tell apart.
chapters.image: L'Estaque - Chemin de la Nerthe - Viaduc ferroviaire du Marinier.jpg

items: To see how he did it, there is a short video in which two art historians look at his painting of the viaduct, with the houses turned into simple shapes.

chapters.heading: Questioned over the Mona Lisa
chapters.text: Cubism made Picasso well known, and in 1911 he nearly became notorious. That August the Mona Lisa disappeared from the Louvre, and nobody knew who had taken it. The police soon turned to Picasso’s friend the poet Guillaume Apollinaire. A former secretary of his had earlier stolen small ancient Iberian stone heads from the museum, and had sold two of them to Picasso. Apollinaire was arrested and spent several days in jail, and Picasso was called in for questioning. Neither of them had anything to do with the Mona Lisa. It turned up two years later in Florence, taken by an Italian handyman who had worked at the Louvre.

items: If you want the whole story, there is a brisk book about the theft and how the empty wall made the painting even more famous.

chapters.place: House of the Black Madonna, Prague
chapters.heading: Cubist buildings
chapters.text: Cubism soon spread beyond Paris, and in Prague it did something it did almost nowhere else: it became architecture. Around 1910 a group of young Czech architects decided that the angles and broken surfaces of Cubist painting could be built. The best example is the House of the Black Madonna, a department store designed by Josef Gočár and finished in 1912, just off the Old Town Square. Its window frames, balconies, and even its staircase are made of crisp, slanting planes. The building is named after a small statue of the Virgin from an older house on the site, which still stands in a cage on the corner. The first floor is a café, the Grand Café Orient, with Cubist lamps and furniture.

items: To see it as part of a longer walk, an introductory tour of Prague starts outside this building and ends across the river in the Lesser Town.

chapters.heading: The first collage
chapters.text: Back in Paris, Picasso and Braque kept pushing. In 1912 Picasso glued a piece of oilcloth onto a small oval still life. The oilcloth was printed to look like the woven cane seat of a chair, and he framed the picture with a length of rope. Putting a ready-made material into a painting was new, and Still Life with Chair Caning is often called the first collage in modern art. It hangs in the Musée Picasso, in a 17th-century mansion in the Marais, the old quarter on the Right Bank. The museum opened in 1985. Most of its collection is work Picasso kept for himself, which went to the French state after his death in 1973 in place of inheritance taxes.

items: For a closer look, there is a short video about the picture and why a piece of oilcloth mattered so much.

chapters.heading: Guernica
chapters.text: The partnership with Braque ended in 1914, when Braque went to fight in the First World War. Picasso went on changing styles for another sixty years, but his most famous painting is about war. On April 26, 1937, during the Spanish Civil War, German and Italian planes supporting General Franco bombed Guernica, a small town in the Basque Country, in the north of Spain. Picasso had been asked to make a painting for the Spanish Republic’s pavilion at the World’s Fair in Paris. He painted Guernica in about five weeks, in black, white, and gray, with a bull, a screaming horse, and a mother holding her dead child. He refused to let it go to Spain while Franco ruled. It arrived in 1981, after Franco’s death, and has hung in the Reina Sofía museum in Madrid since 1992.

mediaNote.lead: There are four good ways into Guernica, from a short video to a long conversation.
items: A video from Smarthistory walks through the painting and its long road to Madrid.
Great Art Explained looks at how he made it in a few weeks, and what the bull, the horse, and the lamp might mean.
In a longer podcast episode, Melvyn Bragg and his guests discuss both the bombing and the painting.
And a short episode of Witness History tells the story through the people who survived the bombing.

title: Opera houses
intro: Opera began at the courts of Italian princes around 1600, and in 1637 Venice opened the first public opera house, where anyone with a ticket could get in. Over the next three centuries, every capital wanted an opera house of its own.
This thread visits some of the grandest of them, and some famous first nights, including a disaster, a revolution, and an assassination.

chapters.heading: Opera goes public
chapters.text: The first opera house open to the paying public was the Teatro San Cassiano in Venice, which opened in 1637. Within a few years the city had several more, competing for audiences at carnival time. The greatest composer working for them was Claudio Monteverdi, who had already been director of music at St. Mark’s Basilica for more than twenty years. In his seventies he wrote his last operas for these theaters. The Coronation of Poppea, from 1643, tells how the Roman emperor Nero puts aside his wife for his mistress. It ends with a love duet that is still one of the most beautiful in opera, though it may have been written by a younger colleague. Monteverdi died later that year, and he is buried in the Frari, a great Gothic church near the Rialto.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of that final duet, “Pur ti miro.”

chapters.heading: San Carlo
chapters.text: By the 1700s, Naples was one of the musical capitals of Europe. Its king, Charles of Bourbon, built the Teatro di San Carlo next to his royal palace and opened it in 1737. It is the oldest opera house in Europe still in use. In the early 1800s it was run by Domenico Barbaja, a former waiter who had made a fortune from gambling tables. He hired the young Gioachino Rossini to write operas for it, and later Gaetano Donizetti. The theater burned in 1816 and was rebuilt within a year.

items: If you want to hear how music runs through the city, there is a radio documentary that goes from old Neapolitan songs to the San Carlo.

chapters.heading: La Scala
chapters.text: Milan’s opera house, La Scala, opened in 1778, replacing the court theater that had burned two years before. It was built on the site of a demolished church, Santa Maria alla Scala, and took its name. It became the most important opera house in Italy. In 1842 Giuseppe Verdi’s Nabucco made his name there. Its chorus of Hebrew slaves longing for home came to be seen as a song for Italians who wanted to free their country from Austrian rule. Not every first night went well. In 1904 Giacomo Puccini’s Madama Butterfly was booed so loudly that he withdrew it after one performance. In the 1950s, La Scala was where the soprano Maria Callas sang many of her greatest roles.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways to get to know La Scala, two of them to listen to.
items: A history podcast tells the story of the theater and the church it replaced.
A recording of “Va, pensiero,” the chorus of Hebrew slaves from Nabucco, is the song that made Verdi’s name.
A recording of “Un bel dì,” from Madama Butterfly, is the aria in which Cio-Cio-San imagines her husband’s ship coming back.
And Maria by Callas, a documentary, tells the soprano’s life in her own words.

chapters.heading: Shot at a masked ball
chapters.text: Opera houses were places to be seen, and sometimes that was dangerous. Gustav III, king of Sweden, loved the theater, and in 1782 he opened a royal opera house in Stockholm. He had also made enemies among the nobles by taking power away from them. On March 16, 1792, he went to a masked ball at his opera house, although he had been warned of a plot. A group of nobles surrounded him, and one of them shot him in the back. He died two weeks later. Verdi later turned the story into an opera, Un ballo in maschera, A Masked Ball. The censors would not allow a king to be murdered on stage, so in the first version the story was moved to Boston.
chapters.image: Kungliga Operan Royal Swedish Opera Stockholm 2016 01.jpg

items: For the whole story, there is a short podcast episode about the king who went to the ball despite the warning.

chapters.heading: An opera starts a revolution
chapters.text: In Brussels, an opera started a revolution. In 1830 what is now Belgium was part of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands, ruled by a Dutch king, and many in the south resented it. On August 25 the city’s opera house, La Monnaie, staged La Muette de Portici, a French opera about a rising in Naples against Spanish rule. During a duet about love of one’s country, the audience grew so excited that some of them rushed out into the streets. The riot that followed that night grew into a revolution, and within months Belgium was independent.
chapters.image: 1004 Royal Theatre of La Monnaie in Brussels Photo by Giles Laurent.jpg

items: To hear more, there is a short radio episode about the night the opera started a revolution.

chapters.heading: Tristan in three cities
chapters.text: Richard Wagner wanted opera to be something bigger. After taking part in a failed revolution in Dresden in 1849, he fled to Switzerland. In Zurich, a wealthy merchant, Otto Wesendonck, gave him a house next to his own villa, and Wagner fell in love with his patron’s wife, Mathilde. He set five of her poems to music, and he began Tristan und Isolde, an opera about forbidden love. When the situation became too much for both households, he left for Venice. There he wrote the second act, in rooms in a palace on the Grand Canal. The opera was so long and difficult that it was called unperformable. It reached the stage only in 1865, in Munich, after the young King Ludwig II of Bavaria paid Wagner’s debts.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways to hear how Tristan came together.
items: “Träume,” one of the songs he wrote to Mathilde’s poems, was a study for the opera.
A recording of the long love duet comes from the second act, the part he wrote in Venice.
The prelude opens with one of the most famous chords in music, which never resolves the way the ear expects.
And a conductor’s podcast episode explains why Tristan was so new, and how a king’s money got it on stage.

chapters.heading: The Palais Garnier
chapters.text: In Paris, Emperor Napoleon III wanted an opera house to match his rebuilt capital. A competition in 1861 was won by Charles Garnier, a young architect who was almost unknown. Building took fourteen years, partly because the ground was so wet that the foundations had to hold back water, and partly because the empire fell in 1870. The Palais Garnier opened in 1875, with a grand marble staircase designed so that the audience could watch each other arrive. The water under the building, held in a great tank in the foundations, gave the novelist Gaston Leroux the idea for the underground lake in The Phantom of the Opera.
chapters.image: Grand Staircase of Palais Garnier, Paris, France.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Two videos cover the building and its ghost.
items: One explains Garnier’s design, from the staircase to the gilded foyer.
The other sorts fact from fiction in The Phantom of the Opera.

chapters.heading: Mahler’s house
chapters.text: Vienna’s Court Opera opened in 1869 as one of the first grand buildings on the Ringstrasse, the boulevard that replaced the old city walls. From 1897 to 1907 it was run by the composer Gustav Mahler. He was a demanding director. He darkened the auditorium during performances, kept latecomers out until a break, and made it one of the best opera houses in Europe. In March 1945, near the end of the Second World War, a bombing raid set it on fire, and most of it burned. Its reopening in 1955, the same year Austria regained its full independence, was celebrated across the country.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Mahler’s house.
items: A short video goes inside the opera house.
And a recording of the Adagietto from his Fifth Symphony, written while he ran the opera, shows Mahler the composer.

chapters.heading: A roof to walk on
chapters.text: The newest stop is a different idea of what an opera house can be. Oslo’s opera house, designed by the Norwegian firm Snøhetta, opened in 2008 on the harbor at Bjørvika, an old industrial waterfront. Its roof is a sloping white plane of marble and granite that rises straight out of the fjord. Anyone can walk up it, with or without a ticket, and on summer evenings people sit up there to watch the sun go down over the water. The building helped turn the area into a new part of the city.
chapters.image: Roof of the Oslo Opera House.jpg

items: If you want to know the thinking behind it, there is a video about the idea of a public building that people can climb.

title: Mozart
intro: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart wrote more than six hundred works in a life of 35 years, and many of them were first heard in rooms you can still visit.

This thread follows him from a palace in Vienna, where he played as a small boy, through the opera houses of Milan, Munich, and Prague, to the Vienna apartment where he wrote The Marriage of Figaro. It ends in Seville, a city he never saw, but where two of his operas are set.

chapters.heading: Playing for the empress
chapters.text: Mozart was born in 1756 in Salzburg, a small city in the Alps ruled by its archbishop. His father, Leopold, was a violinist in the archbishop’s orchestra, and he soon saw that both his children were extraordinary. In 1762 he took them to Vienna, the capital of the Habsburg empire. At Schönbrunn, the imperial family’s summer palace on the edge of the city, six-year-old Wolfgang and his older sister, Nannerl, played for Empress Maria Theresa. A family story says the boy slipped on the polished floor and was helped up by one of the young archduchesses, Marie Antoinette. He thanked her and said he would marry her. Leopold spent much of the next ten years taking the children on tour, from London to Naples.

items: For a look inside, there is a short video tour of the palace and its state rooms.

chapters.heading: Writing down a secret
chapters.text: On the longest of those journeys, father and son spent more than a year in Italy, the home of opera. They reached Rome in Holy Week of 1770. In the Sistine Chapel, in the Vatican, the pope’s choir sang the Miserere by Gregorio Allegri, a setting of a psalm written in the 1630s. It was sung only there, only in that week, and the Vatican did not allow it to be copied. The fourteen-year-old Mozart heard it once, then wrote the whole piece out from memory that evening. He went back later in the week to check a few details. A few months later, the pope made him a knight.
chapters.image: Pope Pius VII in the Sistine Chapel A29940.jpg

items: To hear what he heard, there is a recording of the Miserere, with its high, floating line for a solo soprano.

chapters.heading: His first big opera
chapters.text: Italy gave him his first big chance in opera. Milan, then ruled by Austria, commissioned a serious opera from him for its winter season. Mitridate, re di Ponto, the story of an ancient king and his rival sons, opened on December 26, 1770. The theater was inside the Palazzo Reale, the royal palace next to the cathedral. Mozart was fourteen, and he directed it from the keyboard. Some of the singers had doubted that a boy could write for them, but the opera was a success and ran for more than twenty nights. The theater burned down in 1776, and the city built La Scala to replace it.
chapters.image: Veduta di tre quarti del Palazzo Reale di Milano.jpg

items: For a taste of the opera, there is a recording of its overture.

chapters.heading: Idomeneo
chapters.text: Back home, Mozart worked for the archbishop of Salzburg, and he hated it. The archbishop treated his musicians as servants and rarely let him travel. In 1780 the court of Bavaria, in Munich, commissioned a new opera, and he was given leave to write it. Idomeneo is about a king of Crete who makes a terrible vow to the god of the sea. It opened in January 1781 in the Cuvilliés Theatre, a small, gilded theater in the royal palace. It is his first great opera. A few months later he quarreled with the archbishop in Vienna and resigned. One of the archbishop’s officials, Count Arco, ended the argument by kicking him out of the room.

items: To hear how it begins, there is a recording of the overture.

chapters.heading: Ten years in Vienna
chapters.text: Mozart decided to stay in Vienna and live as a freelance musician, which almost nobody did at the time. He gave concerts, taught pupils, and wrote music for anyone who would pay. In 1782 he married Constanze Weber, a singer, in St. Stephen’s Cathedral. The couple moved house more than a dozen times. The grandest of their homes was an apartment on Domgasse, a narrow street behind the cathedral, where they lived from 1784 to 1787. There he wrote The Marriage of Figaro, a comic opera about servants who outwit their master, with words by the poet Lorenzo Da Ponte. It is the only one of his Vienna homes that survives, and it is now a museum called the Mozarthaus.
chapters.tip: The Mozarthaus museum keeps the Domgasse apartment’s rooms. St. Stephen’s, where he married and where his funeral service was held, is around the corner.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into his years in Vienna.
items: A podcast episode looks at “Dove sono,” an aria from The Marriage of Figaro in which the Countess remembers happier days with her husband.
A short, brisk biography shows him as a working musician, always chasing commissions and money.
And a walking tour of the old town follows him, Beethoven, and Vivaldi, with their music playing as you go.

chapters.heading: The city that loved him most
chapters.text: Figaro did well in Vienna, but in Prague, the capital of Bohemia, it was a sensation. People hummed its tunes in the streets, and Mozart traveled there to see it for himself. The city then commissioned a new opera, and he wrote Don Giovanni, again with Da Ponte, about a nobleman who seduces women and is dragged down to hell. Mozart finished it in Prague and conducted the premiere at the Estates Theatre on October 29, 1787. The story goes that he wrote the overture the night before. “My Praguers understand me,” he is supposed to have said. The theater still stands, almost unchanged, and it still stages his operas.

mediaNote.lead: Two things are worth hearing before a night at the Estates Theatre.
items: A recording of the overture opens with the dark chords that return when a statue comes to drag Don Giovanni away.
A live comedy history podcast follows his whole life, from child star to working musician, and explains why Prague loved him.

chapters.heading: An unfinished Requiem
chapters.text: His last year was one of his busiest. In 1791 he wrote The Magic Flute for a popular theater on the edge of Vienna. He also accepted a strange commission for a Requiem, a mass for the dead, from a patron who wanted to stay anonymous. That autumn he fell ill. He died on December 5, 1791, at his apartment on Rauhensteingasse, a few streets from Domgasse, with the Requiem unfinished. He was 35. The doctors called it a fever, and the real cause is still argued over. The story that he was poisoned by a rival, the composer Antonio Salieri, has no evidence behind it. His widow, Constanze, had the Requiem finished by one of his pupils so that she could be paid for it.

mediaNote.lead: His death left a mystery and an unfinished masterpiece, and there are two good ways to explore both.
items: In a long podcast episode, a conductor explains the Requiem and the mystery around it.
A video by a food historian looks at his last weeks, including the supper some people blame for his death.

chapters.heading: A city he never saw
chapters.text: Two of the operas he wrote with Da Ponte, The Marriage of Figaro and Don Giovanni, are set in Seville, in the south of Spain, a city Mozart never visited. Figaro was based on a French play by Pierre Beaumarchais, the second in a series about Figaro, a clever barber. The first play, The Barber of Seville, became an opera by Gioachino Rossini in 1816, thirty years after Mozart’s. So the prequel reached the stage after the sequel, and it became just as famous. In the old Santa Cruz quarter, guides still point out balconies said to belong to both stories.
chapters.image: Jardines de la plaza de Santa Cruz.jpg

items: If you want the prequel’s story, there is a podcast episode about The Barber of Seville and its disastrous first night.

title: Songs of longing
intro: Many European cities have a song form built on missing something: a home, a lover, a country, a self. Most of them grew up in port districts and poor quarters, often among people who had arrived from somewhere else. Most were looked down on before they became national treasures.
This thread travels from Lisbon in the west to Istanbul in the east. The stops have no timeline, so you can start anywhere, and it is worth listening before you read.

chapters.heading: Saudade in the old quarters
chapters.text: Fado, Lisbon’s song, grew up in the 1800s in the old quarters near the river, Alfama and Mouraria, in sailors’ bars, brothels, and taverns. A singer, the fadista, stands in front of two guitarists, one of them playing the round Portuguese guitar with twelve strings. The mood of fado has a word of its own, saudade, a longing for something lost or something that never was. For a long time respectable Lisbon looked down on it. Then in the 1950s Amália Rodrigues took it around the world, and it became a symbol of Portugal. In 2011 UNESCO listed fado as part of the world’s intangible heritage. Mariza, who grew up in Mouraria, has led its revival.
chapters.tip: Fado houses start late, often after 9 p.m. When a fadista sings, the room goes quiet and stays that way.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three fado singers, and a conversation about the music.
items: “A Casa da Mariquinhas,” sung by Alfredo Marceneiro, has the weathered voice of the old taverns.
“Uma Casa Portuguesa,” sung by Amália Rodrigues, is about a humble house rich in love.
“Ó Gente da Minha Terra,” sung by Mariza, became her signature song.
And a BBC discussion explains fado, and the sense of absence at its heart.

chapters.heading: Deep song across the river
chapters.text: In Seville, the deepest flamenco comes from Triana, the neighborhood across the Guadalquivir River from the cathedral. It was home to Gitano families, the Roma of Spain, along with potters and sailors. The oldest form is called cante jondo, deep song, and its subjects are grief, prison, poverty, and death. Most of it was never written down. It passed from singer to singer in homes and taverns. In the early 1900s, Pastora Pavón, known as La Niña de los Peines, recorded many of the old songs, and she is still thought of as one of the greatest flamenco singers. In 2010 UNESCO listed flamenco as intangible heritage.
chapters.tip: Tablaos are shows for visitors. Peñas, members’ clubs that often let in guests, are where locals listen.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into flamenco.
items: A recording of La Niña de los Peines singing bulerías has the voice of flamenco’s golden age.
A travel podcast visits the city’s flamenco dance museum and talks with its founder.
Duende, by Jason Webster, follows an Englishman who moves to Spain and falls into the flamenco world.
And Flamenco, a film by Carlos Saura, presents thirteen forms of it on a bare stage.

chapters.heading: Songs for the people who left
chapters.text: Naples has a song tradition of its own, the canzone napoletana. Its golden age came in the decades around 1900, just as millions of Neapolitans were emigrating to the Americas, and many songs were written for them or about them. “Santa Lucia luntana,” from 1919, is sung from the deck of a ship as the lights of the bay disappear. “Munasterio ’e Santa Chiara” was written in 1945, after Allied bombs had burned the great church of Santa Chiara in the old center. Its singer is far away and has heard that Naples has been destroyed, but does not want to know if it is true. The best known of all, “’O sole mio,” is simply about the sun.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three songs from Naples.
items: “Munasterio ’e Santa Chiara” is a wartime exile’s song of homesickness.
“Santa Lucia luntana” became the anthem of the emigrants.
And “’O sole mio,” sung by Enrico Caruso, is the most famous Neapolitan song of all.

chapters.heading: One song, played everywhere
chapters.text: In Budapest, one song traveled the world on its own. In 1933 Rezső Seress, a self-taught songwriter, wrote “Szomorú vasárnap,” Sad Sunday, a slow, despairing song about loss. He played the piano most nights at the Kispipa, a small restaurant on Akácfa Street in the old Jewish quarter. The song was translated into English as “Gloomy Sunday,” and newspapers gave it a reputation as cursed. Billie Holiday’s recording from 1941 is the best known in English. Seress, who was Jewish, survived a Nazi forced labor camp, and he went back to playing at the Kispipa after the war.
chapters.image: Akácfa utca a Rákóczi út felől nézve. Fortepan 15309.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here is the song, and a film built around it.
items: A recording of “Szomorú vasárnap” has the melody that went around the world.
And Gloomy Sunday, a German film, imagines a love triangle in a Budapest restaurant, built around the song.

chapters.heading: Refugees in the port
chapters.text: In 1922, after a war between Greece and Turkey, more than a million Greeks were forced to leave Asia Minor, the region that is now western Turkey. Many ended up in shanty towns around Piraeus, the port of Athens. They brought the music of the cafés of Smyrna, the cosmopolitan city they had lost. In the port’s tavernas and hashish dens, it mixed with local songs and became rebetiko, played on the bouzouki and sung about exile, prison, drugs, and love. The dictatorship of Ioannis Metaxas censored it in the late 1930s. After the Second World War it went mainstream, and today it is often called the Greek blues.

mediaNote.lead: To hear how the music sounds and where it came from, here are four places to start.
items: “Frangosyriani,” by Markos Vamvakaris, is a tender love song from the patriarch of rebetiko.
“Synnefiasmeni Kyriaki,” Cloudy Sunday, by Vassilis Tsitsanis, was written in occupied Greece.
An episode of the Ottoman History Podcast tells how refugees from Smyrna and Istanbul turned exile into rebetiko.
And Road to Rembetika, by Gail Holst, explains the music and translates its songs.

chapters.heading: The voice of the old taverns
chapters.text: In Romania, the music of longing belonged to the lăutari, professional musicians, most of them Roma, who played in taverns, at weddings, and at funerals. Maria Tănase grew up in a poor neighborhood on the edge of Bucharest and learned their songs as a girl. From the late 1930s she sang them on the radio and on records, in a deep, dramatic voice, and she became the country’s biggest star. People called her the Piaf of Romania. She died in 1963, at 49, and many Romanians still know her songs by heart.

items: To hear her, there is a recording of “Cine iubește și lasă,” Whoever Loves and Abandons, a curse on a faithless lover.

chapters.heading: Songs for the new arrivals
chapters.text: From the 1960s, millions of people moved from the villages of Anatolia to Istanbul, looking for work. Many built houses on the edges of the city overnight, on land they did not own. Their music was arabesk, which mixed Turkish folk tunes with the sweeping strings of Egyptian film music. Its songs were about fate, heartbreak, and being a stranger in the city. Turkish state radio kept it off the air for years, so it spread on cassettes, sold from the wholesale music market at Unkapanı, by the Golden Horn. Its first great hit was Orhan Gencebay’s “Bir Teselli Ver,” in 1968. The city’s older stars, such as Zeki Müren, sang in the glittering nightclubs called gazinos.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two sides of Istanbul’s music.
items: “Bir Teselli Ver,” Give Me Some Consolation, is the record that started arabesk.
And “Manolyam,” My Magnolia, is sung by Zeki Müren, the most beloved singer Turkey has known.

title: Jazz in Europe
intro: Jazz arrived in Europe after the First World War, with American soldiers and touring bands. Black American musicians soon found that they were treated better in Paris than at home, and within a generation most European cities had players of their own.
This thread starts in the clubs of Montmartre and ends in Reykjavík. On the way it stops in Poland, where jazz was banned and then tolerated, which made it sound like freedom.

chapters.heading: Le jazz hot
chapters.text: After the First World War, Black American musicians who had come over with the army, or on tour, found something in Paris that they could not find at home. They could eat, drink, and live where they liked. In the 1920s they filled the nightclubs of Montmartre, the hilltop district in the north of the city. In 1925 a young dancer from St. Louis, Josephine Baker, arrived with a show called La Revue Nègre. Within months she was the biggest star in Paris, dancing at the Folies Bergère music hall. She later became a French citizen and worked for the Resistance in the Second World War. In 2021 she became the first Black woman to be honored in the Panthéon.
chapters.image: Josephine Baker, Amerikaans,Franse artieste, in de Folies Bergère tijdens een optreden, SFA001007973.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into jazz-age Paris.
items: Paris Noir, by Tyler Stovall, follows Black Americans in Paris from the jazz players of the 1920s onward.
A very short animated video sketches Josephine Baker’s life.
And a comedy history podcast tells her whole story, from St. Louis to the Resistance.

chapters.heading: Banjo
chapters.text: Jazz also arrived through the ports. Claude McKay, a Jamaican-born writer of the Harlem Renaissance, the Black literary movement in New York, lived in Marseille in the 1920s. He set his 1929 novel Banjo on the docks of La Joliette, the port district. Its characters are Black sailors and drifters from Africa, America, and the Caribbean. They live from day to day and play music on the waterfront for whatever they can get. The main character, Banjo, is named after the instrument he plays.
