items: If you want to read it, Banjo is a lively, loose novel of the 1920s waterfront.

chapters.heading: Jazz in Pera
chapters.text: In Istanbul, jazz arrived with refugees. After the Russian Revolution, thousands of Russians who had fought against the Bolsheviks fled to the city, then called Constantinople. Some opened restaurants and nightclubs in Pera, the European quarter above the Golden Horn, and the city discovered cocktails, cabaret, and dance bands. In the 1920s, as the Ottoman Empire ended and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk built a new Turkish republic, the city’s nightlife boomed. The Pera Palace Hotel, built in 1892 for passengers off the Orient Express, was at the center of it.

items: For the whole period, there is Midnight at the Pera Palace, by Charles King, a history of the city between the wars.

chapters.heading: Ježek
chapters.text: In Prague, jazz found its way into the theater. Jaroslav Ježek, a composer who had been almost blind since childhood, wrote the songs and dance numbers for the Liberated Theatre. It was a satirical revue run by two comedians, Jiří Voskovec and Jan Werich. Their shows mocked politicians and, in the late 1930s, Hitler. Ježek’s music mixed jazz, dance band, and classical training. He composed in his apartment, whose walls he had painted a deep blue to rest his eyes. In 1939, after the German occupation of Prague, he and the two comedians fled to New York. He died there in 1942, at 35.

items: To hear his music, there is a recording of “Bugatti Step,” a giddy jazz sprint named after the race car.

chapters.heading: Django
chapters.text: Back in Paris, the most original European jazz musician was Django Reinhardt, a Romani guitarist. At eighteen he was badly burned in a fire in his caravan, and two fingers of his left hand were left paralyzed. He taught himself to play with the other two. With the violinist Stéphane Grappelli, he formed the Quintette du Hot Club de France, a band of string instruments with no drums. During the German occupation, the Nazis persecuted Roma and called jazz degenerate, but Django stayed in Paris and became more popular than ever. In 1940 he wrote “Nuages,” Clouds, which became an anthem of the occupied city. His style, now called gypsy jazz, is still played in the cafés around the flea market at Saint-Ouen, on the northern edge of Paris.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “Nuages,” the heart of gypsy jazz.

chapters.heading: Monica Zetterlund
chapters.text: In the 1950s, Stockholm had one of the liveliest jazz scenes in Europe, centered on Nalen, a dance hall where American stars played on tour. Monica Zetterlund, a singer from a small town in western Sweden, became its great voice. She sang American standards with Swedish words. Her version of “Walkin’ My Baby Back Home,” renamed “Sakta vi gå genom stan,” Slowly We Walk Through Town, became the city’s night song. In 1964 she recorded an album, Waltz for Debby, with the American pianist Bill Evans.

mediaNote.lead: Here is her song, and a film about her.
items: A recording of “Sakta vi gå genom stan” is the Stockholm night song itself.
And Waltz for Monica, a Swedish biopic, follows her from a small town to New York.

chapters.heading: Bluesette
chapters.text: In Brussels, Toots Thielemans was born in 1922 above his parents’ café on the Rue Haute, in the Marolles, an old working-class quarter. He started on the accordion, taught himself guitar by listening to Django Reinhardt, and then took up the harmonica. In 1952 he moved to the United States, where he played with Benny Goodman and George Shearing. He also had an unusual trick: he could whistle in unison with his own guitar. In 1962 he wrote “Bluesette,” a light jazz waltz, and it became a standard.

items: To hear him, there is a recording of “Bluesette,” with its whistling and harmonica.

chapters.heading: Americans in Copenhagen
chapters.text: In the 1960s, several great American jazz musicians settled in Copenhagen, among them the saxophonists Dexter Gordon and Ben Webster. They found steady work, appreciative audiences, and less racism than at home. Many of them played at Jazzhus Montmartre, a club in the old center. The house bassist was a Danish teenager, Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen, who started there at fifteen. He played with the Americans night after night, and he became one of the finest bass players in jazz.

items: To hear him, there is a recording of “My Little Anna,” by the bassist who started at the club as a teenager.

chapters.heading: Polish jazz
chapters.text: In Poland, jazz became political. Under Stalinist rule in the early 1950s it was banned as Western decadence, and musicians played it in private apartments. They called these the catacomb years. After 1956, when the regime loosened its grip, jazz came out into the open, and it became a sound of freedom. Krzysztof Komeda, a pianist who also wrote the music for Roman Polanski’s early films, recorded Astigmatic in Warsaw in 1965. It is often called the greatest Polish jazz album. In Kraków, the trumpeter Tomasz Stańko and the violinist Zbigniew Seifert took the music further, into free jazz.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three recordings from Polish jazz.
items: “Kattorna,” from Komeda’s Astigmatic, comes from the album often called the high point of Polish jazz.
“Litania,” by Tomasz Stańko, is from an album he made in tribute to Komeda.
And “Man of the Light,” by Zbigniew Seifert, shows how he played the violin like a saxophone.

chapters.heading: Garden Party
chapters.text: The last stop is in Reykjavík. In the late 1970s, a group of schoolfriends there formed a jazz-funk band called Mezzoforte. In 1983 their instrumental “Garden Party” reached the top twenty in Britain and was played on radio across Europe. For many people outside Iceland, it was the first music from the island they had ever heard. A few years later the Sugarcubes, with Björk, followed it out into the world.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “Garden Party.”

title: Rock and indie
intro: Rock and roll came from America in the 1950s, and British teenagers copied it in cellars and dance halls. Within a few years, bands from Liverpool and London were selling it back to the world.
This thread follows rock and its indie offspring through eight cities, from a cellar club in Liverpool to the small, strange scene of Reykjavík.
image: The Cavern Club stage 2, Mathew Street, Liverpool, 2008.jpg

chapters.heading: The Cavern
chapters.text: The story starts in a cellar. The Cavern Club, under a warehouse on Mathew Street in Liverpool, opened in 1957 as a jazz club. By 1961 it was booking rock and roll bands at lunchtime for office workers. One of them was the Beatles, four young Liverpudlians just back from playing long nights in Hamburg. They played the Cavern almost three hundred times. In November 1961, a local record-shop manager, Brian Epstein, came down the steps to see them, and he soon became their manager. Two years later, the band had left Liverpool for London and fame.
chapters.image: Cavern Club entrance & John Lennon statue - Mathew Street, Liverpool (2015-11-11 16.11.37 by Loco Steve).jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into the Beatles’ Liverpool.
items: An episode of The Rest Is History tells how four Liverpool teenagers became the Beatles.
Tune In, by Mark Lewisohn, is the long, definitive story of their Liverpool years.
Good Ol’ Freda is a documentary about the teenager who ran their fan club.
And “Penny Lane” is Paul McCartney’s picture of the streets where he grew up.

chapters.place: Eel Pie Island and Waterloo, London
chapters.heading: Swinging London
chapters.text: London had its own bands, and many of them grew up on the blues. On Eel Pie Island, a small island in the Thames at Twickenham, an old hotel ballroom held jazz and blues nights. In 1963, the Rolling Stones played a residency there. By the mid-1960s, London was the center of pop music, and its bands began writing about the city itself. In 1967, Ray Davies of the Kinks wrote “Waterloo Sunset,” about two lovers meeting by the river as the sun goes down.
chapters.image: Eel Pie Island - Twickenham - London, UK - DSC07206.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into 1960s London.
items: A podcast episode tells the story of Eel Pie Island and the rock stars who played there.
And “Waterloo Sunset” is the Kinks’ gentle song about London at dusk.

chapters.heading: Rock behind the Iron Curtain
chapters.text: The new music crossed the Iron Curtain too, and there it became political. In 1960s Prague, the communist government relaxed its grip for a while. A band called Olympic, later nicknamed “the Czech Beatles,” started out backing pop singers at the Semafor, a theater on Wenceslas Square. Then, in August 1968, Soviet-led armies invaded and ended the reforms. A month later, a new band formed, the Plastic People of the Universe, and they refused to change their music for the censors. They were banned, and they played in secret. In 1976 the members were put on trial. The playwright Václav Havel was so angered that he helped start Charter 77, a dissident movement.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two bands from Prague, one tolerated and one banned.
items: “Želva” is a hit by Olympic, the house band at the Rokoko.
And “Muchomůrky bílé” is a song by the Plastic People, the band the regime put on trial.

chapters.place: Harry Street and Windmill Lane, Dublin
chapters.heading: Dublin’s rock stars
chapters.text: In Dublin, rock helped a poor, conservative city find a new kind of confidence. In 1972, Thin Lizzy turned an old folk song, “Whiskey in the Jar,” into a rock hit. Their singer, Phil Lynott, the son of an Irish mother and a Guyanese father, became Ireland’s first rock star. A few years later, four teenagers at a Northside school formed U2. They recorded their early albums at Windmill Lane, a studio near the docks, and by the late 1980s they were among the biggest bands in the world. In 1990, Sinéad O’Connor, from a south Dublin suburb, had a worldwide number one.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three Dublin songs.
items: “Whiskey in the Jar” is Thin Lizzy’s electric version of the old ballad.
“I Will Follow” is U2’s first single, from 1980.
And “Nothing Compares 2 U” is Sinéad O’Connor’s version of a little-known Prince song.

chapters.heading: Heroes
chapters.text: In 1976, David Bowie, worn out by fame and drugs in Los Angeles, moved to West Berlin. He shared a flat in Schöneberg with the singer Iggy Pop, and he worked at Hansa Studios, a few hundred meters from the Berlin Wall. In those years he made three albums with the producer Brian Eno, mixing rock with cold electronic sounds. The best known, “Heroes,” was recorded at Hansa, and its title song is about two lovers kissing by the Wall. Earlier that year, on a train journey through Poland, Bowie had stepped out for a few hours in Warsaw, and its gray streets inspired another track. A few years later, his music became the soundtrack of Christiane F., a film about teenage drug users in West Berlin.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Bowie’s Berlin.
items: “Heroes” is Bowie’s song about two lovers by the Wall.
Christiane F. is the true story of a girl at Bahnhof Zoo, with Bowie’s music and a cameo by Bowie himself.
And “Warszawa” is the wordless track inspired by Bowie’s stop in Warsaw.

chapters.heading: Indie
chapters.text: In the 1980s, British guitar music found a new home in small, independent record labels, and the sound came to be called indie. Its most influential band came from Manchester. The Smiths paired Johnny Marr’s chiming guitar with Morrissey’s gloomy, witty lyrics. In 1986, they posed outside Salford Lads Club, an old boys’ club, for a photograph on an album sleeve. Fans have visited it ever since. At the end of the decade, the Stone Roses mixed guitars with dance music. Then came Oasis, two brothers from Burnage, in south Manchester. In 1996 they played to a quarter of a million people over two nights at Knebworth, a country house north of London.
chapters.image: Salford Lads' Club, Manchester in April 2023 01.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Manchester indie.
items: “This Charming Man” is the song that gave English indie its template.
A short film tells the story of Salford Lads Club and how it became a place of pilgrimage.
“I Wanna Be Adored” opens the Stone Roses’ first album.
And Supersonic is a documentary about Oasis, from a council house to Knebworth.

chapters.heading: The Barrowland
chapters.text: Glasgow had a scene of its own, and a venue that bands loved more than any other. The Barrowland Ballroom, in the East End, was built as a dance hall in 1934. In 1983, Simple Minds filmed a video there, and it became the city’s favorite rock venue. In the 1990s, Glasgow’s art schools and colleges produced a run of indie bands. Belle and Sebastian made their first album as a college music project in 1996. In 2004, Franz Ferdinand, whose singer had booked bands at a small café venue on King Street, had a worldwide hit with “Take Me Out.”

mediaNote.lead: Here are three Glasgow songs.
items: “Waterfront” is the Simple Minds song whose video was filmed at the Barrowland.
“The State I Am In” opens Belle and Sebastian’s first album, made for a college project.
And “Take Me Out” is the song that made Franz Ferdinand famous.

chapters.heading: Iceland
chapters.text: The last stop is the smallest capital on the list. In 1987, a Reykjavík band called the Sugarcubes released a single called “Birthday,” and the British music press fell in love with it. Their singer was Björk. After the band split, she went solo and became one of the most original musicians in the world. In 1999, another Reykjavík band, Sigur Rós, released an album of slow, soaring songs, sung partly in a language they made up. For a city of little more than a hundred thousand people, Reykjavík produced a remarkable amount of music, and people still come to hear it.
chapters.image: Snow in Reykjavik, Harpa concert hall (6905136669).jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Reykjavík’s music.
items: “Birthday” is the Sugarcubes single that first made Björk famous.
“Svefn-g-englar” is ten minutes of Sigur Rós at their most dreamlike.
Screaming Masterpiece is a documentary about Iceland’s music scene.
And in an episode of Song Exploder, Björk takes apart one of her own songs.

title: Electronic music
intro: In the 1970s, musicians in West Berlin, Paris, and Munich began making records almost entirely with synthesizers. By the end of the 1980s that sound had moved into the clubs of Manchester and London, and after the Berlin Wall fell, the empty buildings of East Berlin filled with techno.
Most of the places in this thread are clubs and studios, and some of them are long gone. It ends in Belfast in 2017.

chapters.heading: Tangerine Dream
chapters.text: The story begins in West Berlin, a walled-in island of the West inside communist East Germany. In the late 1960s Edgar Froese founded Tangerine Dream there. In the 1970s the band made long, slow instrumental pieces on synthesizers and sequencers, machines that could play repeating patterns on their own. Their music sounded like nothing on the radio. Albums such as Stratosfear, from 1976, laid down a hypnotic sound that would later fill the city’s clubs.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “Stratosfear,” from 1976.

chapters.heading: Oxygène
chapters.text: In Paris, Jean-Michel Jarre, a young composer who had studied electronic music, recorded Oxygène in a home studio with a handful of synthesizers. It came out in 1976 and sold millions of copies around the world. Jarre went on to play huge free outdoor concerts with lights and lasers. On Bastille Day in 1979, he played on the Place de la Concorde to a crowd of about a million people.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “Oxygène, Part 4,” his best-known piece.

chapters.heading: I Feel Love
chapters.text: In Munich, disco met the synthesizer. Donna Summer, an American singer, had come to the city to perform in the musical Hair, and she stayed. She worked with the Italian producer Giorgio Moroder and the British songwriter Pete Bellotte at Musicland, a recording studio in the basement of the Arabella, a high-rise hotel. In 1977 they made “I Feel Love,” built almost entirely on a Moog synthesizer, with a pulsing bassline that never stops. When the musician Brian Eno heard it, he is said to have told David Bowie that it would change the sound of club music. It led straight to house and techno.

mediaNote.lead: Here is the song, and two stories behind it.
items: A podcast episode tells how a basement studio under a tower block invented the sound of the future.
A recording of “I Feel Love” is the track itself.
And Love to Love You, Donna Summer, a documentary co-directed by her daughter, tells her life from home movies and archive film.

chapters.heading: Belgian electronics
chapters.text: Belgium took to the new machines early. In Brussels, Telex, a deadpan trio, made robotic synth-pop from the late 1970s, including a song about a train to Moscow. In the 1980s Front 242, also from Brussels, made something much harder: marching, aggressive electronic music that they called electronic body music. Their records were played in clubs across Europe, and in Detroit and Chicago, where house and techno were being invented. For a while in the late 1980s, Belgium was one of the centers of club music.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two Brussels records from those years.
items: “Moskow Diskow,” by Telex, is deadpan synth-pop about a train to Moscow.
And “Headhunter,” by Front 242, is the stomping sound of electronic body music.

chapters.heading: The Haçienda
chapters.text: In Manchester, a band and its record label built a club. Factory Records, run by the television presenter Tony Wilson, and its band New Order opened the Haçienda in 1982, in a former yacht showroom on Whitworth Street West. The band put its royalties into it, including money from “Blue Monday,” which became the best-selling twelve-inch single of all time. For years the huge room was half empty. Then in 1988 acid house arrived from Chicago, along with the drug ecstasy, and the Haçienda became the center of a new scene. Local records such as “Voodoo Ray,” made in a bedroom in Moss Side, filled the dance floor. The club lost money the whole time, struggled with gangs and drugs, and closed in 1997.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into the Haçienda.
items: A podcast series tells how New Order gambled a fortune on the club.
“Blue Monday” is the record that helped pay for it.
“Voodoo Ray,” by A Guy Called Gerald, is Manchester acid house in one record.
And 24 Hour Party People, with Steve Coogan as Tony Wilson, is a gleeful and unreliable film about the whole story.

chapters.heading: Soul II Soul
chapters.text: In London, the new sound grew out of sound systems, the mobile discos of Jamaican immigrants and their children. Soul II Soul began as one, led by Jazzie B, playing Sunday nights at the Africa Centre, a cultural center in Covent Garden. Their records mixed soul singing, hip-hop beats, and the deep bass of reggae sound systems. In 1989 “Back to Life” went to number one in Britain, and it is still heard as the start of a new Black British sound.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “Back to Life.”

chapters.heading: After the Wall
chapters.text: Back in Berlin, DJs in the West had been playing house and techno through the late 1980s. When the Wall came down in November 1989, East Berlin was full of empty buildings, and nobody was sure who owned them. Young people from both sides turned bunkers, bank vaults, and power stations into clubs, often illegally. The Love Parade, a street party that started in 1989 with about 150 people, grew to more than a million by the late 1990s. Berlin became the world’s techno capital. Berghain, the best-known club of all, opened in 2004 in a former power station.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into techno Berlin.
items: Der Klang der Familie is an oral history of the years after the Wall, told by the people who were there.
A short video follows the DJ Westbam back to the clubs of 1980s West Berlin.
“For an Angel,” by Paul van Dyk, who grew up in East Berlin, became an anthem of the Love Parade years.
And “Sky and Sand,” by Paul Kalkbrenner, comes from Berlin Calling, a film about a DJ coming apart.

chapters.heading: French touch
chapters.text: In the 1990s, Paris found its own sound. Young producers took old disco and funk records, looped them, and ran them through filters, so that the music seemed to rise and fall like breathing. The press called it French touch. Its best-known act was Daft Punk, two friends who later hid their faces behind robot helmets. The Rex Club, a basement on the Grands Boulevards, was one of the scene’s homes. In 2000 Daft Punk released “One More Time,” which became one of the biggest dance records in the world.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “One More Time.”

chapters.heading: Levels
chapters.text: By the 2010s, dance music had become a global industry, and some of its biggest stars came from Stockholm. Tim Bergling, who called himself Avicii, grew up in the city and started making tracks on his laptop as a teenager. In 2011 his track “Levels,” built around a sample of the American soul singer Etta James, became a hit around the world. He played to huge crowds for years. He died in 2018, at 28, and the city’s large arena was renamed the Avicii Arena in his memory.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “Levels.”

chapters.heading: Glue
chapters.text: The last stop is in Belfast. In the 1990s, during the last years of the Troubles, club nights were among the few places where young people from both sides of the city mixed. One of the longest running was Shine, held at the students’ union of Queen’s University. Two friends, Matt McBriar and Andy Ferguson, went there as teenagers. Later, as the duo Bicep, they became one of the most popular acts in electronic music. Their 2017 track “Glue” is about missing those raves.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “Glue.”

title: Eurovision
intro: The Eurovision Song Contest began in 1956 with seven countries, as a way to bring postwar Europe together through television. It has launched a few global careers, helped start a revolution, and become the place where Europe argues about itself in three-minute songs.
This thread follows a handful of entries back to the cities that sent them, from ABBA in 1974 to a Finnish rapper in a bolero of bright green sleeves.

chapters.heading: Waterloo
chapters.text: The first great Eurovision success story came from Stockholm. ABBA were two couples: Agnetha Fältskog and Björn Ulvaeus, and Anni-Frid Lyngstad and Benny Andersson. In April 1974 they won the contest in Brighton, on the English coast, with “Waterloo,” dressed in glittering platform boots. They went on to become one of the best-selling groups in the history of pop. Both marriages had ended by the early 1980s, and some of their saddest songs were written as they did. Their whole story is told in ABBA The Museum, on the island of Djurgården in Stockholm.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the ABBA story.
items: “Dancing Queen,” from 1976, is the shimmering peak of their records.
A music walk through Stockholm follows their rise from Eurovision to global fame.
And Bright Lights Dark Shadows, by Carl Magnus Palm, is the definitive book on the band.

chapters.heading: A song as a signal
chapters.text: That same spring, Eurovision played a part in a revolution. Portugal had been ruled by a dictatorship for nearly fifty years, and it was fighting long wars to hold on to its colonies in Africa. Its 1974 entry, “E Depois do Adeus,” And After the Goodbye, finished near the bottom. Three weeks later, at five to eleven on the night of April 24, a Lisbon radio station played it as a secret signal to army officers to get ready. Just after midnight, a second station played the next signal, “Grândola, Vila Morena,” a folk song by a singer the regime had kept off the air. The officers moved, and by the next evening the dictatorship had fallen, almost without a shot. It became known as the Carnation Revolution.

items: To hear the signal, there is a recording of “Grândola, Vila Morena,” the song that launched the revolution.

chapters.heading: Rise Like a Phoenix
chapters.text: Eurovision has long had a huge following among gay fans, and in 2014 it became a stage for something more. Austria sent Conchita Wurst, the bearded drag persona of the singer Tom Neuwirth. In some countries, people petitioned for her to be edited out of the broadcast. She won with “Rise Like a Phoenix,” a ballad in the style of a James Bond theme, and on stage she dedicated the win to everyone who believed in a future of peace and freedom. Under the contest’s rules, the winning country hosts the next year, so in 2015 Eurovision came to the Wiener Stadthalle, Vienna’s big arena.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “Rise Like a Phoenix.”

chapters.heading: Portugal finally wins
chapters.text: Portugal first entered Eurovision in 1964, and for more than fifty years it never won. In 2017, against a field of loud pop songs, it sent Salvador Sobral, who sang a quiet, old-fashioned ballad written by his sister, Luísa. “Amar Pelos Dois,” To Love for Both of Us, won by a wide margin. The next year Lisbon hosted the contest, at the arena by the river built for the World’s Fair of 1998. Portugal has kept sending quieter songs, such as Maro’s “Saudade, saudade” in 2022.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two Portuguese entries.
items: “Amar Pelos Dois,” sung by Salvador Sobral, is the ballad that finally won.
And “Saudade, saudade,” by Maro, is a hushed song about longing, partly in English.

chapters.heading: Soldi
chapters.text: Eurovision songs often say something about the country that sends them. Mahmood, a singer with a Sardinian mother and an Egyptian father, grew up in Gratosoglio, a district of high-rise housing on the southern edge of Milan. In 2019 he won the Sanremo festival, Italy’s great song contest, with “Soldi,” Money. It is about a father who left his family, and it has a line in Arabic. Some Italian politicians complained that he was not Italian enough. At Eurovision that May, the song came second.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “Soldi.”

chapters.heading: Måneskin
chapters.text: Two years later, Italy won. Måneskin were four teenagers from Rome who had started out busking on Via del Corso, a long shopping street in the center of the city. Their name means moonlight in Danish, the language of the bass player’s mother. In 2021 they won Sanremo and then Eurovision with “Zitti e buoni,” a loud glam-rock song whose title means roughly shut up and behave. It was Italy’s first win since 1990. They went on to tour the world and play arenas in America.
chapters.image: Crowds on Via del Corso on a weekend afternoon November 2024.jpg

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “Zitti e buoni.”

chapters.heading: In corpore sano
chapters.text: Serbia won the contest in 2007, its first year competing as an independent country, and Belgrade hosted the next year. Its most memorable entry since came in 2022. Konstrakta, the stage name of Ana Đurić, an architect turned performer, sat on stage at a basin and washed her hands while she sang. The song, “In corpore sano,” is a deadpan list of worries about health, health care, and the hair of celebrities. It came fifth, and it was one of the most talked-about entries of the year.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “In corpore sano.”

chapters.heading: Cha Cha Cha
chapters.text: Finland won in 2006 with Lordi, a hard-rock band in monster masks. In 2023 it sent Käärijä, a rapper from Vantaa, a suburb just north of Helsinki. He performed in a bolero with huge bright green sleeves and sang, in Finnish, about letting go with a drink at the end of a hard working week. The song flips from industrial rap into a sing-along chorus. It won the public vote across Europe and came second overall. In Ruskeasanta, the part of Vantaa where he grew up, a mural of him was painted on a wall.
chapters.image: Käärijä Eurovision Song Contest Final 2024 interval act.jpg

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “Cha Cha Cha.”

title: Punk
intro: Punk started in London in 1976 and spread across Europe within a couple of years. It was loud, fast, and cheap: three chords, small clubs, and records made at home.
In each city it also became about something local, from unemployment in Manchester to the Troubles in Belfast. The stops run roughly in the order punk arrived.

chapters.heading: Year zero
chapters.text: It started in a clothes shop. At 430 King’s Road in Chelsea, Malcolm McLaren and the designer Vivienne Westwood sold rubber, bondage gear, and T-shirts with slogans meant to shock. McLaren also managed a band of young regulars, the Sex Pistols. In 1976 they played basement clubs such as the 100 Club on Oxford Street, and that winter a club called the Roxy opened in Covent Garden for the new bands. Britain was in a long economic slump, with high unemployment, and punk gave bored teenagers something to do. By 1979 the Clash, another London band, were singing about the city itself in “London Calling.”

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into London punk.
items: England’s Dreaming, by Jon Savage, is the best book on how it all happened.
A podcast about clothes explains how the safety-pin look came out of that shop.
A radio episode looks at the Roxy, and how punk mixed with reggae there.
And “London Calling” shows where the Clash had taken punk by 1979.

chapters.heading: Forty people
chapters.text: Punk spread fast because people who saw it went home and started bands. On June 4, 1976, the Sex Pistols played the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester, a small room above a concert hall. Only about forty people came. Among them, by most accounts, were young men who went on to form Joy Division and the Fall. The two students who had booked the gig were already starting a band of their own, called Buzzcocks. The gig became a legend, and later many more people claimed to have been there. Manchester went on to have one of the richest music scenes in Britain.

mediaNote.lead: Here is the gig, and three songs from the bands that came out of it.
items: A podcast episode tells the story of the night itself.
“Ever Fallen in Love,” by Buzzcocks, is two minutes of perfect lovesick punk.
“Love Will Tear Us Apart,” by Joy Division, was recorded weeks before their singer, Ian Curtis, died.
And “Totally Wired,” by the Fall, is Mark E. Smith at his most scratchy and restless.

chapters.heading: Good Vibrations
chapters.text: In Belfast, punk meant something more. In the late 1970s the city was in the middle of the Troubles, the long and violent conflict over whether Northern Ireland should stay in the United Kingdom. Catholics and Protestants lived largely apart, and there were soldiers on the streets. Punk was one of the few scenes that young people from both sides shared. Terri Hooley ran a record shop called Good Vibrations on Great Victoria Street, and he started a label to put out records by local bands. In 1978 he released “Teenage Kicks” by the Undertones, a band from Derry, which became one of the best-loved singles of the decade.

mediaNote.lead: Three stories bring Belfast punk back.
items: A podcast episode looks at Hooley’s life and the scene that grew up around his shop.
“Alternative Ulster,” by Stiff Little Fingers, shouts about growing up under the Troubles.
And Good Vibrations, a warm comedy-drama, tells Hooley’s story.

chapters.heading: Ça plane pour moi
chapters.text: On the continent, punk sometimes turned into pop. In 1977 a Belgian singer called Plastic Bertrand had a hit across Europe with “Ça plane pour moi,” a fast, happy song with nonsense lyrics in French. It sounded like punk, but it was made in a studio as a novelty record. Years later it came out that Plastic Bertrand did not even sing on it. The vocals were by its producer, Lou Deprijck. It is still played at parties all over Europe.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of the song, pinned to the Ancienne Belgique, a Brussels concert hall.

chapters.heading: Zurich burns
chapters.text: In Zurich, women were at the front of punk. Kleenex was a band of young women who formed in 1978. Their records came out on Rough Trade, an independent label in London, and they were played on British radio. The company that made Kleenex tissues threatened to sue, so they changed their name to LiLiPUT. Zurich’s young people also wanted somewhere to play. In 1980 they rioted for a youth center of their own, in protest at the city spending millions on its opera house. The city eventually gave them the Rote Fabrik, an old factory on the lake, which is still a cultural center.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two songs from Zurich’s scene.
items: “Ain’t You,” by Kleenex, is snarling and joyful at once.
“Tubel Trophy,” by Baby Jail, is the kind of dialect fun-punk that filled the Rote Fabrik.

chapters.heading: West Berlin
chapters.text: West Berlin was a strange place for punk, and a good one. It was an island of West Germany surrounded by the communist East, with cheap rent and empty buildings. Young men moved there to avoid military service, which did not apply in the city. In Kreuzberg, a district against the Wall, the club SO36 became the center of the punk and post-punk scene from 1978. The singer Nina Hagen had moved to the West from East Berlin in 1976, after the East German state expelled her stepfather, a singer who criticized the regime. Her wild, operatic voice made her the godmother of German punk.

mediaNote.lead: Two things give the feel of punk in West Berlin.
items: B-Movie, an archive documentary, follows the city’s underground through the 1980s.
And “African Reggae,” from 1979, is Nina Hagen at full force.

chapters.heading: Ebba Grön
chapters.text: In Sweden, punk came from the suburbs. Rågsved, in the south of Stockholm, is one of the concrete housing areas the city built after the Second World War. Its youth center gave rehearsal space to local bands. The best-known band to come out of it was Ebba Grön, which took its name from a police code word. In 1980 they recorded “Staten och kapitalet,” The State and Capital, a cover of a 1970s protest song. It became one of the best-known songs in Swedish rock.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of the song that became the anthem of Swedish punk.

chapters.heading: Rokk í Reykjavík
chapters.text: Punk reached Iceland last, and the scene there was tiny but loud. In 1981 and 1982 a handful of bands played in Reykjavík, the capital, often at Hótel Borg, a hotel on Austurvöllur, the square in front of the parliament. Purrkur Pillnikk, one of the best, played songs that were often over in less than two minutes. Its singer, Einar Örn, later sang in the Sugarcubes with Björk. The scene was filmed in Rokk í Reykjavík, a documentary released in 1982. One of the teenage punks of that time was Jón Gnarr, who became a comedian and, in 2010, the mayor of Reykjavík.

mediaNote.lead: Here is a song from the scene, and the story of one of its fans.
items: “Ekki enn,” Not Yet, by Purrkur Pillnikk, is a typical burst of Reykjavík punk.
And Gnarr, a documentary, follows Jón Gnarr from punk comedian to mayor.

title: Hip-hop
intro: Hip-hop came to Europe from New York in the early 1980s, through records, films, and breakdancers on television. Within a few years, teenagers in Paris were rapping in French.
Almost everywhere, it took root in the same kind of place: the big postwar housing projects on the edge of the city. This thread follows it from Paris to Belfast, one city at a time.
image: Des moyens pour l education mural Marseille 2026.JPG

chapters.heading: The banlieue
chapters.text: In 1984, French television began showing H.I.P. H.O.P., a weekly program about breakdancing, hosted by a young DJ called Sidney. It was one of the first hip-hop shows anywhere in the world. Its biggest audience was in the banlieue, the ring of suburbs around Paris, where many immigrant families lived in huge concrete housing projects. In Seine-Saint-Denis, north of the city, two graffiti writers, JoeyStarr and Kool Shen, formed a rap group called Suprême NTM. Their songs were angry and political, about police, poverty, and being shut out of Paris. In 1995, the same year as their landmark album, Mathieu Kassovitz’s film La Haine showed that anger to the whole country.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways to hear and see the banlieue.
items: “Paris sous les bombes,” by Suprême NTM, is named after the graffiti, not real bombs.
La Haine follows three friends through the day after a riot, from their housing project into central Paris.
And a short video meets a Paris hip-hop dancer at the Gare de Lyon.

chapters.place: Le Panier and the Old Port, Marseille
chapters.heading: Planet Mars
chapters.text: Marseille built its own scene, and it was proud not to be Paris. The city is a port, with families from Italy, Armenia, North Africa, and the Comoros, and its rap sounded like it. In 1991, a group called IAM released their first album, and they called their city “planet Mars.” Their singer, Akhenaton, later co-directed a film about young men drifting through days in Le Panier, the old quarter above the port. By the 2010s, Marseille rappers were among the best-selling in France. In 2020, Jul, the best-selling of them all, gathered the city’s rappers for one long song, and it spent twelve weeks at number one in France.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Marseille rap.
items: “Je danse le Mia,” IAM’s first big hit, pokes fun at the posers of 1980s Marseille.
Comme un aimant, made by IAM’s Akhenaton, drifts through Le Panier with a group of young men.
And “Bande organisée” is the six-minute song that lined up the whole city’s rappers in 2020.

chapters.heading: Welcome to the suburbs
chapters.text: Sweden had its own banlieue. In the 1960s and 1970s, the government built a million new homes in ten years, many of them in tower blocks on the edges of cities. By the 1990s, these suburbs were home to many immigrant families. In Alby, south of Stockholm, three young men with Latin American roots formed the Latin Kings. Their first album, in 1994, was called “Welcome to the Suburbs,” and they rapped in the mixed slang spoken there. Twenty years later, a Stockholm teenager called Yung Lean showed how far the music had traveled. He made strange, sleepy songs in his bedroom, and they found fans around the world online.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two Stockholm rap songs, twenty years apart.
items: “Välkommen till förorten” is the Latin Kings’ song about the suburbs where they grew up.
And “Ginseng Strip 2002” is the bedroom recording that made Yung Lean an internet star.

chapters.heading: Chelas
chapters.text: In Lisbon, hip-hop arrived with families from Portugal’s former colonies, especially Cape Verde and Angola. Many of them settled in the housing projects of the east side and the suburbs across the river. Rap in Portuguese grew up alongside rap in Cape Verdean Creole. One of its central figures was Sam the Kid, a rapper and producer from Chelas, a district of public housing in eastern Lisbon. He made his records at home and rapped about ordinary life in the neighborhood. His 2002 album is still seen as a landmark of Portuguese hip-hop.

items: To hear it, there is “Sobre(tudo),” Sam the Kid’s 2002 song about everyday life in his corner of Lisbon.

chapters.heading: Grime
chapters.text: London took longer to find its own voice, and when it did, it did not sound American at all. Around 2002, young MCs in Bow, in East London, began rapping over fast, harsh electronic beats on pirate radio. The music was called grime. Its first star was Dizzee Rascal, who grew up on a housing project in Bow. In 2003, at eighteen, he won the Mercury Prize, Britain’s top album award, for his debut. Grime faded for a while, then came back stronger in the 2010s. In 2019, Stormzy, from Croydon in South London, became the first Black British solo artist to headline the Glastonbury Festival.
chapters.image: Tower block by the Bow roundabout - geograph.org.uk - 6279820.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into London rap.
items: “Fix Up, Look Sharp” comes from Dizzee Rascal’s prize-winning first album.
A short video from Vox explains how grime came out of Bow.
“Vossi Bop” is Stormzy’s 2019 number one.
And “Introvert,” by Little Simz from North London, shows how far London rap has traveled since.

chapters.heading: My block
chapters.text: German rap had grown up in the 1990s, but in Berlin it took a harder turn. The Märkisches Viertel is a vast estate of concrete towers in the north of the city, built in the 1960s and 1970s. A rapper called Sido grew up there. In 2004 he released “Mein Block,” a cartoonish tour of his tower block, with its neighbors, dealers, and parties. It was a hit, and it made Berlin the center of German street rap. A decade later, Capital Bra, who had come to Berlin as a child from the former Soviet Union, had more number ones than anyone in German chart history.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two Berlin rap hits.
items: “Mein Block” is Sido’s guided tour of his housing project.
And “Berlin lebt,” by Capital Bra, is a swaggering shout-out to his adopted city.

chapters.heading: Dear Italy
chapters.text: In Milan, rap became the voice of a new generation of Italians. Marracash, born to Sicilian parents, grew up in the Barona housing projects on the southwest edge of the city. His first album, in 2008, helped take Milan street rap into the Italian charts. Ten years later, Ghali, whose parents came from Tunisia, released “Cara Italia,” or “Dear Italy.” It was a love letter to the country, and it asked who gets to count as Italian.
chapters.image: Milano - quartiere INA-Casa Baggio II - edificio dei negozi.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two songs from Milan’s edges.
items: “Badabum Cha Cha” is the single that took Marracash into the charts.
And “Cara Italia” is Ghali’s love letter to the country he was born in.

chapters.heading: Kneecap
chapters.text: The last stop is West Belfast, where hip-hop met an old language. In 2017, three young men from the area formed a rap group called Kneecap. They rapped in Irish as well as English, with jokes about drugs, police, and politics. The name is a dark joke too, about the punishment shootings of the Troubles. They became stars in Ireland, and their songs drew young people to the language. In 2024 they played themselves in a film about their own story, and it won awards around the world.
chapters.image: Belfast - International Wall along Falls Road (A501) - Murals - geograph.org.uk - 3977059.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Kneecap.
items: “C.E.A.R.T.A.” is the song about a member who refuses to speak English to the police.
And Kneecap is the loosely true film in which they play themselves.

title: The Roman Empire
intro: At its height, Rome ruled from Scotland to Syria, and it left roads, walls, theaters, and towns that later cities were built on top of. Much of it is now underground, in basements, under squares, and under office buildings.
This thread starts in Rome with the first emperor, then travels out to the provinces. It ends with the people who fled when the empire fell apart in the west.

chapters.place: Ara Pacis and the Forum, Rome
chapters.heading: Augustus
chapters.text: Rome was a republic for nearly five hundred years, until civil wars tore it apart in the first century BC. The winner was Octavian, the adopted heir of Julius Caesar. In 27 BC the Senate gave him the name Augustus, and he ruled for forty years. He was careful never to call himself king. He said he was only the first citizen, and he kept the old offices of the republic while holding all the real power. The Forum, the old center of the city, filled with new temples and monuments in his name. In 13 BC the Senate voted to build him the Altar of Peace, the Ara Pacis, near the Tiber. His statue from the villa of his wife, Livia, shows him as a young general, though he was in his forties when it was made.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Augustus’s Rome.
items: An audio guide explains how the altar lined up with a giant sundial, so that a shadow crossed it on his birthday.
A podcast episode reads the statue from Livia’s villa, from the pose to the messages on his breastplate.
And a short video explains the Roman Forum, where Romans voted, traded, and worshipped.

chapters.heading: Londinium
chapters.text: From Rome, the empire spread to the edges of the known world. The Romans invaded Britain in AD 43, and a few years later they founded a town by a bridge over the river Thames. They called it Londinium. In AD 60 or 61, Boudica, the queen of the Iceni, a British tribe, led a rebellion and burned it to the ground. Archaeologists still find the layer of burned red earth it left behind. The town was rebuilt and became the largest in Roman Britain, with a stone wall around it. Under an office building in the City of London, you can visit the remains of a temple to Mithras, a god popular with soldiers and merchants. Stretches of the wall survive near the Tower of London.
chapters.image: London Roman Wall - surviving section by Tower Hill gardens full section.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Two guides show what is left of Roman London.
items: A walking tour with the historian Tristan Hughes follows the city from its founding to its abandonment in 410.
And a podcast episode with a London guide explains the Roman ruins hidden in the modern city.

chapters.heading: Pompeii
chapters.text: For a picture of ordinary Roman life, the best place is Pompeii, a busy town on the Bay of Naples. In AD 79 Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried it under several meters of ash and pumice. Most of the people fled, but many died, and the town was lost for more than sixteen centuries. Excavations began in the 1700s, and they are still going on. The streets have bakeries with their ovens, bars with counters for hot food, and walls covered in election slogans, advertisements, and rude graffiti. Many of the best finds, such as the great mosaic of Alexander the Great in battle, are now in the archaeological museum in Naples.

mediaNote.lead: Two works bring Pompeii to life.
items: Mary Beard’s Pompeii reconstructs the daily life of the town, from its bakeries to its plumbing.
And a podcast episode looks closely at the Alexander Mosaic, made of about a million tiny stones.

chapters.heading: Emperors from Spain
chapters.text: The provinces did more than pay taxes. They produced emperors. Itálica, just outside Seville, was founded in 206 BC by the Roman general Scipio for wounded soldiers, after a victory over Carthage nearby. Three centuries later, Trajan, who was born there, became the first emperor from outside Italy, and he took the empire to its greatest size. His successor, Hadrian, also came from an Itálica family. Hadrian was a great builder. In Rome he rebuilt the Pantheon, a temple to all the gods, with a concrete dome that is still the largest unreinforced one in the world. Itálica itself has the ruins of one of the biggest amphitheaters in the empire.
chapters.image: Anfiteatro de las ruinas romanas de Itálica, Santiponce, Sevilla, España, 2015-12-06, DD 34-45 PAN HDR.JPG

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to follow the emperors from Spain.
items: A podcast episode tells how a settlement for veterans produced two emperors.
And a short video looks at the Pantheon, Hadrian’s great temple in Rome.

chapters.heading: Olisipo
chapters.text: At the far western edge of the empire was Olisipo, the town that became Lisbon. It was an important port, and it was known for its garum, a salty fish sauce that the Romans put on almost everything. In the first century AD the town built a theater on the hillside below the castle, with seats for a few thousand people. Later it was buried and forgotten. Its remains were found in 1798, when the neighborhood was being rebuilt after the great earthquake of 1755. They can be seen today in a small museum on the slope of the Alfama.

items: For a walk through these layers, there is a tour led by an archaeologist that passes the Roman theater on its way down from the castle.

chapters.heading: Singidunum
chapters.text: On the Danube, the empire’s northern frontier, Rome built forts to hold back the peoples beyond the river. One of them stood on the ridge above the point where the Sava meets the Danube. It was the base of a legion, the Fourth Flavian, and the town that grew beside it was called Singidunum. That town is now Belgrade. The fortress hill, now the park called Kalemegdan, has been fortified again and again by every power that has held the city since. One of the city’s main streets still follows the line of the Roman road that ran out of the camp.

items: For a walk through all of its layers, there is a tour by a local historian that follows the old Roman road.

chapters.heading: Capital of the West
chapters.text: By the end of the 200s, the empire was too big to rule from one city. The emperor Diocletian split it into an eastern and a western half, and in the west the capital moved to Milan, closer to the frontiers. In 313 the emperor Constantine and his co-emperor, Licinius, met in Milan and agreed to tolerate Christianity, which had been persecuted. Milan became one of the great centers of the new faith. Its bishop, Ambrose, was powerful enough to stand up to emperors. In the 380s he founded a church just outside the walls, and he is buried in its crypt. It is now the Basilica of Sant’Ambrogio.

items: For a closer look at his church, there is a video about the basilica and its arcaded forecourt.

chapters.heading: Constantine
chapters.text: Constantine had come to power by force. In 312 he defeated his rival, Maxentius, at the Milvian Bridge, just north of Rome. Later Christian writers said he had seen a sign in the sky before the battle and fought under the sign of Christ. In 315 the Senate dedicated a triumphal arch to him beside the Colosseum. Many of its carvings were taken from monuments to earlier emperors, with the old faces recut to look like Constantine. In 330 he moved the capital to a new city in the east, on the site of Byzantium, and named it Constantinople after himself.

items: For a closer look, there is a video about the arch and its borrowed carvings.

chapters.heading: After Rome
chapters.text: In the 400s and 500s, the western half of the empire fell apart. Armies from beyond the frontiers, among them the Huns and later the Lombards, swept through northern Italy. People from the towns on the mainland fled to the muddy islands of the Venetian lagoon, where horsemen could not follow. Refugees from Altinum, a Roman town on the shore, settled on Torcello, and they built with stone carried from the old Roman towns. Torcello’s cathedral was founded in 639. Over the following centuries, the settlements on the islands grew into Venice, which liked to say it had been born free and owed nothing to Rome.
chapters.image: Venedig Torcello Basilica di Santa Maria Assunta-4345.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to see how Venice rose from the ruins.
items: A short video looks for the Roman stones hidden in a city that claims it was never Roman.
And a podcast episode tells how refugees on a muddy lagoon built a city out of almost nothing.

image: Colosseum and Arch of Constantine seen from Palatine.jpg

title: Byzantium
intro: The Roman Empire carried on in the east for a thousand years after Rome itself fell, ruled from Constantinople, the city that is now Istanbul. Its people called themselves Romans, and for centuries their capital was the richest city in the Christian world.
Much of what survives was carried away. This thread starts in the city and then follows the loot to Venice, Paris, and London.

chapters.heading: Hagia Sophia
chapters.text: In 330 the emperor Constantine moved his capital to Byzantium, a Greek town on the strait between Europe and Asia, and renamed it Constantinople. Two centuries later, in 532, riots destroyed much of the city, including its great church. The emperor Justinian rebuilt it on a scale nobody had attempted. Hagia Sophia, Holy Wisdom, was finished in 537, and for nearly a thousand years its dome was the largest in the world. Forty windows around its base make it seem to float on light. After the Ottoman conquest in 1453 it became a mosque. It was a museum from 1934, and it became a mosque again in 2020. Mosaics of Christ, the Virgin, and the emperors survive in the upper galleries.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Hagia Sophia.
items: A video explains how Justinian’s builders made the dome seem to float.
A short one looks at the Deësis mosaic in the upper gallery.
Another asks what changed when it became a mosque again.
And John Julius Norwich’s A Short History of Byzantium tells the empire’s whole thousand-year story.

chapters.heading: The walls
chapters.text: Constantinople was surrounded by water on three sides. On the fourth, the emperor Theodosius II built a great line of land walls in the early 400s, running about six kilometers from the Sea of Marmara to the Golden Horn. It was really three barriers: a wide moat, an outer wall, and a taller inner wall with nearly a hundred towers. For a thousand years these walls turned back every army that besieged the city, including Huns, Avars, Arabs, and Bulgars. Much of them still stands, crumbling in places and restored in others.

items: For more, there is a video about the three lines of stone that held off invaders for a thousand years.

chapters.heading: The Fourth Crusade
chapters.text: The walls could not stop an enemy that came by sea. In 1202 a crusader army gathered in Venice, meaning to attack Egypt. It could not pay the Venetians for the fleet they had built, and it was drawn into a dispute over the Byzantine throne. In 1204 the crusaders, fellow Christians, attacked Constantinople from the water and broke in. For three days they looted the city, stripping its churches, including Hagia Sophia, and they put one of their own leaders on the throne. The Byzantines took the city back in 1261, but the empire never recovered its strength.
chapters.image: The Entry of the Crusaders into Constantinople - 1840 - Eugène Delacroix - Louvre - Inv 3821.jpg

items: For the story, there is a podcast episode about the crusaders who sacked the church they had come to save.

chapters.heading: The loot in Venice
chapters.text: Venice took one of the largest shares of the spoils. Its doge, Enrico Dandolo, an old and nearly blind man, had led the attack himself. The four bronze horses that stood over the entrance to St. Mark’s Basilica for centuries came from the Hippodrome, Constantinople’s great racetrack, and they are now kept inside the basilica. The Tetrarchs, a carving in purple porphyry of four Roman co-emperors embracing, were set into the outer corner of the basilica. Much of the treasury inside came from the same sack. Venice used its share, including trading rights and islands across the eastern Mediterranean, to build a sea empire.
chapters.image: Horses of Basilica San Marco bright.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways to see what Venice took.
items: A long podcast episode tells how the doge steered the crusade to Constantinople.
A short video tours St. Mark’s Basilica, glittering with loot.
Another looks at the Tetrarchs on the basilica’s corner.
And City of Fortune, by Roger Crowley, tells how Venice won and lost its sea empire.

chapters.heading: The Barberini Ivory
chapters.text: Smaller treasures traveled too. In the 500s, carvers in Constantinople made a panel of ivory showing an emperor on a rearing horse, with a defeated barbarian beside him and Christ blessing him from above. It probably shows Justinian. Over the centuries it passed through several hands, and in the 1600s it belonged to the Barberini, a powerful family in Rome whose name it still carries. It is now in the Louvre in Paris.

items: For a closer look, there is a short video about the ivory and the emperor it shows.

chapters.heading: The Archangel Michael
chapters.text: The largest single panel of Byzantine ivory to survive is in London. Carved around 525, probably in Constantinople, it shows the archangel Michael standing at the top of a flight of steps, holding an orb and a staff. It may once have been one half of a pair. It is now in the British Museum, one of the finest works left from the city at its height.

items: For a closer look, there is a short video about the archangel panel.

title: Vikings
intro: For about three centuries, from the late 700s, Scandinavians raided, traded, and settled from Ireland to the Black Sea. Several of today’s capitals began as their towns, or were shaped by them.
This thread starts in their homelands, in Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, and follows them west to Dublin and Iceland.

chapters.heading: At home
chapters.text: The people we call Vikings were mostly farmers, fishermen, and craftsmen. Going viking, raiding by sea, was something some men did in the summer, for plunder and fame. The Danes raided England and France, and in the 800s they conquered much of eastern England. The National Museum of Denmark, in Copenhagen, holds much of what survives of daily life in the period, from swords and jewelry to combs and tools. Copenhagen itself began later, as a small fishing and trading town on the harbor.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Viking Denmark.
items: The Children of Ash and Elm, by Neil Price, is the best popular book on who the Vikings really were.
And a walking tour traces Copenhagen’s thousand years of fires and rebuilding, from a square by the old harbor.

chapters.heading: East to Byzantium
chapters.text: Vikings from what is now Sweden mostly went east. They sailed across the Baltic and down the great rivers of Russia and Ukraine, dragging their boats overland between rivers, all the way to Constantinople and the Caspian Sea. Some served as guards to the Byzantine emperor. They traded furs and slaves for silver, and tens of thousands of silver coins from the Islamic world, some minted as far away as Baghdad, have been found buried in Sweden. The Swedish History Museum in Stockholm has many of them. Runestones carved with the names of men who traveled east still stand around the country, and one is set into a wall in Stockholm’s Old Town.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Viking Sweden.
items: The Children of Ash and Elm, by Neil Price, explains their world, from their gods to their ships.
And a historian’s walk through the Old Town passes a Viking runestone set into a wall.

chapters.place: Museum of the Viking Age, Oslo
chapters.heading: The Oseberg ship
chapters.text: In Norway, the Vikings buried their most important dead in ships. In 834, two women were laid in a beautifully carved ship at Oseberg, near the Oslo fjord, with sledges, a cart, beds, animals, and food for the next life. The ship was covered with a mound of clay and turf, which kept it almost whole for more than a thousand years. It was dug up in 1904 and taken to Oslo. It now stands with two other ships in the Museum of the Viking Age on the Bygdøy peninsula. The museum is being rebuilt around them, because they are too fragile to move far. Oslo itself was founded later, around 1050.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the ships and the city.
items: A video tells the story of the two women buried in the Oseberg ship.
Another shows how the museum is being rebuilt around ships too fragile to move.
And a podcast episode traces Oslo from a Viking outpost to a modern capital.

chapters.heading: Dyflin
chapters.text: Vikings began raiding Ireland at the end of the 700s, attacking monasteries for their treasures. In 841 a group of them built a fortified camp beside a black pool, dubh linn in Irish, where a small stream met the river Liffey. It grew into a busy trading town, and one of the biggest slave markets in western Europe. In the 1970s the city decided to build its new civic offices on Wood Quay, on top of the excavated remains of the Viking town. Archaeologists found over a hundred houses. Tens of thousands of people marched in protest, but the offices were built.

items: For the full story, there is a podcast episode about the port the Vikings founded and how it still shapes Dublin.

chapters.heading: Iceland
chapters.text: Norse settlers reached Iceland, an empty island far out in the North Atlantic, around 870. According to the sagas, the first permanent settler, Ingólfur Arnarson, threw the carved pillars of his high seat overboard as he approached the coast. He promised to settle wherever the gods brought them ashore. His slaves found them in a bay with steaming hot springs, and he named it Reykjavík, smoky bay. In 2001, builders working on a hotel on Aðalstræti, in the old center, found the remains of a Viking longhouse. It is now displayed where it was found, in a museum called the Settlement Exhibition.

items: For the legend, there is a podcast episode about the chieftain whose pillars chose Iceland’s capital.

title: Queens
intro: Most European thrones passed to sons, so a woman who ruled usually got there by accident, by marriage, or by outliving the men around her.

This thread visits ten of them, from a queen of Naples in the 1300s to an empress of Austria at the end of the 1800s. Each stop is the room, church, or square where her reign turned, and several of them ended badly.

chapters.heading: Joanna I
chapters.text: Joanna inherited the kingdom of Naples in 1343, when she was sixteen, from her grandfather, King Robert. She had been married as a child to her cousin Andrew, a prince from the Hungarian branch of the family, who wanted to rule in his own right. In 1345 he was strangled at a castle outside the city. Many people blamed Joanna, although nothing was ever proved. Andrew’s brother, the king of Hungary, invaded to avenge him, and Joanna fled for a time. She came back and ruled for nearly forty years from the Castel Nuovo, the great castle by the harbor, and she married four times in all. In the end another cousin, with Hungarian support, took Naples, and in 1382 he had her killed.

items: For more on her long and dangerous reign, there is a podcast episode about the queen and the accusations that followed her.

chapters.heading: Crowned king
chapters.text: In Poland, a girl was crowned king. In 1384 Jadwiga, a daughter of the king of Hungary and Poland, was about ten when she was crowned in Wawel Cathedral in Kraków. She took the title king, because Polish law had no place for a queen who ruled in her own right. Two years later the Polish nobles married her to Jogaila, the grand duke of Lithuania, who was baptized and became king of Poland. The marriage joined Poland and Lithuania for four centuries. Jadwiga died in 1399, still in her twenties. She left her jewels to refound Kraków’s university, which is now named after the dynasty her marriage began, the Jagiellonian University.

items: For the whole story, there is a podcast episode about the girl who was crowned king.

chapters.heading: Isabella of Castile
chapters.text: A century later, Isabella came to the throne of Castile, in Spain, in 1474, after a war over the succession. Her husband, Ferdinand, was king of Aragon, and together they ruled most of what became Spain. They often held court in the Alcázar of Seville, a palace built by earlier Muslim and Christian rulers. In 1478 they set up the Spanish Inquisition to hunt down converts suspected of secretly keeping their old faith. In 1492 they took Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain, and expelled all Jews who would not convert. That same year, Isabella paid for Christopher Columbus’s first voyage across the Atlantic. In 1503 the House of Trade, which ran Spain’s new empire in the Americas, opened in the palace.
chapters.image: Baths of Maria de Padilla, Alcázar of Seville.jpg

items: If you want more, there is a podcast episode about how she built an empire, and an inquisition to police it.

chapters.heading: Hürrem
chapters.text: In Istanbul, the most powerful woman of the 1500s started as a captive. Hürrem, known in Europe as Roxelana, was taken as a girl in a raid on what is now western Ukraine. She was sold into the harem of the Ottoman sultan, Süleyman the Magnificent, and she became his favorite. Then Süleyman did something no sultan had done for centuries: he freed her and married her. She advised him on politics, wrote to foreign rulers, and paid for mosques, schools, and soup kitchens. Her rivals at court called her a witch. Mimar Sinan, the great imperial architect, built a bathhouse in her name near Hagia Sophia, and it is open again as a hamam today.
chapters.image: İstanbul - Ayasofya Hürrem Sultan Hamamı r3 - Şub 2013.jpg

mediaNote.lead: If you want to know how she did it, there are two good places to start.
items: A podcast episode tells how a kidnapped teenager became the sultan’s only wife.
And Leslie Peirce’s Empress of the East is a full biography, based on careful scholarship.

chapters.heading: Catherine de’ Medici
chapters.text: Catherine de’ Medici was born in 1519 in the Medici family palace in Florence, and both her parents died within weeks. Her family arranged a grand marriage for her. At fourteen she was sent to France to marry the king’s second son, Henry, who unexpectedly became heir and then King Henry II. For years she was overshadowed by his mistress. Then, in 1559, Henry was killed in a jousting accident, and three of their sons became king in turn. Catherine ruled through them for thirty years, while France was torn apart by war between Catholics and Protestants. She was blamed for the St. Bartholomew’s Day massacre of 1572, when thousands of Protestants were murdered in Paris and other cities.

items: For her side of the story, there is a podcast episode about the orphaned Medici who became France’s most feared queen.

chapters.heading: Mary, Queen of Scots
chapters.text: Mary became queen of Scotland as a baby, in 1542, and was raised in France. In 1561, after the death of her young French husband, she came home to a country that had just turned Protestant, while she stayed Catholic. She lived at Holyrood, the royal palace at the bottom of the Royal Mile in Edinburgh. In 1565 she married her cousin Lord Darnley, and the marriage was a disaster. In 1566 a group of lords, with Darnley among them, burst into her supper room and stabbed her secretary, David Rizzio, to death in front of her. Less than a year later, the house where Darnley was staying blew up, and he was found strangled in the garden. Mary then married the man most people suspected, and within months she was forced to give up her throne.
chapters.image: Palace of Holyroodhouse quadrangle Edinburgh 2025 dllu.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways to follow her story through Edinburgh.
items: A short video from the Royal Collection tells the story of the murder in her supper room.
A podcast episode looks at Darnley’s murder and how it led to her downfall.
And a walking tour of the Royal Mile retells her reign, starting at the palace.

chapters.heading: Christina of Sweden
chapters.text: In Sweden, Christina became queen at five, in 1632, when her father, King Gustavus Adolphus, was killed in battle in Germany. She was brought up like a prince, learned several languages, and read everything. In 1650 she was crowned in Storkyrkan, Stockholm’s great church, with the title king. She invited scholars to her court, among them the French philosopher René Descartes. He died there of pneumonia after a few months of giving her lessons at five in the morning. She refused to marry. In 1654, at 27, she gave up the throne, became a Catholic, and moved to Rome. She is one of very few women buried in St. Peter’s Basilica.

items: For more, there is a podcast episode about the young queen who was crowned king and then gave up the throne.

chapters.heading: Caroline Matilda
chapters.text: Caroline Matilda was a sister of King George III of Britain. In 1766, at fifteen, she was married to King Christian VII of Denmark, who was mentally ill and treated her coldly. In 1768 a German doctor, Johann Struensee, joined the court to look after the king. He became the king’s closest adviser, and the queen’s lover. For about two years, Struensee ran Denmark. He passed hundreds of reforms inspired by the Enlightenment, from freedom of the press to ending torture. In January 1772, after a masked ball at the palace theater, his enemies arrested him in a coup. Struensee was executed. The queen was divorced and sent into exile in Germany, where she died at 23.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to get to know this scandal.
items: A Royal Affair, a Danish film with Mads Mikkelsen, dramatizes the queen, the doctor, and the coup.
And a history podcast tells how Struensee rose and fell.

chapters.heading: Marie Antoinette
chapters.text: Marie Antoinette was the youngest daughter of Empress Maria Theresa of Austria. In 1770, at fourteen, she was sent from Vienna to marry the heir to the French throne, the future Louis XVI. At Versailles she was mocked for her spending, her clothes, and her foreign birth, and pamphlets accused her of every vice. She became the face of everything the French Revolution hated. After the monarchy fell in 1792, the king was tried and executed. The queen spent her last weeks in the Conciergerie, a prison on the Île de la Cité in the middle of Paris. She was guillotined on October 16, 1793. She probably never said “Let them eat cake.”

mediaNote.lead: Two podcast episodes take her from palace to prison.
items: One takes an irreverent look at her whole life, starting at Versailles.
The other follows her last months in the Conciergerie.

chapters.heading: Sisi
chapters.text: The last stop is in Vienna, with an empress who never wanted the job. Elisabeth of Bavaria, known as Sisi, married the Austrian emperor, Franz Joseph, in 1854, when she was sixteen. She never settled at the stiff Viennese court. She spent as much time away as she could, traveling, riding, and walking for hours, and she was devoted to Hungary, where she was much loved. Her only son, Crown Prince Rudolf, died in 1889, and she wore black for the rest of her life. In 1898, as she walked along the lakefront in Geneva, an Italian anarchist stabbed her with a sharpened file. She died within hours.
chapters.image: Schoenbrunn Palace as seen from Neptune Fountain, September 2016.jpg

mediaNote.lead: If you are visiting her rooms in the Hofburg, two things will help.
items: A podcast episode tells her lonely, glittering story.
And Sissi, the 1955 film with Romy Schneider, shows the fairy tale that Austria still loves.

image: John Opie (1761-1807) - The Murder of Rizzio - 49 - Guildhall Art Gallery.jpg

title: The Ottoman frontier
intro: For more than three centuries, the Ottoman Empire pushed into Europe, and Europe pushed back. The frontier ran through cities that changed hands, held out against sieges, and still carry the marks.
The stops run in date order, from the fall of Constantinople in 1453 to the Greek war of independence in the 1820s.

chapters.heading: Constantinople falls
chapters.text: By the 1400s, the Byzantine Empire had shrunk to little more than its capital, Constantinople, surrounded by Ottoman lands. In April 1453 the young sultan Mehmed II besieged it with a huge army and enormous cannons, built for him by a Hungarian engineer. After 53 days, on May 29, his troops broke through the thousand-year-old land walls. The last Byzantine emperor died in the fighting. Mehmed made the city his capital, and he built the Topkapı Palace on the point above the Bosphorus, where the sultans lived for nearly four centuries. The city came to be called Istanbul.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Ottoman Istanbul.
items: A BBC discussion tells how the cannons finally broke the walls.
A short video visits the courtyards of Topkapı.
And Constantinople, by Philip Mansel, is a portrait of the Ottoman city over five centuries.

chapters.heading: The gate to Hungary
chapters.text: Three years later, Mehmed turned on Belgrade, the fortress where the Sava meets the Danube, which guarded the road to Hungary. In July 1456 a Hungarian commander, John Hunyadi, held the fortress against him and drove the Ottomans back. The pope had ordered church bells to ring at noon to call for prayers for the defenders, and in many places they still ring at noon in memory of the victory. Belgrade held out for another 65 years. In 1521 Suleiman the Magnificent, the greatest of the sultans, took it, and it stayed in Ottoman hands, with breaks, until the 1860s.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two podcast episodes about the fortress.
items: One tells how Hunyadi held Belgrade against Mehmed II.
The other tells how Suleiman took it in 1521.

chapters.heading: Vlad the Impaler
chapters.text: North of the Danube, the princes of Wallachia, in what is now southern Romania, tried to hold off the Ottomans. The most famous was Vlad III. He had spent part of his youth as a hostage at the Ottoman court. As prince, he fought the sultan’s armies, and he became notorious for impaling his enemies on stakes, which earned him the name Vlad the Impaler. He was also called Dracula, son of the dragon, after an order of knights his father had joined. A charter he signed in 1459 is the first document known to mention Bucharest. The ruins of his princely court are in the Old Town.

items: For his story, there is a podcast episode about the real Dracula and how he ruled.

chapters.heading: Ottoman Buda
chapters.text: In 1526 Suleiman crushed the Hungarian army at the Battle of Mohács, and the Hungarian king was killed. In 1541 the Ottomans took Buda, the royal castle town on the hills above the Danube, and they held it for 145 years. They turned churches into mosques and built bathhouses over the hot springs, and some of those baths, such as Rudas and Király, are still in use. On a hill nearby is the tomb of Gül Baba, a dervish who died in 1541, which is still visited by pilgrims from Turkey. In 1686 a Habsburg army took Buda back after a long and bloody siege.
chapters.image: Rudas Baths central part and Gellert Hill in Tabán, 2016 Budapest.jpg

items: For the bigger story, there is Budapest: Between East and West, a history of the city pulled between empires.

chapters.place: Arsenale and the Grand Canal, Venice
chapters.heading: Lepanto
chapters.text: Venice lived by trade with the Ottomans, and it also fought them. In 1570 the Ottomans attacked Cyprus, a Venetian island. Venice joined Spain and the pope in a Holy League, and its Arsenale built much of the fleet. On October 7, 1571, the two fleets met off Lepanto, on the coast of Greece, in one of the largest sea battles ever fought with oared galleys. The Christian fleet won. But Venice still lost Cyprus, and within a few years it made peace and went back to trading. Turkish merchants in Venice had their own trading house on the Grand Canal, the Fondaco dei Turchi, which is now a natural history museum.
chapters.image: (Venice) Battaglia di Lepanto - Andrea Vicentino - Correr Museum.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two BBC discussions about Venice and the Ottomans.
items: One tells the story of the battle of Lepanto.
The other explains how Venice built a trading empire stretching to the Black Sea.

chapters.heading: The second siege
chapters.text: The Ottomans had besieged Vienna once before, in 1529, and failed. In 1683 they came back, with an army of more than 100,000 men under the grand vizier, Kara Mustafa. They surrounded the city in July and dug tunnels to blow up its walls. The defenders held out for two months. On September 12 a relief army arrived, and the Polish king, Jan III Sobieski, led a huge cavalry charge down the slopes of the Kahlenberg, the hill north of the city. The Ottoman army broke and fled. It was the high point of Ottoman power in Europe, and from then on the frontier moved south. Viennese legend says the city’s coffeehouses began with sacks of coffee the Ottomans left behind.

items: For the whole story, there is a podcast episode about the siege and the charge that broke it.

chapters.heading: Sobieski’s palace
chapters.text: Jan III Sobieski came home a hero, hailed as the savior of Christian Europe. He was the elected king of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, a large state whose nobles chose their kings. In the years after the siege, he rebuilt a manor south of Warsaw as a grand baroque summer palace, Wilanów. Its decoration celebrates his victories and compares him to the heroes of ancient Rome. It survived the Second World War, unlike most of Warsaw, and it is now a museum.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Sobieski’s world.
items: A tour of Wilanów tells the story of his victory at Vienna through the palace.
And a BBC discussion explains the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, the republic that elected its kings.

chapters.heading: The Parthenon explodes
chapters.text: In 1687, during a war between Venice and the Ottomans, a Venetian army besieged Athens. The Ottoman garrison had stored gunpowder inside the Parthenon, the ancient temple on the Acropolis, which had survived almost intact for two thousand years. A Venetian mortar shell landed in it, and the explosion blew out the middle of the building. The ruin we see today is largely the result. Greece stayed under Ottoman rule for well over another century. In 1821 the Greeks rose up, and after years of war, with help from Britain, France, and Russia, Greece became independent. Athens, by then a small town, was made its capital in 1834.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the Acropolis and Greek independence.
items: A video tells the story of the shell that blew up the Parthenon.
And Mark Mazower talks about his history of the Greek revolution, and its chaotic road to a nation.

image: Relief of Vienna 1683 - Wien Museum - 2 (photo by Andrew Nash).jpg

title: The Habsburgs
intro: For four hundred years, one family married and inherited its way into ruling much of Europe, from Spain and the Netherlands to Bohemia and Hungary. Its palaces, crypts, and art collections are still among the main sights in half a dozen cities.
This thread follows the family from Brussels to Budapest, and through to its end in 1918.

chapters.heading: Charles V
chapters.text: The Habsburgs began as minor lords in what is now Switzerland, but by the 1500s a series of marriages had brought them an astonishing inheritance. Charles V was born in Ghent in 1500 and grew up in the Netherlands. In 1515, at fifteen, he was declared of age in the great hall of the Coudenberg Palace in Brussels. He went on to rule the Netherlands, Spain and its new empire in the Americas, much of Italy, and the Holy Roman Empire. In 1555, worn out by forty years of wars, he gave up his thrones in the same hall, leaning on the shoulder of a young prince, William of Orange. The palace burned in 1731, and its remains lie under the Place Royale.
chapters.image: Brussels, straatzicht Place Royale met église Saint-Jacques-sur-Coudenberg oeg2043-01020 en standbeeld van Godefroid de Bouillon foto3 2015-06-07 13.53.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Charles’s Brussels.
items: A podcast episode tells the story of the day he gave up his empire.
Another tells how he was declared of age in the same hall, at fifteen.
And a video shows the Ommegang, a parade held every summer to re-create one given for Charles in 1549.

chapters.heading: The Spanish branch
