chapters.text: Charles divided his lands. His brother Ferdinand took the Austrian lands and the imperial title, and his son Philip II took Spain, the Netherlands, and the Americas. Philip made Madrid the capital of Spain in 1561. The Spanish Habsburgs were great collectors, and their paintings became the core of the Prado. In 1656 Diego Velázquez, the court painter, painted Las Meninas. It shows the young princess Margarita among her ladies-in-waiting, with Velázquez himself at his easel and the king and queen glimpsed in a mirror at the back. Generations of marriages between cousins took their toll, and the Spanish line ended in 1700 with Charles II, who was sickly and had no children.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the Spanish Habsburgs’ painter.
items: A long video from Great Art Explained unpicks Las Meninas, and who is looking at whom.
And The Vanishing Velázquez, by Laura Cumming, is a gripping book about a lost portrait, and about looking at paintings.

chapters.heading: Rudolf’s court
chapters.text: In the Austrian branch, the emperor Rudolf II moved his court from Vienna to Prague in 1583. He was shy and moody, and more interested in art and science than in governing. He filled Prague Castle with painters, astronomers, and alchemists, and with a famous cabinet of curiosities. The astronomers Tycho Brahe and Johannes Kepler worked for him. After his death, the religious tensions he had held off broke out. In 1618 Protestant nobles threw two of the emperor’s Catholic governors and their secretary out of a high window of the castle. All three survived. It started the Thirty Years’ War, which devastated central Europe.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Rudolf’s Prague.
items: The Mercurial Emperor, by Peter Marshall, describes Rudolf’s court of astronomers, alchemists, and painters.
A podcast from Radio Prague tells the story of the men thrown from the window.
And The Emperor and the Golem, a much-loved Czech comedy from 1951, imagines Rudolf, his baker, and a clay giant.

chapters.heading: The imperial capital
chapters.text: Vienna was the family’s main seat. In 1683 an Ottoman army besieged it for two months before a relief army drove it off, and after that the city grew into a grand imperial capital. The Habsburgs lived in the Hofburg, a sprawling palace in the center, and spent the summers at Schönbrunn, on the edge of the city. Empress Maria Theresa ruled for forty years in the 1700s and had sixteen children. In the 1800s the family’s art collections went into the new Kunsthistorisches Museum, and its crowns and regalia into the Treasury of the Hofburg. Franz Joseph became emperor in 1848, at eighteen, and reigned for 68 years.
chapters.image: Hofburg Neue Burg section, Heldenplatz. Statue of Archduke Charles.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Habsburg Vienna.
items: A short video tours Schönbrunn and its 1,441 rooms.
Another visits the Kunsthistorisches Museum and its Bruegels.
A third looks at the crowns and relics in the Treasury.
And A Nervous Splendor, by Frederic Morton, tells the story of one winter in Vienna, from 1888 to 1889.

chapters.heading: Austria-Hungary
chapters.text: Hungary had been part of the Habsburg lands since the 1600s, but many Hungarians resented rule from Vienna, and in 1848 they rebelled. The rising was crushed. Then in 1866 Austria lost a short war to Prussia, and Franz Joseph needed the Hungarians’ support. In 1867 he agreed to share power. Austria and Hungary became two countries with their own parliaments, under one monarch. Budapest boomed. To rival Vienna, it built a huge parliament on the Danube, an opera house, wide boulevards, and the first underground railway on the continent.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Budapest in its golden age.
items: Budapest: Between East and West, by Victor Sebestyen, is a personal history of the city.
And Sunset, a film by László Nemes, follows a young woman through Budapest in 1913, a year before the catastrophe.

chapters.heading: The end
chapters.text: The family’s last decades were full of loss. Franz Joseph’s only son, Crown Prince Rudolf, died with his young lover, Mary Vetsera, at the hunting lodge of Mayerling in 1889. His wife, Elisabeth, was murdered in Geneva in 1898. His nephew and new heir, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, was shot in Sarajevo in June 1914, and the war that followed destroyed the empire. Franz Joseph died in 1916. In 1918 the last emperor, Charles I, gave up power, and the empire broke apart into new countries. The Habsburgs are buried in the Imperial Crypt, beneath the Capuchin church in Vienna.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the end of the empire.
items: A podcast episode tells the story of Crown Prince Rudolf and Mary Vetsera.
And The Radetzky March, by Joseph Roth, follows one family through three generations as the empire declines.

title: Napoleon
intro: Napoleon Bonaparte rose from an artillery officer to emperor of the French in less than ten years. By 1810 he controlled most of continental Europe, and the cities he took still show the marks.
This thread follows his rise and fall, from a street fight in Paris to the battlefield at Waterloo, and ends at his tomb under a golden dome.

chapters.heading: A whiff of grapeshot
chapters.text: Napoleon was born in 1769 on Corsica, an island in the Mediterranean that had become French only the year before. He trained as an artillery officer in France, and the French Revolution, which began in 1789, gave ambitious young officers fast promotion. In October 1795, royalist crowds marched on the revolutionary government in Paris. The government put the 26-year-old Bonaparte in charge of its guns. He brought up cannon and fired on the rebels near the church of Saint-Roch, on the Rue Saint-Honoré, killing hundreds. The historian Thomas Carlyle later called it “a whiff of grapeshot.” It made Bonaparte’s name, and within months he had command of an army in Italy.

items: To hear what happened that day, there is a podcast episode about the fight outside the church.

chapters.heading: The end of a republic
chapters.text: In Italy he beat the Austrians again and again, and in 1797 his army reached the edge of the Venetian lagoon. Venice had been an independent republic for about eleven hundred years, ruled by elected doges and a Great Council of noble families. Its power had come from trade, and from the Arsenale, the vast state shipyard that was said to build a war galley in a day. By 1797 it had little left to fight with. On May 12 the Great Council voted to dissolve the republic. Napoleon then handed Venice to Austria in a peace treaty, and his soldiers took the four bronze horses from the front of St. Mark’s Basilica to Paris.

items: If you want the longer story, a historian of Venice explains how the city grew rich on its navy, and how Napoleon brought it down.

chapters.heading: The picture of power
chapters.text: Napoleon understood that power depended on pictures. In 1799 he seized control of the French government, and the next year he led an army across the Alps into Italy. He made the crossing on a mule, led by a local guide. But he asked the painter Jacques-Louis David to show him calm on a fiery horse, and David painted a rearing stallion against a stormy sky, in five versions. The first hangs at Malmaison, the country house west of Paris that Napoleon shared with his wife, Josephine. Another painter, Antoine-Jean Gros, showed him touching plague victims in Jaffa, in Palestine, to answer reports that he had left his sick soldiers to die. In 1804, in Notre-Dame, he crowned himself emperor.

mediaNote.lead: Two of the paintings made for him are worth a closer look.
items: A video from Great Art Explained shows how David’s portrait was made as propaganda.
A shorter one looks at Gros’s picture of the plague hospital, which now hangs in the Louvre.

chapters.heading: King of Italy
chapters.text: In 1805 he took a second crown. In Milan Cathedral he crowned himself King of Italy, using the old Iron Crown of the Lombard kings. His government closed many churches and monasteries across northern Italy and took their paintings. The best were gathered in Milan, in the Brera palace, where they became one of Italy’s great galleries, the Pinacoteca di Brera. Among them is a painting by Tintoretto, brought from Venice, of the body of Saint Mark being found in Alexandria. Other pictures went to the Louvre in Paris, which was then called the Musée Napoléon. Many came back after his fall, but some never did, among them a Titian taken from a church in Milan.
chapters.image: Pinacoteca di Brera - Milano - il cortile interno.JPG

mediaNote.lead: Here are two of the paintings his armies moved.
items: A video looks at Tintoretto’s Finding of the Body of Saint Mark, with men pulling bodies from tombs in a long, dark hall.
Another looks at Titian’s Crowning with Thorns, the painting from Milan that is still in the Louvre.

chapters.heading: The second and third of May
chapters.text: Spain was next. In 1808 he forced the Spanish king to give up the throne and made his own brother Joseph king instead. French troops were already in Madrid, and on May 2 the people of the city rose against them, fighting with knives and stones. The French crushed the rising, and that night and the next morning they shot hundreds of prisoners on the hills outside the city. The war that followed lasted six years. When it was over, in 1814, Francisco Goya, the Spanish court painter, painted both days. His Third of May, with a man in a white shirt raising his arms before a firing squad, hangs in the Prado.
chapters.image: El Tres de Mayo, by Francisco de Goya, from Prado (cropped).jpg

mediaNote.lead: If you are going to the Prado, two things will help.
items: A video explains how Goya’s painting works, and why it has shaped how artists show war.
A costume drama by Miloš Forman follows Goya through the years of the Inquisition and the French invasion, though it is uneven.

chapters.heading: The Congress of Vienna
chapters.text: The Spanish war drained his armies, and in 1812 he lost most of what was left in Russia. Vienna knew him well. His troops had occupied the city twice, and in 1810 he married Marie Louise, the daughter of the Austrian emperor. In 1814 he was beaten and sent into exile on Elba, an island off the Italian coast. The rulers of Europe then met in Vienna to decide what to do with the continent. For nine months, Prince Metternich, the Austrian foreign minister, ran the talks from his office on the Ballhausplatz, while the court kept the visitors busy with balls and banquets. One guest joked that the congress danced a great deal but did not move forward.

items: To understand what was decided there, there is a podcast episode about the diplomats who redrew the map of Europe between banquets and balls.

chapters.heading: Waterloo
chapters.text: While they were still talking, Napoleon escaped from Elba. In March 1815 he landed in the south of France, marched to Paris, and took back power without a fight. He ruled for about a hundred days. The allied armies gathered in Belgium, and on June 18 he attacked a British-led army under the Duke of Wellington near the village of Waterloo, south of Brussels. The fighting lasted all day. In the evening a Prussian army under Marshal Blücher arrived, and the French broke and ran. Napoleon was sent to Saint Helena, a tiny British island in the South Atlantic. A tall mound topped by an iron lion now marks the battlefield.
chapters.image: Belgique Butte du Lion dit de Waterloo.jpg

items: For the battle itself, there is a podcast episode in which Dan Snow and his father, Peter Snow, go through the day.

chapters.heading: Back to Paris
chapters.text: He died on Saint Helena in 1821, at 51. By then the French had begun to remember him more kindly, as the general who had made France great, and in 1840 the king, Louis-Philippe, asked the British to return his body. It was carried up the Seine and through Paris in a huge procession. It now lies in a tomb of red stone under the golden dome of Les Invalides, a hospital for old soldiers built by Louis XIV. Other traces of him are all over the city. The column on Place Vendôme is covered in bronze from captured cannon, and the Arc de Triomphe celebrates his victories.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to see Napoleon’s Paris.
items: A short video at his tomb tells the story of his rise and fall.
A walking tour starts at the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel, passes the column on Place Vendôme, and ends at the tomb.

title: Dictators
intro: Twentieth-century Europe produced dictators of every kind. Some were soldiers, one was a professor, and one was a failed painter.

Most of these men had nothing to do with each other, but their stories have the same shape: a way in, years of control, and an ending. This thread takes them in order, from a men’s hostel in Vienna in 1908 to a square in Bucharest in 1989. Each stop is a place where one regime started or ended.

chapters.heading: Hitler, a failed painter in Vienna
chapters.text: The story starts with a young man who wanted to be a painter. Adolf Hitler moved to Vienna, then the capital of the Austrian empire, hoping to study at its Academy of Fine Arts. The Academy turned him down twice. He stayed anyway, living in cheap lodgings and then in a men’s hostel on Meldemannstraße, a poor street. He got by selling watercolors of the city’s sights. Vienna also gave him his politics. Its mayor, Karl Lueger, won votes by blaming Jews for the city’s problems, and Hitler took note. He left for Munich, in Germany, in 1913. Twenty years later he was running that country.

mediaNote.lead: Two things here show you the Vienna that shaped him.
items: A book describes the city Hitler knew, a place of cheap hostels and resentment.
An audio tour walks you past his lodgings and the academy that rejected him.

chapters.place: Palazzo Venezia, Rome, and Piazzale Loreto, Milan
chapters.heading: Mussolini invents Fascism
chapters.text: Hitler was not the first, though. His model was an Italian. Benito Mussolini was a blacksmith’s son and a former socialist newspaper editor. In 1919 he founded the Fascist movement at a meeting in a hall on Piazza San Sepolcro, a small square in Milan. Three years later he was in power. He ruled from Palazzo Venezia, a palace in the center of Rome, and spoke to crowds from its balcony. The end came from his own side. In July 1943, with the war going badly, his Fascist Grand Council voted him out. In April 1945 he was shot by partisans, the Italian resistance fighters. They hung his body upside down in Piazzale Loreto, a square in Milan.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways to follow Mussolini from start to finish.
items: One podcast episode covers his rise, starting with the meeting in Milan.
Another covers his fall in 1943.
A book follows what happened to his body after Piazzale Loreto, which was buried, stolen, and fought over for years.

chapters.heading: Salazar, the professor who ruled Portugal
chapters.text: Not every dictator shouted from a balcony. António de Oliveira Salazar was an economics professor who kept out of the public eye. He ran Portugal for 36 years, from 1932. His secret police, known as the PIDE, did the work that speeches did elsewhere. They held political prisoners in the Aljube, a jail beside Lisbon’s cathedral. Salazar kept Portugal out of the Second World War. Later he fought long wars to hold on to its colonies in Africa. Those wars finished the regime, though he did not live to see it. In April 1974 young army officers, tired of fighting them, overthrew his successors in a single day. People put carnations in the soldiers’ gun barrels. The Aljube is now a museum about the prisoners.

mediaNote.lead: To see what the regime did, and how it ended, there are three things here.
items: A documentary tells the story of the secret police using only prisoners’ mugshots and survivors’ voices.
A feature film re-creates the day of the 1974 coup.
A book covers the same day in more detail.

chapters.heading: Franco and the silence after him
chapters.text: Next door in Spain, the dictator got there by war. Francisco Franco was a general who rose against the elected government in 1936. Three years of civil war followed, and he won in 1939. The killing did not stop with the war. Tens of thousands of people were executed in the years after it, many of them against the wall of the Almudena cemetery in Madrid. Franco ruled until 1975 and died in bed. After his death, Spain agreed not to prosecute the crimes of his regime. The families of the dead are still pushing against that silence.

mediaNote.lead: Two things here go deeper into the killing and the silence.
items: A documentary follows victims of the regime as they go to court decades later.
A long history book counts the civilians killed by Franco’s side.

chapters.heading: Quisling, the name that means traitor
chapters.text: Franco stayed out of Hitler’s war. Norway was not given the choice. Germany invaded in April 1940, and one Norwegian politician had asked for it. Vidkun Quisling had urged Hitler to occupy the country, and on the day of the invasion he announced himself prime minister. From 1942 he led a puppet government, one that took its orders from Berlin. He lived in a villa on Bygdøy, a peninsula on the edge of Oslo, and called it Gimle. After the war he was tried for treason, and he was shot in October 1945. His surname became a word for traitor.

items: For the full story of Quisling, there is a podcast episode about him, and about how his name became an insult.

chapters.heading: Hitler’s last days in the bunker
chapters.text: By then the man Quisling served was already dead. In early 1945 Hitler moved underground, into a bunker beneath the garden of the Reich Chancellery, his headquarters in Berlin. He spent his last weeks there while the Red Army, the army of the Soviet Union, fought its way into the city. Mussolini was shot on April 28. Two days later, on April 30, 1945, Hitler killed himself. The bunker was later demolished. Today the site is a parking lot with a single information board.

mediaNote.lead: There are two ways to get inside the bunker.
items: A short video shows the rooms as they were found, and what became of them.
Downfall is a German feature film about Hitler’s last ten days, based on his secretary’s memoir.

chapters.heading: Tito, who defied Stalin
chapters.text: The war that destroyed Hitler made the next dictator. Josip Broz, known as Tito, led the partisans, the communist fighters who resisted the German occupation of Yugoslavia. In 1945 he took power. Three years later he broke with Joseph Stalin, the Soviet leader, who expected communist countries to obey Moscow. Few people thought Tito would last. He did. He ran Yugoslavia as a one-party state, but one that let its people travel and work abroad. He died in 1980 and is buried in the winter garden of his residence in Belgrade, now called the House of Flowers. About a decade after his death, the country came apart in war.

mediaNote.lead: If Tito interests you, there are three things to try.
items: One podcast episode covers the break with Stalin.
Another covers his death and what followed.
There is also a short biography.

chapters.heading: The colonels who seized Greece
chapters.text: Tito was still in power when soldiers took over the country to his south. On April 21, 1967, a group of Greek army colonels seized the government in a coup, with almost no bloodshed. They banned political parties and censored newspapers, books, and songs. Opponents were jailed and tortured. The challenge came from students. In November 1973 they occupied the Polytechnic, a university in central Athens. The army sent a tank through its gate. The occupation was crushed, but the regime never recovered, and it fell the following summer.

mediaNote.lead: Two short podcast episodes here bring these years closer.
items: In one, a resistance fighter describes the coup and what happened to him afterward.
The other reports on the students at the Polytechnic.

chapters.heading: Ceaușescu and the crowd that booed
chapters.text: The last dictator in this thread held on longest. Nicolae Ceaușescu led communist Romania from 1965. Like Tito, he defied Moscow, and in the 1970s Western governments courted him for it. The 1980s were different. He decided to pay off all of Romania’s foreign debt, and his people went hungry while he did it. At the same time he bulldozed a fifth of old Bucharest to build himself a palace. On December 21, 1989, he summoned a crowd to the city’s central square to cheer him. They booed instead. Four days later, on Christmas Day, he and his wife were shot.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Ceaușescu’s last decade.
items: A podcast episode covers the speech and the execution.
A short video is about the palace.
In another podcast episode, a British diplomat describes watching Romania go hungry in the early 1980s.

image: Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest (51878975552).jpg

title: Spies
intro: For most of the 20th century, Europe’s cities were where spies met, traded secrets, and sometimes died. Neutral capitals, divided cities, and grand hotels were where the work got done.
This thread runs in date order, from a nurse shot in Brussels in the First World War to a poisoned cup of tea in London in 2006.

chapters.heading: A nurse before a firing squad
chapters.text: The story starts in the First World War, in Brussels, which the German army occupied in 1914. Edith Cavell, a British nurse, ran a nursing school and clinic in the city. With Belgian friends, she hid British and French soldiers who had been cut off behind the lines, and helped about two hundred of them escape to the neutral Netherlands. The Germans arrested her in 1915, and on October 12 she was shot by a firing squad at the Tir National, a shooting range on the edge of the city. Britain made her a martyr, and her face appeared on recruiting posters. For a long time she was remembered only as a nurse who saved lives. Some historians now argue that her network was also passing military intelligence to the British.

items: If you want the case for Cavell as a spy, there is a podcast episode in which a historian sets out the evidence.

chapters.heading: Orwell’s war
chapters.text: In the 1930s, Europe divided between fascism and communism, and the spying turned on ordinary people. In the Spanish Civil War, which began in 1936, the Soviet Union backed the Republic against General Franco, and it sent its secret police along too. George Orwell, the English writer, came to Barcelona to fight for the Republic. He joined the militia of the POUM, a small left-wing party that Moscow saw as an enemy. His wife, Eileen O’Shaughnessy, worked in Barcelona while he was at the front, in an office that looked after the British volunteers. In 1937 the POUM was banned and its members were arrested. Soviet-backed agents had been watching the couple, and they escaped to France in June, just in time.
chapters.image: 13 Edifici Telefònica, av. Portal de l'Àngel - pl. Catalunya (Barcelona).jpg

items: To hear her side of it, there is a podcast episode about Eileen running the office while Orwell fought, with informers all around her.

chapters.heading: The neutral port
chapters.text: When the Second World War began, Portugal stayed neutral, and Lisbon became one of the last open doors out of Europe. Refugees from across the continent crowded into the city, waiting for visas and a place on a ship to America. Spies came too. British and German agents watched each other in the same hotels and cafés, and in the casino at Estoril, a resort along the coast. Ian Fleming, then a British naval intelligence officer, passed through in 1941. The casino is said to have given him an idea for his first James Bond novel.

items: For a walk through it, there is a tour of the Baixa and Bairro Alto about the city’s rebuilding after the earthquake of 1755 and its wartime spies.

chapters.heading: The Third Man
chapters.text: After the war, the Cold War cut straight through some cities. Vienna, like Berlin, was divided between the four victorious powers: the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, and France. Soldiers from all four patrolled the old center together. The city was bombed out and short of everything, and a black market thrived. In 1948 the novelist Graham Greene and the director Carol Reed made The Third Man there. It is a thriller about an American writer searching for a friend who sells watered-down penicillin on the black market. Much of it was filmed in the real ruins, with a famous chase through the sewers and a meeting on the Riesenrad, the giant Ferris wheel in the Prater park.

items: If you have a free evening, the film itself is the best guide to postwar Vienna, and the Ferris wheel is still there to ride.

chapters.heading: The front line
chapters.text: Berlin was the front line. The city sat deep inside East Germany, divided between East and West, and from 1961 the Wall ran through it. Both sides filled it with agents. The Americans and British built a listening station on Teufelsberg, a hill in the west of the city made from the rubble of bombed buildings. From there they picked up radio traffic from the East. On the Glienicke Bridge, which crosses the river Havel between West Berlin and Potsdam, the two sides exchanged captured spies. The first swap came in 1962, when the Soviet agent Rudolf Abel was traded for Francis Gary Powers, an American pilot shot down over the Soviet Union. After East Germany collapsed in 1989, its citizens won the right to read the files the Stasi, the secret police, had kept on them.

mediaNote.lead: Berlin has more spy stories than any other stop, and here are four of them.
items: Steven Spielberg’s film Bridge of Spies tells the true story of the 1962 exchange, through the American lawyer who negotiated it.
A short radio report visits the abandoned listening station on Teufelsberg.
In a podcast episode, the director of the Allied Museum tells stories of espionage in the divided city.
And a historian at the Stasi Archives explains how the secret police worked, and how its files were saved.

chapters.heading: Radio across the Curtain
chapters.text: Not all Cold War spying was about stealing secrets. Some of it was about news. From 1951, Radio Free Europe, paid for by the American government, broadcast to Eastern Europe from a building on the edge of the English Garden, Munich’s large central park. Its sister station, Radio Liberty, broadcast to the Soviet Union from the same city. Communist governments jammed the signals and planted agents among the staff. In 1981 a bomb wrecked part of the Radio Free Europe building. It was later traced to a terrorist working for Romania’s secret police.

items: For a story from inside, there is a podcast episode in which a woman describes the day her husband, an editor at Radio Liberty, confessed that he had been spying for the KGB.

chapters.heading: Between the blocs
chapters.text: Between the two blocs sat Yugoslavia. Its leader, Josip Broz Tito, broke with Stalin in 1948 and refused to join either side, so both East and West courted him, and spied on him. That made Belgrade, the capital, a meeting ground. The café of the Hotel Moskva, a grand building from 1908 on Terazije, the city’s main square, was a favorite place for diplomats, journalists, and agents to watch one another. After Tito died in 1980, the country began to weaken, and the spying grew more urgent.
chapters.image: Hotel Moskva and the fountain in Belgrade.jpg

items: To hear how it worked, there is a podcast episode in which a former CIA officer describes meeting a Yugoslav source in Belgrade’s cafés and hotels.

chapters.heading: Reading your own file
chapters.text: Some secret police spied mostly on their own people. In Romania under Nicolae Ceaușescu, the Securitate built one of the largest networks of informers in the Eastern bloc, and ordinary people learned to watch what they said. Foreigners were watched too. Katherine Verdery, an American anthropologist, did research in Romania from the 1970s. Years after the regime fell in 1989, she read the file the Securitate had kept on her. In it she appears as a spy, and she found that some of her friends had been informing on her.

items: If you want to read it, her book describes the file, the informers, and what happened when she went back to meet them.

chapters.heading: Polonium in Mayfair
chapters.text: The Cold War ended, but the spying did not. Alexander Litvinenko was a former officer of the FSB, Russia’s security service, who had accused his superiors of corruption and fled to London in 2000. On November 1, 2006, he had lunch at a sushi bar on Piccadilly, then met two Russian men for tea at the Millennium Hotel in Mayfair. Within hours he was ill. Doctors found he had been poisoned with polonium-210, a rare radioactive element, and he died three weeks later. In 2016 a British public inquiry concluded that the killing had probably been approved by President Vladimir Putin.

items: To hear the story from people close to it, there is a short Witness History episode about the poisoning.

title: Cities under bombs
intro: In the Second World War, bombing cities became a strategy rather than an accident. Warsaw, London, Belfast, Naples, and Berlin all spent months or years under air raids, and the ruins shaped how they were rebuilt.
This thread visits cities that were bombed, from Warsaw in 1939 to Belgrade in 1999, and shows how they remember it.

chapters.heading: Warsaw
chapters.text: The war in Europe began with the bombing of cities. On September 1, 1939, Germany invaded Poland, and within days its planes and artillery were bombarding Warsaw. The city held out for nearly three weeks, without power or water, as fires spread. The Royal Castle, the home of Polish kings, was set ablaze. Warsaw surrendered on September 28. Worse was to come, because after the uprising of 1944 the Germans destroyed most of what was left. The castle was rebuilt from photographs and rescued fragments in the 1970s.

items: For the siege, there is a podcast episode about the three weeks in September 1939 when the city held out.

chapters.heading: The Blitz
chapters.text: From September 1940 to May 1941, German bombers attacked London on most nights. It became known as the Blitz. More than 40,000 people were killed across Britain, about half of them in London. Many Londoners sheltered at night on the platforms of Underground stations. The prime minister, Winston Churchill, and his government worked from a reinforced basement under government offices in Whitehall, now a museum called the Churchill War Rooms. The danger did not end with the Blitz. In March 1943, during an air-raid alert, 173 people were crushed to death on the stairs of Bethnal Green station, in the East End.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into London in the Blitz.
items: A video goes through the Churchill War Rooms, from the map room to the cabinet room.
The Splendid and the Vile, by Erik Larson, tells Churchill’s first year as prime minister through the Blitz.
Fires Were Started is a wartime film made with real firemen.
And a Witness History episode tells the story of the Bethnal Green disaster.

chapters.heading: The May Blitz
chapters.text: Liverpool was the main port for supplies coming from America, so it was bombed more heavily than any British city outside London. The worst week came at the start of May 1941, when German planes attacked every night. More than 1,700 people were killed, and thousands of homes were destroyed. St. Luke’s Church, at the top of Bold Street, was hit by a firebomb and burned out. It was left roofless as a memorial, and local people call it the bombed-out church.
chapters.image: St. Luke's Church "Bombed out Church", Liverpool - geograph.org.uk - 7378089.jpg

items: For more, there is a talk from the National Archives about how the government tracked the morale of Liverpool during the Blitz.

chapters.heading: Belfast
chapters.text: Belfast built ships and planes for the war, but its leaders thought it was too far away for German bombers to reach, and the city had almost no shelters. On the night of Easter Tuesday, April 15, 1941, about two hundred German bombers attacked, mostly hitting the crowded working-class streets in the north of the city. About 900 people died, the most killed in a single night anywhere in Britain outside London. Fire engines came from Dublin, across the border in neutral Ireland, to help.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the Belfast Blitz.
items: A podcast episode with Dan Snow tells how German bombers found a city with almost no shelters.
And These Days, a novel by Lucy Caldwell, follows two sisters through the raids.

chapters.heading: Naples
chapters.text: Naples, Italy’s main port in the south, was bombed by the Allies more than a hundred times between 1940 and 1943, and thousands of people were killed. Families sheltered in the ancient tunnels and cisterns under the city, dug by the Greeks and Romans, and some lived down there for weeks at a time. The actress Sophia Loren grew up in Pozzuoli, just west of the city, during the raids, and as a child she was cut by flying shrapnel. Allied troops entered the city in October 1943, after its people had driven out the Germans in four days of street fighting.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into wartime Naples.
items: A local guide leads a podcast host into the tunnels under the city.
And on Desert Island Discs, Sophia Loren talks about growing up under the bombs.

chapters.heading: A mistake
chapters.text: Some bombs fell by mistake. In March 1945 the Danish resistance asked the British to bomb the Gestapo’s headquarters in Copenhagen, where captured resistance members were held. The raid hit its target, and some prisoners escaped. But one of the low-flying planes hit a lamppost and crashed near the Institut Jeanne d’Arc, a Catholic school known as the French School. Later planes saw the smoke, took it for the target, and bombed the school. In the school, 86 children and 18 adults were killed.

items: For the story, there is The Bombardment, a Danish film about the raid, which is hard to watch.

chapters.heading: Rubble
chapters.text: Germany was bombed far more heavily than Britain. By 1945, Allied raids and the final battle for the city had left much of Berlin in ruins, and its people cleared the rubble by hand. Women known as Trümmerfrauen, rubble women, passed bricks from hand to hand to clean and reuse them. The broken tower of the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church, on the Kurfürstendamm, was kept as a reminder, beside a new church built in the 1960s. In 1947 the Italian director Roberto Rossellini filmed Germany Year Zero in the real ruins, following a boy trying to survive in the wrecked city.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Berlin in ruins.
items: A walking tour along the Kurfürstendamm starts and ends at the bombed church.
Germany Year Zero, Rossellini’s film, shows the real rubble of 1947.
And Berlin: The Downfall 1945, by Antony Beevor, tells the story of the last months of the war in the city.

chapters.heading: Belgrade
chapters.text: The last stop is more recent. In 1999 NATO bombed Yugoslavia for 78 days to force its government to stop its campaign against ethnic Albanians in Kosovo. In Belgrade, missiles hit the headquarters of the Yugoslav army, a pair of red stone buildings by the architect Nikola Dobrović on Kneza Miloša Street. They still stand there as ruins, while the city argues over what to do with them. On May 7, American bombs hit the Chinese embassy in New Belgrade, killing three people. NATO said it had used an out-of-date map.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two stories from the bombing of Belgrade.
items: A short radio report looks at the bombed army headquarters, and what might happen to it.
And a Witness History episode tells the story of the strike on the Chinese embassy.

title: Resistance
intro: Under Nazi rule, most people kept their heads down. Some wrote leaflets, hid their neighbors, forged papers, or took up guns.
This thread starts in Berlin itself and moves through occupied cities across Europe, ending in the summer and autumn of 1944.

chapters.heading: In the capital
chapters.text: Resistance began in Germany itself, though it was rare and dangerous. Otto and Elise Hampel were a working-class couple in Berlin. After Elise’s brother was killed in the war, they spent two years writing postcards against Hitler and leaving them in stairwells around the city. They were caught and beheaded in 1943. The novelist Hans Fallada turned their story into Alone in Berlin. That same year, the Gestapo arrested Jewish men married to non-Jewish women and held them in a building on Rosenstraße. Their wives gathered in the street outside, day after day, and most of the men were released.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three stories of resistance in Berlin.
items: Alone in Berlin, by Hans Fallada, is the novel based on the Hampels.
Rosenstraße, a German film, tells the story of the women’s protest, though historians dispute some of it.
And Aimée & Jaguar, by Erica Fischer, is the true story of a Jewish woman in hiding and the wife of a Nazi officer who fell in love.

chapters.heading: Hunger and the flag
chapters.text: Germany occupied Greece in April 1941. The occupiers took the country’s food for their own armies, and that winter tens of thousands of people starved in Athens. Defiance started early. On the night of May 30, 1941, two students, Manolis Glezos and Apostolos Santas, climbed the Acropolis and pulled down the swastika flag. Over the next three years the Greek resistance grew into one of the largest in Europe, and the occupiers answered with mass reprisals. On May 1, 1944, the Germans shot 200 prisoners at the firing range in Kaisariani, a refugee district on the edge of the city.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into occupied Athens.
items: Inside Hitler’s Greece, by Mark Mazower, is the clearest account of the occupation.
And a Witness History episode hears from a woman who lived through the famine.

chapters.place: Warsaw Zoo and the Arsenal, Warsaw
chapters.heading: The zoo and the scouts
chapters.text: In Warsaw, the resistance was organized on a huge scale, with an underground army, schools, and courts. Some people resisted by hiding others. Jan Żabiński, the director of the Warsaw Zoo, and his wife Antonina hid about 300 Jews during the war, in the empty animal enclosures and in their own villa inside the zoo. Others fought. In March 1943, scouts in the Home Army ambushed a Gestapo truck near the old Arsenal on Długa Street to free a captured friend, Jan Bytnar. They got him out, but he died a few days later from the torture he had suffered. The story was told in Stones for the Rampart, a book written in secret that same year.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two stories from wartime Warsaw.
items: The Zookeeper’s Wife, by Diane Ackerman, tells how the Żabińskis hid people at the zoo.
And Stones for the Rampart is a Polish film based on the book about the scouts and their raid.

chapters.heading: The White Rose
chapters.text: In Munich, a few students at the university, with one of their professors, formed a group called the White Rose. In 1942 and 1943 they wrote and printed leaflets calling on Germans to resist Hitler, and they mailed them to people across the country. On February 18, 1943, Hans Scholl and his sister Sophie carried a suitcase of leaflets into the university’s main building. They dropped the last of them from the floor above into the atrium. A caretaker saw them and called the Gestapo. They were tried four days later and beheaded the same afternoon. Sophie was 21.
chapters.tip: A memorial of bronze leaflets is set into the sidewalk outside the main university building.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the story of the White Rose.
items: Sophie Scholl: The Final Days, a German film, is built from the Gestapo’s transcripts of her interrogation.
And The White Rose, by their sister Inge Scholl, tells the story of the group.

chapters.heading: Flame and Citron
chapters.text: Denmark was occupied in 1940 with a light touch: the Danish government stayed in office, and life went on fairly normally. In August 1943, after strikes and sabotage, the government resigned, and the resistance grew. Two young members of the Holger Danske group, Bent Faurschou-Hviid and Jørgen Haagen Schmith, known as Flame and Citron, shot informers and collaborators in Copenhagen. Both were dead by October 1944, cornered by the Gestapo. Resistance fighters who were executed are buried at Mindelunden, a memorial park in Ryvangen, on the site where many of them were shot.

items: For their story, there is Flame & Citron, a Danish film about the two men that does not make it simple.

chapters.heading: Open city
chapters.text: Germany occupied Rome in September 1943, after Italy changed sides in the war. On March 23, 1944, Italian partisans set off a bomb against a column of German police marching along Via Rasella, killing 33 of them. The next day the Germans took 335 men and boys from the city’s prisons and streets, shot them in caves on the Via Ardeatina, and blew up the entrances. The site is now a memorial, the Fosse Ardeatine. Meanwhile, priests hid Jews and escaped prisoners of war in convents, monasteries, and buildings belonging to the Vatican. In 1945, months after the Germans left, Roberto Rossellini filmed Rome, Open City in the same streets.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into occupied Rome.
items: Death in Rome, by Robert Katz, reconstructs both days, hour by hour.
Rome, Open City, Rossellini’s film, was shot in the streets months after the Germans left.
And a Witness History episode tells how an Irish priest in the Vatican ran a secret rescue network.

chapters.heading: Hiding and fighting
chapters.text: In the Netherlands, many resisted by hiding people. Anne Frank, her family, and four others hid in rooms behind a bookcase at her father’s business on the Prinsengracht for two years, until they were betrayed in August 1944. Only her father survived. Others fought. The teenage sisters Truus and Freddie Oversteegen, with their friend Hannie Schaft, lured collaborators into the woods to be shot. The banker Walraven van Hall secretly funded the resistance with money taken from the Dutch central bank. In the last winter of the war, the Hunger Winter of 1944 and 1945, about 20,000 people died of starvation and cold.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four stories from the Dutch resistance.
items: A short podcast tells the story of Freddie Oversteegen.
The Resistance Banker is a Dutch film about Walraven van Hall.
Anne Frank Remembered, an Oscar-winning documentary, includes interviews with Miep Gies, who helped hide the family.
And a Witness History episode tells of surviving the Hunger Winter.

chapters.heading: Liberation
chapters.text: In August 1944, Allied armies were advancing across France toward Paris. On August 19 the resistance in the city rose. Fighters, many of them police officers, seized the Hôtel de Ville, the city hall, and put up barricades in the streets. The communist commander, Henri Rol-Tanguy, ran the uprising from an underground bunker beneath the Place Denfert-Rochereau. Hitler ordered that Paris should be destroyed rather than given up. The German commander, Dietrich von Choltitz, did not carry out the order, and on August 25 he surrendered the city intact to French troops.
chapters.image: Crowds of French patriots line the Champs Elysees-edit2.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the Liberation of Paris.
items: A Witness History episode tells the story of the fighters who took the Hôtel de Ville.
A short video visits the Liberation of Paris Museum and the bunker below it.
And a walking tour traces the occupation and the Resistance across the city.

chapters.heading: The last months
chapters.text: Hungary was Germany’s ally, but in March 1944 the Germans occupied it, and in a few weeks they deported more than 400,000 Hungarian Jews, most of them to Auschwitz. Hannah Szenes, a young poet born in Budapest, had moved to Palestine before the war. She joined a British mission, parachuted into Yugoslavia, and then crossed into Hungary. She was caught, tortured, and shot in November 1944, at 23. In Budapest, a young Jewish man, Pinchas Rosenbaum, put on the uniform of the Arrow Cross, the Hungarian fascists, and pulled people out of the lines being marched to their deaths. On the bank of the Danube, sixty pairs of iron shoes remember the people the Arrow Cross shot into the river.
chapters.image: Girl contemplates Shoes on the Danube Bank (Budapest, Hungary).jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two stories from Budapest in 1944.
items: A history podcast tells the story of Hannah Szenes.
And Walking with the Enemy is a film based on the story of Pinchas Rosenbaum.

image: Press used by the Dutch resistance (25671677677).jpg

title: Uprisings
intro: For forty-five years after the Second World War, people in Central and Eastern Europe kept trying to take their cities back. Most attempts were crushed within days or weeks. Each one was remembered, and in 1989 the anniversaries, the funerals, and the songs came back.
This thread runs from the Warsaw Uprising of 1944 to the fall of Ceaușescu in 1989. Each stop is a place you can still stand in.

chapters.heading: Warsaw rises
chapters.text: By the summer of 1944, the Red Army was pushing the Germans back across Poland, and it reached the outskirts of Warsaw. On August 1, the Polish Home Army, the underground army loyal to the government in exile in London, rose against the German occupiers. It hoped to free the city before the Soviets arrived. But the Red Army stopped on the far bank of the Vistula and waited. The fighting lasted 63 days. Up to 200,000 civilians were killed. When the Home Army surrendered, the Germans expelled the survivors and blew up most of what was left of the city. The Warsaw Rising Museum, in an old tram power station, tells the story.
chapters.image: Warsaw Uprising - Soldiers from Parasol on Warecka Street.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into the Uprising.
items: A Witness History episode hears from a former scout who carried messages during the fighting.
Rising ’44, by Norman Davies, is the full history of the battle.
Kanał, Andrzej Wajda’s film, follows a company escaping through the sewers as the Uprising collapses.
And “Godzina W,” by the rock band Lao Che, comes from a whole album about the Uprising.

chapters.heading: Builders strike in East Berlin
chapters.text: After the war, the Soviet Union set up communist governments across Eastern Europe, and the first uprising against one came in East Berlin. In June 1953 the East German government raised the amount of work required for the same pay. On June 16, construction workers building the grand new Stalinallee walked off the job in protest. The next day hundreds of thousands of people were on strike across the country, calling for free elections. In Berlin, crowds marched to the government offices near Potsdamer Platz. Soviet tanks put the uprising down, and dozens of people were killed.
chapters.image: Bundesarchiv B 145 Bild-F005191-0040, Berlin, Aufstand, sowjetischer Panzer.jpg

items: For more, there is a Witness History episode about the uprising of 1953.

chapters.heading: Budapest fights the tanks
chapters.text: Three years later it was Hungary’s turn. On October 23, 1956, students marched through Budapest calling for reforms, and by evening crowds had pulled down a giant statue of Stalin. Fighting broke out with the secret police and Soviet troops. Young fighters, many of them teenagers, held the Corvin Passage, a cinema courtyard, against Soviet tanks. A reforming communist, Imre Nagy, became prime minister and announced that Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact, the Soviet military alliance. On November 4 the Soviet army came back in force. About 2,500 Hungarians were killed, and 200,000 fled the country. Nagy was arrested and, in 1958, hanged.
chapters.image: 1956, Budapest, Üllői út - Ferenc körút, Kilián laktanya.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the revolution of 1956.
items: A podcast episode looks back at the uprising and why it mattered.
Children of Glory, a Hungarian film, tells it through the water polo team that played the Soviets at the Olympics that year.
And Journey to a Revolution, by Michael Korda, is a memoir by a student who drove medical supplies into Budapest.

chapters.heading: Students against the censors
chapters.text: In Poland in 1968, the trouble began in a theater. The National Theatre in Warsaw was staging Forefathers’ Eve, a play by Adam Mickiewicz, Poland’s great Romantic poet, which includes lines against Russian rule. Audiences cheered those lines, and the authorities closed the production. Students at the University of Warsaw protested, and police beat them at the university gate. The government blamed the protests on Zionists, and it followed with an antisemitic campaign that drove about 13,000 Polish Jews out of the country.

items: For more, there is a Witness History episode about the students who stood up to the censors.

chapters.heading: The end of the Prague Spring
chapters.text: That same year, in Czechoslovakia, the new communist leader, Alexander Dubček, promised “socialism with a human face”: less censorship, more debate, and more freedom to travel. People called it the Prague Spring. Moscow saw it as a threat. On the night of August 20, 1968, the armies of the Soviet Union and its allies invaded, and tanks filled Wenceslas Square. The reforms were rolled back. In January 1969, a student named Jan Palach set himself on fire at the top of Wenceslas Square in protest, and he died three days later. The singer Marta Kubišová recorded “Modlitba pro Martu,” A Prayer for Marta, which became an anthem of resistance. She was banned from performing for nearly twenty years.
chapters.image: 10 Soviet Invasion of Czechoslovakia - Flickr - The Central Intelligence Agency.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into 1968 in Prague.
items: A podcast episode hears from a journalist who saw the tanks arrive.
A recording of “Modlitba pro Martu” is the song that became the anthem.
Jan Palach, a Czech film, follows the last months of the student’s life.
And The Unbearable Lightness of Being, Milan Kundera’s novel, is set as the tanks crush the Prague Spring.

chapters.heading: A funeral, thirty-one years late
chapters.text: For years, the uprising of 1956 could not be mentioned in Hungary. Imre Nagy had been buried in an unmarked grave in a far corner of a Budapest cemetery. By 1989 the communist government was weakening, and it agreed to rebury him with honors. On June 16, 1989, the thirty-first anniversary of his execution, his coffin lay in state in Heroes’ Square, and about a quarter of a million people came. A young speaker named Viktor Orbán called for Soviet troops to leave the country. It was clear that the regime could no longer control what people said in public.

items: For more, there is a Witness History episode about the state funeral, thirty-one years late.

chapters.heading: The Wall opens
chapters.text: In East Germany, crowds marched in the streets through the autumn of 1989, and in October the longtime leader, Erich Honecker, was pushed out. On the evening of November 9, at a press conference, a Politburo spokesman, Günter Schabowski, announced new rules that would let East Germans travel. Asked when they took effect, he looked at his notes and said, “immediately.” He was wrong, but thousands of people went straight to the border crossings. At Bornholmer Straße, the guards could not get clear orders, and just before midnight they opened the gate. The Berlin Wall had fallen.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the end of East Germany.
items: A short video from Vox explains the small mistake that opened the Wall.
A Witness History episode tells the story of Honecker’s fall.
And Good Bye, Lenin!, a funny and sad film, follows a son who pretends East Germany still exists so the news won’t harm his sick mother.

chapters.heading: The Velvet Revolution
chapters.text: In Prague, the end came quickly. On November 17, 1989, police beat students who were marching on Národní, the avenue by the river. Within days, hundreds of thousands of people were filling Wenceslas Square every evening. The playwright Václav Havel, who had been jailed for years as a dissident, spoke to them from the balcony of the Melantrich building, a publishing house. Marta Kubišová, banned since 1970, stood up there beside him and sang. Within weeks the communist government had resigned, and by the end of December Havel was president. Because almost no one was hurt, it was called the Velvet Revolution.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the Velvet Revolution.
items: A podcast episode tells how a playwright came to address 300,000 people from a balcony.
The Magic Lantern, by Timothy Garton Ash, is an eyewitness account of the revolutions of 1989.
And Citizen Havel, a documentary filmed over thirteen years, follows Havel as president.

chapters.heading: Ceaușescu’s last speech
chapters.text: The last of the revolutions of 1989 was the bloodiest. In Romania, Nicolae Ceaușescu had ruled for twenty-four years, and the country was poor, hungry, and watched by the secret police. In December, protests broke out in the city of Timișoara, and the army fired on the crowds. On December 21, Ceaușescu spoke to a large rally he had organized in front of the Central Committee building in Bucharest. The crowd began to boo him, live on television, and he stood on the balcony looking confused. The next day he fled by helicopter. He and his wife, Elena, were caught, tried by a hasty military court, and shot on December 25. More than a thousand people were killed in the revolution.
chapters.image: PSL during the Romanian Revolution of 1989.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Romania’s revolution.
items: A documentary episode tells how Ceaușescu went from a leader courted by the West to a hated despot.
A podcast episode hears from a Reuters correspondent who reported from the streets.
And The Paper Will Be Blue, a Romanian film, follows one night of the revolution in real time.

image: Berlin 1989, Fall der Mauer, Chute du mur 10.jpg

intro: 1913 was the last full year of peace before the First World War. Europe looked richer and more modern than ever, and in many cities, artists and thinkers were tearing up the old rules.
This thread visits eight cities through that year. Most of the people in it had no idea what was coming.

chapters.heading: Strangers in Vienna
chapters.text: The year begins in Vienna, the capital of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. In January 1913, a young Georgian revolutionary arrived on a false passport, and spent a month writing an essay on nationalism. His name was Joseph Stalin. Another Russian revolutionary, Leon Trotsky, had been living in the city for years, and spent his evenings playing chess at the Café Central. Across town, a failed painter, Adolf Hitler, was living in a men’s hostel and selling watercolors of the sights. In his apartment at Berggasse 19, Sigmund Freud was seeing patients. None of them could have guessed what the others would become.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Vienna in 1913.
items: A walking tour follows Hitler’s years in Vienna, past the places he lived.
And Becoming Freud, by Adam Phillips, is a short book on how Freud became Freud.

chapters.heading: Freud and Jung
chapters.text: Freud’s closest ally had been a Swiss psychiatrist, Carl Jung, who made his name at the Burghölzli, the university psychiatric hospital in Zurich. Freud had seen Jung as his heir. But Jung doubted Freud’s view that sex lay behind almost everything in the mind. In January 1913, Freud wrote to Jung proposing that they end their personal relationship, and Jung agreed. The split left Jung shaken. Late that year he began a long, private descent into his own visions, which shaped his ideas for the rest of his life.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Jung’s break with Freud.
items: A podcast episode follows Jung’s work at the Burghölzli and his break with Freud.
And Memories, Dreams, Reflections is Jung’s own account of his inner life.

chapters.heading: The Futurists
chapters.text: In Milan, a group of artists wanted to tear up the past altogether. They called themselves the Futurists, and they loved speed, machines, and noise. In March 1913, one of them, the painter Luigi Russolo, published a manifesto called The Art of Noises, calling for music made from the sounds of factories and traffic. That same year, the sculptor Umberto Boccioni made a striding figure that seems to be dissolving into motion. A bronze cast of it is in the Museo del Novecento, by the cathedral, and it appears on Italy’s twenty-cent coin. The Futurists also loved war. When it came, Boccioni joined the army, and he died in 1916 after a fall from a horse.
chapters.image: Museo del 900 - Milan - Boccioni - Forme uniche della continuità nello spazio - Unique Forms of Continuity in Space.jpg

items: For more, there is a short video about the Futurist painters and their love of speed and the modern city.

chapters.heading: The Rite of Spring
chapters.text: In Paris, the most famous night of the year came in a brand-new theater. On May 29, 1913, the Ballets Russes, a Russian dance company, gave the first performance of The Rite of Spring at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées. Igor Stravinsky’s music was harsh and pounding, and the dancers stamped instead of floating. The audience began to jeer, others shouted back, and the noise nearly drowned out the orchestra. Later that year, in November, a writer called Marcel Proust paid to publish the first volume of a long novel, Swann’s Way. It became one of the great books of the century.

items: If you want to know Proust without reading three thousand pages, Edmund White’s short biography is the place to start.

chapters.heading: The suffragettes
chapters.text: In London, women had been campaigning for the vote for decades. The most militant of them, the suffragettes, smashed windows, set fire to empty buildings, and went on hunger strike in prison. In April 1913, the government passed a law allowing it to release hunger strikers and rearrest them once they recovered. It became known as the Cat and Mouse Act. On June 4, at the Derby horse race at Epsom, a suffragette called Emily Wilding Davison stepped onto the track and was struck by the king’s horse. She died four days later, and thousands marched at her funeral through London.
chapters.image: Epsom Downs, Home of the Derby - geograph.org.uk - 2224106.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the suffragettes.
items: Suffragette is a film about a laundry worker drawn into the militant campaign.
A short video from Vox shows how the suffragettes used spectacle.
And Rise Up, Women!, by Diane Atkinson, tells the story through the women themselves.

chapters.heading: The baths
chapters.text: Budapest, the empire’s second capital, was booming. In June 1913, it opened the Széchenyi Bath in the City Park, a palace of thermal pools fed by hot springs. It was one of the largest bathing complexes in Europe, and it is still full of people playing chess in the steaming water. The city had grown faster than almost any in Europe, with grand boulevards, cafés, and the first underground railway on the continent. The film Sunset follows a young woman through Budapest in that same year, a city of luxury with something dark beneath it.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Budapest in 1913.
items: A short video from Rick Steves visits the Széchenyi Bath.
And Sunset, by László Nemes, follows a young milliner through Budapest in 1913.

chapters.heading: The Lockout
chapters.text: Dublin showed the other side of the prosperous years. Its poor lived in tenements, old Georgian mansions divided into single rooms, with whole families in each. In August 1913, a union led by James Larkin called a strike on the city’s trams. Employers, led by the businessman William Martin Murphy, locked out workers who belonged to the union. At the height of the dispute, about twenty thousand were on strike or locked out. On August 31, police baton-charged a crowd on Sackville Street, now O’Connell Street. Days later, two tenement houses on Church Street collapsed, killing seven people. The Lockout dragged on until early 1914, and the workers went back defeated.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Dublin’s tenements.
items: Dublin Tenement Life is an oral history of people who grew up in these houses.
And a short video hears from former residents of Henrietta Street, where one house is now a museum.

chapters.heading: Street scenes
chapters.text: The year ends in Berlin, the fast-growing capital of the German Empire. The painter Ernst Ludwig Kirchner had moved there from Dresden, and in 1913 his group of artists, called Die Brücke, broke up. He began painting the city’s streets at night, with women in feathered hats walking among men in dark coats, in jagged lines and sickly colors. His Potsdamer Platz shows two women on a traffic island in the city’s busiest square. In June 1914, the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne was shot dead in Sarajevo. Within weeks, Europe was at war.

items: For a closer look, there is an episode of Inside the Masterpiece on Kirchner’s Potsdamer Platz.

intro: In 1968, protest moved across Europe in months, not years. Students in Warsaw and Paris, workers in France, reformers in Prague, and singers in Barcelona had different enemies, but they were watching each other.
The chapters follow the calendar, from a banned play in Warsaw in March to an album about Belfast in November.

chapters.heading: A banned play
chapters.text: The year began in a theater in Warsaw. In January the National Theatre was staging Forefathers’ Eve, a play by Adam Mickiewicz, Poland’s great Romantic poet, with lines against Russian rule that audiences cheered. The communist authorities closed it. In March, students at the University of Warsaw held a rally for free speech, and police and plainclothes militia beat them at the university gate. Protests spread to other cities. The government blamed Zionists, and it followed with an antisemitic campaign that drove about 13,000 Polish Jews out of the country.

items: For more, there is a Witness History episode about the students who stood up to the censors.

chapters.heading: Easter riots
chapters.text: In West Germany, students were angry about the Vietnam War, about former Nazis still in power, and about the newspapers of Axel Springer, which attacked them every day. On April 11 a young man shot Rudi Dutschke, the best-known student leader, on a Berlin street. Dutschke survived, though he never fully recovered. Students blamed the Springer press for stirring up hatred, and over the Easter weekend they blockaded its printing plants and offices across the country. In Munich, a photographer and a student were killed in the clashes. Schwabing, the city’s student and artists’ district, had just been the setting of the year’s comedy hit, Zur Sache, Schätzchen, about a lazy songwriter who drifts into trouble with the police.

items: For a lighter view of Schwabing that year, there is Zur Sache, Schätzchen, the film that defined the old bohemian quarter.

chapters.heading: Barricades in the Latin Quarter
chapters.text: In Paris, the protests began at the university. On May 3 police cleared students occupying the courtyard of the Sorbonne, in the Latin Quarter. The arrests brought out thousands more. On the night of May 10, students tore up the paving stones and built barricades across the streets, and riot police attacked them. Workers then joined in. By the end of the month, around ten million people were on strike, and France had come to a standstill. Slogans on the walls said things like “Be realistic, demand the impossible.” President Charles de Gaulle left the country briefly, came back, and called an election. In June his party won it easily.
chapters.image: Prenez vos désirs pour des réalités - 1968.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into May in Paris.
items: A podcast episode tells the story of the student revolt and the general strike.
The Dreamers, Bernardo Bertolucci’s film, follows three young film lovers in Paris as the revolt breaks out.
And “Il est cinq heures, Paris s’éveille,” a hit by Jacques Dutronc that year, is about the city waking up at dawn.

chapters.heading: Students against the “red bourgeoisie”
chapters.text: The protests even reached Yugoslavia, a communist country that was not part of the Soviet bloc. In June, students in Belgrade clashed with police and then occupied their university for a week. They complained about unemployment and about the privileges of the party officials they called the red bourgeoisie. The government expected trouble. Instead, the leader, Josip Broz Tito, went on television, said that the students were partly right, and promised reforms. The students cheered him, and the protest ended. Few of the reforms came.

chapters.heading: The tanks arrive
chapters.text: In Czechoslovakia, the change had come from the top. Since January the new communist leader, Alexander Dubček, had lifted censorship and allowed open debate, in what was called the Prague Spring. Moscow saw it as a threat. On the night of August 20, the armies of the Soviet Union and its allies invaded. In the morning, crowds on Wenceslas Square argued with the young Soviet soldiers on their tanks, many of whom did not know where they were. The singer Marta Kubišová recorded “Modlitba pro Martu,” A Prayer for Marta, which became the song of the occupation. The reforms were slowly rolled back.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into August in Prague.
items: A podcast episode hears from a journalist who saw the tanks arrive.
A recording of “Modlitba pro Martu” is the song of the occupation.
And Pelíšky, Cosy Dens, a much-loved Czech film, follows two families in one apartment block through the Prague Spring and the invasion.

chapters.heading: The stake
chapters.text: In Spain, Franco was still in power, and the Catalan language was restricted in schools, the press, and public life. In 1968 Lluís Llach, a young Catalan singer, wrote “L’Estaca,” The Stake. In the song, an old man explains that we are all tied to a rotten stake, and that if we all pull together, it will fall. Llach was often banned from performing, and his concerts became protests. The song traveled far beyond Barcelona. In Poland in 1978, a singer wrote new words for it, and as “Mury,” Walls, it became an anthem of the Solidarity movement.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “L’Estaca.”

chapters.heading: Astral Weeks
chapters.text: In Northern Ireland, 1968 was the year the civil rights movement began. Catholics marched for equal rights in housing, jobs, and voting, and in October police beat marchers in Derry. In Belfast, students at Queen’s University founded People’s Democracy. In November, Van Morrison, who had grown up on Hyndford Street in east Belfast, released Astral Weeks, an album of long, dreamy songs about the streets of his childhood. One of them is named after Cyprus Avenue, a leafy, well-off street nearby. Within a year the city had turned violent, and the Troubles had begun.

items: To hear it, there is a recording of “Cyprus Avenue,” from Astral Weeks.

title: Jewish quarters
intro: Jews have lived in European cities for more than two thousand years. In many of them, the Jewish quarter was where they were allowed, or required, to live, and its streets, synagogues, and cemeteries are among the oldest parts of town.
This thread goes roughly in the order the communities were founded, from Rome to Copenhagen. It includes the Holocaust, but it starts long before it, and in some cities it does not end with it.

chapters.heading: The oldest community
chapters.text: The oldest Jewish community in Europe is in Rome, where Jews have lived since the second century BC. In AD 70 a Roman army destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem, and the Arch of Titus, in the Forum, shows soldiers carrying off its great seven-branched candlestick, the menorah. For centuries Rome’s Jews lived freely near the river. In 1555 a pope ordered them walled into a small, crowded ghetto beside the Tiber, which was locked at night. It lasted until 1870, when Rome became part of united Italy. On October 16, 1943, German soldiers rounded up more than a thousand of the old quarter’s residents and deported them to Auschwitz. Sixteen came back. The quarter, with its great domed synagogue, is still the center of Jewish Rome.
chapters.tip: Restaurants along Via del Portico d’Ottavia serve carciofi alla giudia, whole artichokes fried twice.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Jewish Rome.
items: A short video walks through the old ghetto beside the ancient Portico of Octavia.
A podcast episode looks at the Arch of Titus, a monument to the destruction of the Temple.
A Witness History episode tells the story of the gold ransom and the raid of 1943.
And a food writer shows how carciofi alla giudia, the artichokes of the ghetto, are flattened and fried twice.

chapters.heading: Sepharad
chapters.text: In medieval Spain, Jews lived for centuries alongside Christians and Muslims, and the country had one of the largest Jewish populations in Europe. In Seville they lived in the judería, the Jewish quarter, now Santa Cruz, the maze of whitewashed lanes beside the cathedral. In 1391 a preacher stirred up riots against the Jews here, and the violence spread across Spain. Thousands were killed, and many more converted to save their lives. In 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella ordered every Jew who would not convert to leave the country. The exiles and their descendants, who spread across the Mediterranean and beyond, are called Sephardic Jews, from Sepharad, the Hebrew name for Spain. Today Santa Cruz is the most photographed quarter in Seville.

items: For a quick look, there is a short video walking through the lanes of the old Jewish quarter.

chapters.heading: The first ghetto
chapters.text: In Venice, Jews were allowed to live in the city from 1516, but only in one place. It was a small island in the district of Cannaregio, on the site of an old foundry, or getto in Venetian. Its gates were locked at night and guarded by Christian watchmen whom the Jews had to pay. The word ghetto spread from here to the rest of Europe. Jews from Germany, Italy, Spain, and the Ottoman lands lived side by side, each group with its own synagogue. With no room to spread out, the buildings grew upward, some of them seven stories high, taller than anywhere else in the city. Five synagogues survive, hidden on the upper floors of ordinary-looking houses.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the world’s first ghetto.
items: A video explains how the ghetto began, and why its buildings grew so tall.
A radio documentary marks the ghetto’s five hundredth anniversary with a visit to Cannaregio.
And The Merchant of Venice, Shakespeare’s play about the moneylender Shylock, is set in the city of the ghetto, though it never names it.

chapters.heading: A refuge
chapters.text: In Spain and Portugal, many Jews had been forced to convert, and the Inquisition watched to see whether they secretly kept their faith. From the 1590s some of them escaped to Amsterdam, where the Dutch Republic let them live and worship openly. They prospered as merchants. In 1675 they opened the Portuguese Synagogue, a vast, plain building that is still lit by hundreds of candles, with no electric light. The community was strict about its own beliefs. In 1656 it expelled one of its sons, the young philosopher Baruch Spinoza, for ideas about God that it considered dangerous. Spinoza went on to become one of the great thinkers of the Enlightenment.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Jewish Amsterdam.
items: Betraying Spinoza, by Rebecca Goldstein, is a warm, personal book about the philosopher and why he was cast out.
And a long walking tour of the old east side covers its maritime and Jewish history.

chapters.heading: The Old-New Synagogue
chapters.text: Prague has had a Jewish quarter since the Middle Ages. Its Old-New Synagogue, built around 1270, is the oldest synagogue in Europe still in use. A famous legend says that in the 1500s Rabbi Judah Loew made a giant out of clay, the Golem, to protect the community. Its body is said to lie in the synagogue’s attic still. Next door is the Old Jewish Cemetery. It had no room to expand, so new graves were laid on top of old ones, in some places twelve layers deep, and thousands of tombstones lean together among the trees. Around 1900 most of the old quarter was demolished and rebuilt with grand apartment blocks. On the walls of the Pinkas Synagogue are the names of nearly 80,000 Czech Jews murdered in the Holocaust.
chapters.image: Old New Synagogue- Jewish Town Hall (Prague).jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Prague’s Jewish quarter.
items: A short video visits its synagogues and the wall of names.
A podcast episode tells the legend of the Golem, and where it came from.
A longer film looks at the crowded old cemetery.
And a heritage walk takes in the cemetery and the oldest working synagogue in Europe.

chapters.heading: Kazimierz
chapters.text: In Kraków, King Casimir the Great founded Kazimierz as a separate town across the river in 1335. In 1495 Kraków’s Jews were moved there, and for more than four centuries it was one of the great centers of Jewish life in Poland, with synagogues, schools, and markets. When the Germans occupied Kraków in 1939, they forced the Jews out. In March 1941 they moved them across the Vistula into a walled ghetto in Podgórze, and in 1943 they cleared it. Most of its people were murdered. The businessman Oskar Schindler saved about 1,200 of his Jewish workers by keeping them at his factory. Since the 1990s Kazimierz has come back to life, with restored synagogues, cafés, and a festival of Jewish culture every summer.
chapters.image: Wolf Popper Synagogue, Entrance gate, 16 Szeroka street, Kazimierz, Kraków, Poland.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Jewish Kraków.
items: A short video visits the synagogues and courtyards of Kazimierz.
“Es brent,” It Is Burning, was written by Mordechai Gebirtig, a carpenter and poet of Kazimierz who was murdered in the ghetto.
A Witness History episode recalls the move into the ghetto in 1941.
And Schindler’s Ark, by Thomas Keneally, is the book behind Spielberg’s film.

chapters.heading: The largest community in Europe
chapters.text: Before the Second World War, Warsaw had the largest Jewish community in Europe, about a third of the city. The writer Isaac Bashevis Singer grew up on Krochmalna Street, a poor street of traders and workshops, where his father was a rabbi. Nearby, the doctor and children’s author Janusz Korczak ran an orphanage for Jewish children. In 1940 the Germans sealed more than 400,000 people into a ghetto. Inside, the historian Emanuel Ringelblum and a secret group collected documents about life there and buried them in milk cans and metal boxes. In 1942 most of the ghetto’s people were deported to the death camp at Treblinka. Korczak refused offers of rescue and went with his children. In April 1943 the last people in the ghetto rose up, and the Germans burned it street by street.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into the story of Jewish Warsaw.
items: In My Father’s Court is Singer’s memoir of his boyhood on Krochmalna Street.
The King of Children, by Betty Jean Lifton, is a biography of Janusz Korczak.
Who Will Write Our History is a documentary about Ringelblum’s secret archive.
And a Witness History episode tells the story of a ghetto fighter who led survivors out through the sewers.

chapters.heading: Europe’s largest synagogue
chapters.text: In Budapest, Jews played a large part in the city’s growth in the 1800s, and in 1859 they finished the Dohány Street Synagogue. It is the largest synagogue in Europe, with seats for nearly three thousand people. Theodor Herzl, the writer who imagined a Jewish state, was born next door in 1860. In 1944, near the end of the war, Germany occupied Hungary, and in a few weeks more than 400,000 Hungarian Jews were deported, most of them to Auschwitz. In Budapest, diplomats from neutral countries tried to save those who were left. Raoul Wallenberg, a Swedish diplomat, gave out thousands of protective passes and set up safe houses. In January 1945 he went to meet the Soviet army and disappeared.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Jewish Budapest.
items: A short video visits the synagogue and the memorial garden behind it.
A podcast episode tells how Theodor Herzl, born next door, founded modern Zionism.
A Witness History episode tells the story of Raoul Wallenberg.
And Fatelessness, by Imre Kertész, is a novel about a Budapest boy sent to Auschwitz, by a survivor who won the Nobel Prize.

chapters.heading: A family’s netsuke
chapters.text: In Vienna around 1900, many of the city’s bankers, doctors, writers, and composers came from Jewish families. One of them was the Ephrussi family, bankers who lived in a palace on the Ringstrasse. When Germany annexed Austria in 1938, the Nazis took everything. A collection of tiny Japanese carvings, called netsuke, survived because a maid, Anna, hid them in her mattress. The potter Edmund de Waal, a descendant of the family, followed the netsuke through five generations in his book The Hare with Amber Eyes. On Judenplatz, the square at the center of the medieval Jewish quarter, stands the city’s Holocaust memorial, by the artist Rachel Whiteread. It is a concrete library whose books face inward and can never be opened.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Jewish Vienna.
items: The Hare with Amber Eyes, by Edmund de Waal, follows his family’s netsuke from Paris to Vienna to Tokyo.
Still Alive, by Ruth Klüger, is the memoir of a Vienna girl who was deported as a child and survived.
And a long walking tour covers Jewish Vienna and the city’s part in the Holocaust.

chapters.heading: Across the Sound
chapters.text: The thread ends with a rescue. In October 1943, the German occupiers of Denmark planned to round up the country’s Jews, about 7,500 people. A German diplomat leaked the plan. Ordinary Danes, from doctors and students to fishermen, hid their Jewish neighbors and took them at night in small boats across the Øresund, the narrow strait to neutral Sweden. In a few weeks about 7,000 people escaped, and the great majority of Denmark’s Jews survived the war. The Danish Jewish Museum in Copenhagen tells the story.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the story of the rescue.
items: A Witness History episode tells how Jews escaped by boat from occupied Denmark to Sweden.
And Countrymen, by Bo Lidegaard, tells the story through the letters and diaries of the people involved.

image: Old Jewish Cemetery in Josefov, Prague - 8363.jpg

title: Exiles
intro: Europe’s cities have always taken in people who could not go home: poets thrown out by their rivals, revolutionaries waiting for their moment, and refugees from war. Some cities became waiting rooms, where people sat for months hoping for a visa or a ship.
This thread follows exiles from Dante, thrown out of Florence in 1302, to refugees arriving in Europe today.

chapters.heading: Dante
chapters.text: In the 1290s, Dante Alighieri, a poet, was also a politician in Florence.
