The city was split between two factions, and in 1302, while he was away on a mission to the pope, the other side took power. Dante was sentenced to exile and fined, and he was later condemned to be burned alive if he ever came back. He never did. For the rest of his life he moved between the courts of northern Italy. In exile he wrote the Divine Comedy, an epic journey through hell, purgatory, and heaven, and he put several of his enemies in hell. He died in Ravenna in 1321, and he is buried there. Florence has asked for his remains back ever since.

items: For his life, there is a short biography of the poet who wrote the greatest poem in Italian while in exile.

chapters.heading: Lenin, Joyce, and Dada
chapters.text: During the First World War, neutral Switzerland filled with refugees, draft dodgers, and revolutionaries. In 1916, on Spiegelgasse, a short street in Zurich’s old town, a group of artists and poets opened the Cabaret Voltaire. Disgusted by the war, they staged nonsense poems and noise, and they called the movement Dada. A few doors up the same street lived Vladimir Lenin, the exiled Russian revolutionary. Across town, James Joyce was writing Ulysses. In April 1917, after the tsar fell, the German government let Lenin cross Germany in a sealed train, hoping he would cause trouble in Russia. He did.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into wartime Zurich.
items: A short Witness History episode tells how war refugees invented Dada.
Lenin on the Train, by Catherine Merridale, tells the story of his journey like a thriller.
A podcast episode explains how the journey was arranged, and what it led to.
And Travesties, Tom Stoppard’s comedy, imagines Lenin, Joyce, and a Dada poet meeting in Zurich.

chapters.heading: A passport for the stateless
chapters.text: After the First World War and the Russian Revolution, millions of people in Europe were refugees, and many had lost their citizenship. Without a passport, they could not legally travel or work. Fridtjof Nansen, a Norwegian polar explorer famous for crossing Greenland on skis, became the League of Nations’ first High Commissioner for Refugees. In 1922 he created a travel document for stateless people, which became known as the Nansen passport. More than fifty countries recognized it, and it helped hundreds of thousands of people. That year he won the Nobel Peace Prize. His polar ship, the Fram, is now in a museum in Oslo.

items: For his story, there is a BBC discussion about the polar hero who became a champion of refugees.

chapters.heading: The exchange
chapters.text: In 1922 a Greek army that had invaded Anatolia was defeated by the Turkish nationalists, and Greek communities that had lived on that coast for thousands of years fled. In 1923 the two countries agreed to exchange their minorities, by religion rather than language. More than a million Orthodox Christians were sent to Greece, and several hundred thousand Muslims to Turkey. Athens was overwhelmed. The refugees built new districts on its edges and named them after the towns they had lost, such as Nea Smyrni, New Smyrna, and Nea Ionia.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the story of the exchange.
items: Twice a Stranger, by Bruce Clark, tells how the exchange uprooted people on both sides.
And “Vradiazei,” Night Falls, is sung by the great mournful voice of postwar Greece, who was born in Nea Ionia.

chapters.heading: Leaving Vienna
chapters.text: In March 1938 Germany annexed Austria, and within days Vienna’s Jews were being beaten in the streets, robbed, and forced out of their jobs. About two thirds of the city’s Jewish population, well over a hundred thousand people, managed to emigrate before the war closed the borders. Most had to leave almost everything behind. Maria Altmann, a young woman from a wealthy family, escaped with her husband to the United States. Their family’s property, including a gold portrait of her aunt Adele by Gustav Klimt, was taken. Decades later, she won the painting back from Austria.
chapters.image: Palacio Belvedere, Viena, Austria, 2020-02-01, DD 93-95 HDR.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two films about leaving and returning.
items: Woman in Gold, with Helen Mirren, tells Maria Altmann’s fight to recover the painting.
And Welcome in Vienna, by Axel Corti, follows two émigrés who come back as American soldiers in 1945.

chapters.heading: Marseille
chapters.text: When France fell to Germany in 1940, the north was occupied, and refugees from all over Europe fled south to Marseille, hoping to find a ship. They needed visas, exit permits, and transit papers, and they waited for months. Varian Fry, an American journalist, came to the city that summer with a list of artists and intellectuals in danger. Working from a hotel and then a small office, he helped about 2,000 people escape, among them the painter Marc Chagall, the philosopher Hannah Arendt, and the poet André Breton. The novelist Anna Seghers, herself one of the refugees, turned the endless waiting into a novel, Transit.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Marseille in 1940.
items: A podcast episode tells how Varian Fry smuggled Europe’s artists past the Nazis.
Surrender on Demand is Fry’s own account of those months.
Transit, by Anna Seghers, is a hypnotic novel about the waiting.
And Christian Petzold’s film Transit sets her story in the present day.

chapters.heading: The last port
chapters.text: For refugees who made it across the Pyrenees and through Spain, the last stop was Lisbon. Portugal was neutral, and ships still sailed from its harbor to New York and South America. Tens of thousands of people waited in the city for a visa or a place on a ship, sometimes for months. They filled the cafés around the Rossio, the old central square. Many of them had got this far thanks to Aristides de Sousa Mendes, the Portuguese consul in Bordeaux, who issued thousands of visas against his government’s orders in June 1940. He was punished for it and died poor.
chapters.image: Westward view from the south end of Rossio, Lisbon, 2010.jpg

items: For the whole story, there is a book about neutral Lisbon in the war, full of refugees, spies, and smugglers.

chapters.heading: Brodsky’s winters
chapters.text: Exile did not end with the war. Joseph Brodsky, a young poet from Leningrad, was put on trial in 1964 for “social parasitism,” because the state did not consider poetry a job. In 1972 the Soviet Union expelled him. He settled in the United States, and in 1987 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature. For seventeen years he spent most winters in Venice, a city that reminded him of his own, and he wrote a short book about it, Watermark. He died in 1996, and he is buried on San Michele, the cemetery island in the lagoon.

items: If you want to read it, Watermark is a short book about Venice in winter: fog, water, and light.

chapters.heading: Arriving now
chapters.text: The latest exiles are arriving now. The war in Syria, which began in 2011, drove millions of people from their homes. In 2015 and 2016, more than a million people came to Europe seeking safety, many of them on foot. One of them, the Syrian filmmaker Thaeer Muhreez, arrived at Amsterdam’s Centraal Station in 2016 after a long journey across the continent. In Paris, the Agency of Artists in Exile gives artists who have fled their countries a place to work, tools, and a community.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two stories of arriving.
items: A podcast episode follows a Syrian filmmaker building a new life in the Netherlands.
And a short video visits the Paris agency that helps exiled artists keep working.

title: The Atlantic slave trade
intro: For four centuries, European ships carried about 12.5 million Africans across the Atlantic to forced labor in the Americas. The trade was run from Europe’s ports, and the money built warehouses, banks, town halls, and country houses that are still standing.
This thread visits six of those cities, from Lisbon, where it began, to Glasgow. Each has started, at different speeds, to say so in public.

chapters.heading: Where it started
chapters.text: The trade began with Portugal. In the 1440s Portuguese ships sailing down the west coast of Africa began taking captives and bringing them back to sell in Lisbon and other towns. Within a century the trade had crossed the Atlantic. Portugal went on to carry more Africans to the Americas than any other country, most of them to work on the sugar plantations of Brazil. The trade was run by the crown from the waterfront in Lisbon, near today’s Praça do Comércio. In the 1500s about one in ten people in Lisbon was Black. Portugal banned its slave trade in 1836, though slavery in Brazil went on until 1888.
chapters.image: Blue facades of waterfront buildings at Ribeira das Naus in Lisbon, Portugal, 20250604 2033 9639.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two short videos about Lisbon and the trade.
items: One explains the human cost of Portugal’s trading empire.
And the other looks at Afro-Portuguese culture in the city today.

chapters.heading: The Dutch West India Company
chapters.text: In the 1600s the Dutch joined in. The Dutch West India Company, founded in 1621, took forts on the Gold Coast of West Africa, in what is now Ghana. From there it shipped captives to Dutch colonies in the Caribbean and South America, among them Suriname. The profits flowed back to Amsterdam, the same city that was celebrating its Golden Age. The Netherlands abolished slavery in its colonies only in 1863, one of the last countries in Western Europe to do so. Even then, the freed people had to keep working on the plantations for another ten years. In 1934 Anton de Kom, a writer from Suriname, published We Slaves of Suriname, the first history of the colony told from the side of the enslaved. In 2023 the Dutch king apologized for his country’s part in slavery.

items: If you want to read it, We Slaves of Suriname was banned, then forgotten, and then became a bestseller in the Netherlands nearly ninety years after it was written.

chapters.heading: Denmark’s islands
chapters.text: Denmark, too, had colonies in the Caribbean: the islands of St. Thomas, St. John, and St. Croix, now the US Virgin Islands. It bought captives at its forts on the Gold Coast and shipped them across the Atlantic to work on sugar plantations. The sugar and rum came back to warehouses in Copenhagen, such as the large West Indian Warehouse on the harbor, built in 1781. In 1792 Denmark became the first country to pass a law banning the slave trade, though it took effect only in 1803. Slavery itself continued on the islands until 1848, when the enslaved people of St. Croix rose up and forced the governor to free them.

items: For more, there is a podcast episode about how Denmark and Norway ran forts in Ghana and plantations in the Caribbean.

chapters.heading: The capital of the trade
chapters.text: London was where much of the British trade was organized. From 1672 the Royal African Company, backed by the king, held a monopoly on the English trade with West Africa, including the trade in people. Even after the monopoly ended, the City of London financed the voyages, insured the ships, and invested the profits. Black Londoners, some free and some enslaved, lived in the city throughout. Among the objects in the British Museum is a drum made by the Akan people of West Africa, which was carried to Virginia on a slave ship in the 1700s. Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807, and slavery in most of its colonies in 1833. The slave owners were paid compensation. The enslaved were paid nothing.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into this history.
items: A short radio episode looks at the Akan drum, and what it carries of the trade.
And Black and British, by David Olusoga, shows how far back Black British history goes.

chapters.heading: The biggest slaving port
chapters.text: By the end of the 1700s, Liverpool had become the biggest slaving port in Europe. Its ships carried goods to West Africa, captives across the Atlantic, and sugar, cotton, and tobacco back home, a route often called the triangular trade. Liverpool ships carried well over a million Africans. The money paid for docks, the Town Hall, and merchants’ houses, and many streets are named after slave traders. In 2007, the two hundredth anniversary of the abolition of the British trade, the International Slavery Museum opened at the Royal Albert Dock, close to where slaving ships were once fitted out.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Liverpool’s past.
items: A short video introduces the International Slavery Museum.
A podcast episode looks at how the city has come to remember the trade that built its wealth.
A walking tour visits the buildings and street names that still carry those ties.
And The Slave Ship, by Marcus Rediker, tells the human history of the ships themselves.

chapters.heading: Tobacco and sugar
chapters.text: In Glasgow, the money came from what enslaved people grew. In the 1700s the city’s merchants dominated Britain’s trade in tobacco from Virginia, and later its trade in sugar and cotton from the Caribbean. The richest of them were known as the tobacco lords. They built mansions and warehouses in what is now called the Merchant City, east of the center, and streets there are still named Virginia Street and Jamaica Street. One of their mansions is now the city’s Gallery of Modern Art. In recent years Glasgow has begun to study and acknowledge these links openly.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the story.
items: It Wisnae Us, by Stephen Mullen, is a short guide to how slavery paid for the city center.
And a walking tour of the Merchant City covers the trade, and the city’s part in abolition.

title: Queer Europe
intro: For most of the 20th century, gay men in much of Europe could be jailed for their relationships, and queer life went on in bars, magazines, and private clubs. In 1989 Denmark became the first country to recognize same-sex couples, and in 2015 Ireland voted for same-sex marriage.
This thread follows that change through the places where it happened, from Berlin in the 1920s to Dublin in 2015.

chapters.heading: Weimar Berlin
chapters.text: In the 1920s, after the First World War, Berlin became one of the freest cities in Europe. Sex between men was still illegal in Germany, but the law was loosely enforced, and the streets around Nollendorfplatz, a square in Schöneberg, were full of gay and lesbian bars and clubs. The doctor Magnus Hirschfeld ran an Institute for Sexual Science, which studied sexuality and campaigned for equal rights. The English writer Christopher Isherwood lodged nearby, and he wrote stories about the city that later became the musical Cabaret. In May 1933, months after the Nazis took power, students ransacked Hirschfeld’s institute and burned its library in public. The Nazis went on to send thousands of gay men to concentration camps.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into queer Weimar Berlin.
items: A comedy history podcast looks at queer life in the city in the 1920s.
Goodbye to Berlin is Isherwood’s book of stories, the source of Cabaret.
Cabaret, with Liza Minnelli, sets the songs against the rise of the Nazis.
And a design podcast explains how Hirschfeld’s institute became the first target of the Nazi book burnings.

chapters.heading: Sent away
chapters.text: In Fascist Italy, homosexuality was not made a crime, because the regime preferred to pretend it did not exist. Instead the police sent gay men into internal exile, called confino, on remote islands and in mountain villages. Ettore Scola’s 1977 film A Special Day takes place on the day of a great parade for Hitler’s visit to Rome in May 1938. While the rest of their apartment block goes to the parade, a lonely housewife, played by Sophia Loren, meets a neighbor, played by Marcello Mastroianni. He is a radio announcer who has lost his job for being gay and is about to be sent away.

items: To see it, A Special Day is a quiet and moving film set in one apartment block.

chapters.heading: Der Kreis
chapters.text: Switzerland legalized sex between adult men in 1942, during the Second World War, and Zurich became a place where gay men could meet, carefully. A club and magazine called Der Kreis, The Circle, held discreet dances in the old town and published its magazine in German, French, and English. It had readers all over Europe and America. In the late 1950s, after several murders of gay men, the police cracked down, and the club finally broke up in 1967.

items: For the story, there is Der Kreis, a Swiss docudrama about the club, a love affair, and the crackdown that broke it up.

chapters.heading: Alan Turing
chapters.text: In Britain, sex between men was a crime until 1967, and men were regularly prosecuted. One of them was Alan Turing, the mathematician who had helped break German codes at Bletchley Park during the war. Afterward he worked on one of the first computers at the University of Manchester. In 1952 he reported a burglary at his house, told the police about his relationship with a young man, and was convicted of gross indecency. To avoid prison, he was made to take hormone treatment. He died in 1954, at 41. In 2009 the British government apologized, and in 2013 he received a royal pardon. A statue of him sits on a bench in Sackville Gardens, in Manchester’s gay village.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into his life.
items: A BBC discussion looks at Turing’s work and his prosecution.
And Alan Turing: The Enigma, by Andrew Hodges, is the definitive biography.

chapters.heading: Tom of Finland
chapters.text: In Finland, homosexuality was illegal until 1971. Touko Laaksonen had fought in the Second World War and then worked in advertising in Helsinki. In private he drew muscular, cheerful gay men in leather and uniforms. In 1957 an American magazine began publishing his drawings under the name Tom of Finland, and they became famous among gay men around the world. At home he stayed almost unknown for decades. In 2014 Finland put his drawings on a set of postage stamps.
chapters.image: Statue of Johan Ludvig Runeberg on Esplanadi in Helsinki, Finland.jpg

items: For his story, there is Tom of Finland, a Finnish film about his life.

chapters.heading: Pride
chapters.text: In 1984 Britain’s coal miners went on strike against pit closures, and the strike lasted a year. A group of gay and lesbian activists in London, who had been harassed by the police themselves, decided to support them. They called themselves Lesbians and Gays Support the Miners. They met at Gay’s the Word, a bookshop in Bloomsbury, and raised money for a mining community in South Wales. The miners were wary at first, and then they became friends. In 1985 miners from Wales marched at the front of London’s Pride parade.
chapters.image: Gay's the Word, London, Bloomsbury, WC1 b.jpg

items: For the full story, there is Pride, a warm and funny film about the activists and the village.

chapters.heading: After Franco
chapters.text: In Spain, the Franco dictatorship treated gay people as criminals and dangers to society. Franco died in 1975, and in 1979 homosexuality was removed from the law used to persecute it. In the 1980s Madrid exploded with music, film, and nightlife in what was called the Movida. The singer Alaska’s 1986 song “A quién le importa,” Who Cares, became an anthem of being yourself. Chueca, a run-down neighborhood in the center, grew into the city’s gay district. In 2005 Spain became one of the first countries in the world to allow same-sex marriage.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Madrid after Franco.
items: “A quién le importa,” by Alaska, is the anthem of the Movida.
And an architecture walk through Salamanca and Chueca traces how the districts grew.

chapters.heading: The first partnerships
chapters.text: On October 1, 1989, Denmark became the first country in the world to let same-sex couples register their partnership, with most of the rights of marriage. Eleven couples signed at Copenhagen City Hall that day. Among them were Axel and Eigil Axgil, who had founded Denmark’s first gay rights organization forty years before. Denmark went on to allow full marriage in 2012.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two stories from that day.
items: A short video shows the couples signing at City Hall.
And a Witness History episode tells the story of two of the first couples, Ivan Larsen and Ove Carlsen.

chapters.heading: The vote
chapters.text: In Ireland, sex between men was illegal until 1993. The law was finally changed after a long campaign by David Norris, a lecturer at Trinity College, who took his case to the European Court of Human Rights and won. Twenty-two years later, in May 2015, Ireland held a referendum on same-sex marriage. It became the first country to allow it by popular vote, and 62 percent voted yes. Crowds gathered in the courtyard of Dublin Castle to watch the results come in.
chapters.image: Dublin Castle Upper Castle Yard Panorama 01.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into queer Dublin.
items: A podcast tells the story of the referendum and the day the results came in.
And a tour of Kilmainham Gaol, the old city jail, looks for the queer lives behind its walls.

title: Assassinations
intro: Political killings tend to happen in ordinary places: a theater, a church during Mass, a shopping street, a car at a red light. Several of the spots are marked, and a few are still just street corners.
This thread runs from the death of Julius Caesar in 44 BC to a street in Amsterdam in 2004. Some of these killings changed what happened next, and some changed very little.

chapters.heading: Caesar
chapters.text: On the Ides of March, March 15, 44 BC, a group of senators stabbed Julius Caesar to death at a meeting of the Senate. It was held in a hall attached to the Theater of Pompey, in the center of Rome. Caesar had won a civil war and made himself dictator for life, and the conspirators, led by Brutus and Cassius, said they were saving the Republic. Instead, his death led to more civil war and to the rule of his adopted son, who became Augustus, the first emperor. The site is now Largo di Torre Argentina, a sunken square of ancient temples, where volunteers run a shelter for the city’s stray cats.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the death of Caesar.
items: A short video visits the square, and the cats that live in the ruins.
And Rubicon, by Tom Holland, tells how the Roman Republic destroyed itself.

chapters.heading: The Pazzi conspiracy
chapters.text: In Florence, the most famous killing took place in the cathedral. On Sunday, April 26, 1478, during Mass, men hired by the Pazzi, a rival banking family, attacked the two Medici brothers who ruled the city. Giuliano de’ Medici was stabbed to death in front of the altar. His brother Lorenzo, later called the Magnificent, was wounded but escaped into the sacristy. The people of Florence sided with the Medici and hunted down the conspirators within days, and some were hanged from the windows of the town hall. Sixty years later, in 1537, another Medici, Lorenzino, lured his cousin Alessandro, the first duke of Florence, to an apartment and stabbed him.
chapters.image: Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence Cathedral, interior, 223756.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two Medici murders, sixty years apart.
items: A podcast episode tells the story of the attack during Mass.
And another tells how Lorenzino lured the duke to his death.

chapters.heading: Mary’s court
chapters.text: In Edinburgh, the court of Mary, Queen of Scots, saw two murders in less than a year. In March 1566 a group of Protestant lords, with Mary’s husband, Lord Darnley, among them, burst into her supper room at the Palace of Holyroodhouse. They dragged out her Italian secretary, David Rizzio, and stabbed him dozens of times. Mary was six months pregnant. In February 1567 the house where Darnley was staying blew up, and he was found strangled in the garden. Mary married the Earl of Bothwell, the man most suspected of the murder, and within months she had lost her throne.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the murders at Mary’s court.
items: A short video from the Royal Collection tells the story of the murder in her supper room.
And a podcast episode looks at Darnley’s murder and how it led to her downfall.

chapters.heading: A masked ball
chapters.text: In Stockholm, King Gustav III loved the theater, and he built the city’s royal opera house. He had also taken power from the nobles, and some of them wanted him dead. On March 16, 1792, he went to a masked ball at his opera house, although he had received a letter warning him of a plot. A group of masked nobles surrounded him, and one of them, Jacob Johan Anckarström, shot him in the back. The king died two weeks later. Verdi later turned the story into the opera A Masked Ball.
chapters.image: Kungliga Operan Royal Swedish Opera Stockholm 2016 01.jpg

items: For the whole story, there is a short podcast episode about the king who went to the ball despite the warning.

chapters.heading: The regicide
chapters.text: In Portugal, the monarchy was unpopular by the early 1900s, and republicans wanted it gone. On February 1, 1908, King Carlos I and his family were driving through Lisbon in an open carriage, back from a stay in the country. As the carriage turned out of the Praça do Comércio, the great square by the river, two gunmen opened fire. The king and his heir, Prince Luís Filipe, were killed. The younger son, Manuel, was wounded, and he became king. Two years later, in 1910, a revolution ended the monarchy, and Portugal became a republic.

items: For the story, there is a podcast episode about the regicide and how it led to the end of the monarchy.

chapters.place: Church of Sts Cyril and Methodius, Prague
chapters.heading: Heydrich
chapters.text: During the Second World War, Reinhard Heydrich, one of the chief organizers of the Holocaust, ruled the occupied Czech lands from Prague Castle. The Czechoslovak government in exile in London trained a team of parachutists to kill him. On May 27, 1942, two of them, Jozef Gabčík and Jan Kubiš, ambushed his car at a sharp bend in a Prague street. Gabčík’s gun jammed, but Kubiš threw a bomb, and Heydrich died of his wounds a week later. The Nazis took terrible revenge. They destroyed the villages of Lidice and Ležáky and killed their people. The parachutists hid in the crypt of the Church of Saints Cyril and Methodius, where they were betrayed and died fighting in June.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the story of the parachutists.
items: A podcast episode tells the story of the operation and its aftermath.
HHhH, by Laurent Binet, is a novel about the killing, by a writer who agonizes over how to tell it.
And Anthropoid, a film shot in Prague, follows the parachutists to their last stand in the crypt.

chapters.heading: Carrero Blanco
chapters.text: In Spain, General Franco was old by the 1970s, and he had chosen his closest ally, Admiral Luis Carrero Blanco, as prime minister to carry on his regime. On December 20, 1973, Carrero Blanco was driving home from daily Mass in Madrid. Members of ETA, the armed Basque separatist group, had dug a tunnel under Calle Claudio Coello and packed it with explosives. The blast threw his car over the roof of a five-story building, and it landed in an inner courtyard. He was killed. Franco died two years later, and Spain moved to democracy.

items: For the story, there is a Witness History episode about the assassination.

chapters.heading: Palme and Lindh
chapters.text: Sweden thought of itself as a safe, open country, where leaders could walk the streets. On the night of February 28, 1986, the prime minister, Olof Palme, sent his bodyguards home and went to the cinema with his wife. As they walked home along Sveavägen, the main street, a gunman shot him in the back. He died there on the sidewalk. A man was convicted and then acquitted, and in 2020 prosecutors named a different suspect, who had died years before. In 2003 the foreign minister, Anna Lindh, was stabbed while shopping in a department store a short walk away, days before a national vote on the euro. She died the next day.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the two killings.
items: A long read tells the story of the Palme case and the decades of investigation.
Palme, a documentary, looks at the life of the prime minister, loved and loathed.
And a Witness History episode tells the story of Anna Lindh’s death.

chapters.heading: Đinđić
chapters.text: In Serbia, Zoran Đinđić became prime minister after the fall of Slobodan Milošević in 2000. In 2001 he sent Milošević to the war crimes tribunal in The Hague. He also began to go after the gangsters and paramilitaries who had grown rich in the wars of the 1990s. On March 12, 2003, a sniper shot him as he got out of his car outside the government building on Nemanjina Street. The killers came from a special police unit with close ties to organized crime.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into his killing.
items: McMafia, by Misha Glenny, has a sharp chapter on Belgrade’s gangsters and the murder.
And a Witness History episode hears from people who were there.

chapters.heading: Theo van Gogh
chapters.text: The last stop is in Amsterdam. Theo van Gogh was a filmmaker and columnist who liked to provoke, and he was distantly related to the painter Vincent van Gogh. In 2004 he made Submission, a short film about the treatment of women in Islam, with the politician Ayaan Hirsi Ali. On the morning of November 2, 2004, as he cycled to work, a young Islamist shot and stabbed him on a street near the Oosterpark. The killing shocked a country that had seen itself as a model of tolerance. A jagged steel sculpture called The Scream stands in the park in his memory.

items: For more, there is Murder in Amsterdam, by Ian Buruma, which asks what the killing cost the Dutch idea of tolerance.

image: Vincenzo Camuccini - La morte di Cesare.jpg

title: Heretics and witches
intro: For four centuries, believing the wrong thing could get you burned. Catholic and Protestant churches, and the states behind them, tried and killed reformers, scientists, women accused of witchcraft, and people who read the wrong books.
This thread follows it from the burning of Jan Hus in 1415 to the end of the Spanish Inquisition in 1834.

chapters.heading: Jan Hus
chapters.text: In the early 1400s, Jan Hus, a priest and teacher at the university in Prague, preached at the Bethlehem Chapel in Czech, the language of ordinary people, not in Latin. He attacked the wealth and corruption of the Church. In 1414 he was summoned to a great council of the Church at Constance, in Germany, and promised safe conduct by the emperor. Once he arrived, he was arrested and tried. He refused to take back his views, and in July 1415 he was burned at the stake. His followers, the Hussites, rose up and fought off five crusades sent against them. A huge monument to Hus stands in the Old Town Square.

items: For his story, there is a podcast episode about Jan Hus and the wars that followed his death.

chapters.heading: The Inquisition begins
chapters.text: In Spain, Ferdinand and Isabella set up the Spanish Inquisition in 1478, and it held its first auto-da-fé, a public ceremony of judgment, in Seville in 1481. Six people were burned. Its first targets were converts from Judaism suspected of secretly keeping their old faith. For three centuries its headquarters in Seville was the Castillo de San Jorge, a castle by the river in Triana. Later it turned on Protestants. Around 1560 it burned a group of monks from a monastery near Seville who had been reading Lutheran books and translating the Bible into Spanish. The ruins of the castle are now a small museum under the Triana market.
chapters.tip: The castle’s ruins are now a small museum under the Triana market.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the Inquisition’s early years.
items: The Spanish Inquisition, by Henry Kamen, looks past the legend at how it really worked.
And a five-minute podcast tells the story of the monks who translated a forbidden Bible.

chapters.heading: Savonarola
chapters.text: In Florence in the 1490s, a Dominican friar, Girolamo Savonarola, preached against luxury, corruption, and the Medici. When the Medici were driven out in 1494, he became the most powerful man in the city. In February 1497 his followers went from house to house collecting mirrors, playing cards, cosmetics, fine clothes, books, and paintings. They burned them all in a great bonfire in the Piazza della Signoria, the Bonfire of the Vanities. The pope excommunicated him, and Florence turned against him. In May 1498 he was tortured, hanged, and burned in the same square. A round plaque in the paving marks the spot.
chapters.image: Savonarola's execution memorial, Piazza della Signoria, Florence (26073214863).jpg

items: For more, there is a podcast episode about the friar and his bonfire.

chapters.heading: Veronica Franco
chapters.text: In Venice, the city’s government kept the Inquisition on a short leash. Veronica Franco was one of the city’s best-known courtesans, a woman paid for her company by rich and powerful men, and she was also a published poet. In 1580 she was brought before the Inquisition on a charge of witchcraft, made by her son’s tutor. She defended herself with confidence, and she was acquitted, probably helped by her friends among the city’s nobility.

items: To see her story, there is Dangerous Beauty, a glossy film about her life.

chapters.heading: Scotland’s witch trials
chapters.text: In Scotland, the fear of witches became a panic. In 1590 King James VI sailed home from Denmark with his new bride, and storms nearly sank his ship. He blamed witches, and dozens of people from North Berwick, a town east of Edinburgh, were tortured until they confessed. James later wrote a book about witchcraft. Over the next century and more, Scotland tried several thousand people for witchcraft, most of them women. Hundreds of the accused were strangled and then burned on Castlehill, at the top of the Royal Mile, by the castle. A small fountain there, the Witches’ Well, remembers them. In 2022 the Scottish government formally apologized.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two walks that cover the witch trials.
items: One follows Scotland’s witch trials and the women persecuted in them, from Holyrood Palace to the castle.
The other walks the full Royal Mile, starting at the Witches’ Well on the castle esplanade.

chapters.heading: Giordano Bruno
chapters.text: In Rome, the Inquisition put a former friar, Giordano Bruno, on trial. Bruno argued that the universe was infinite, that the stars were other suns, and that they might have planets with life of their own. He also held views about God that the Church considered heretical. He was tried for eight years and refused to take back his ideas. On February 17, 1600, he was burned alive in the Campo de’ Fiori, a market square near the river. In 1889 a hooded bronze statue of him was put up on the spot, facing toward the Vatican. The market still runs around it every morning.
chapters.image: Statue of Giordano Bruno, Campo de' Fiori (45788557464).jpg

items: For more, there is a podcast episode about the friar who burned for insisting the universe has no edge.

chapters.heading: Galileo
chapters.text: Galileo Galilei was luckier. With his telescope, he found evidence that the Earth goes around the sun, and he said so in a book in 1632. The next year the Inquisition in Rome found him vehemently suspected of heresy. He was made to kneel and take back his views, and the book was banned. He was not burned. He spent the last nine years of his life under house arrest in a villa at Arcetri, in the hills above Florence. He went blind there, but he kept working and wrote one of his most important books on physics. He died in 1642.

items: For his last years, there is a podcast episode about the condemned astronomer who kept working under house arrest.

chapters.place: Plaza Mayor and the Prado, Madrid
chapters.heading: The last trials
chapters.text: The grandest auto-da-fé of all was held in Madrid’s Plaza Mayor in 1680, before the young King Charles II, and it lasted from morning until late at night. More than a hundred people were sentenced, and some were burned afterward outside the city. By the time of the painter Francisco Goya, a century later, the Inquisition was weaker, but it was still dangerous. Goya was questioned about his painting of a nude woman, the Naked Maja. Napoleon abolished the Inquisition when he invaded Spain in 1808. The Spanish king brought it back after the French left, and it was finally ended in 1834.

items: To see Goya’s Madrid, there is Goya’s Ghosts, a costume drama by Miloš Forman about the painter and the Inquisition, though it is uneven.

image: Pedro Berruguete - Saint Dominic Presiding over an Auto-da-fe (detail) - c. 1491-1499 - 02.jpg

title: Heists
intro: Some of the most famous objects in Europe are famous partly because someone took them. Others are still being argued over, two centuries after they were removed.
This thread runs from the Parthenon in Athens to a jewelry vault in London. The thieves range from a British ambassador and the Nazi leadership to a museum handyman and a gang of pensioners.

chapters.heading: The Parthenon sculptures
chapters.text: The oldest argument starts on the Acropolis in Athens. Around 1801, when Greece was part of the Ottoman Empire, agents of Lord Elgin, the British ambassador in Istanbul, began removing sculptures from the Parthenon, the great temple of the goddess Athena. They took about half of what survived, including much of the long frieze, and shipped it to Britain. Elgin said he had permission from the Ottoman authorities, but whether he really did is still disputed. In 1816 he sold the sculptures to the British Museum, which still has them. Greece has asked for them back for decades. In 2009 it opened the Acropolis Museum, with a glass-walled top floor that looks up at the Parthenon and leaves space for the missing pieces.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to see both sides.
items: A podcast episode visits the Acropolis Museum and the gallery built for the missing marbles.
And a video from Smarthistory looks at the sculptures themselves, in their long gallery at the British Museum.

chapters.heading: The Mona Lisa
chapters.text: The most famous theft of all was simple. On a Monday morning in August 1911, when the Louvre was closed, Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman who had worked at the museum, took the Mona Lisa off the wall. He removed the frame, hid the painting under his workman’s smock, and walked out. Nobody noticed for a day. When the news broke, crowds came to the Louvre to stare at the empty space on the wall. Peruggia kept the painting in his room in Paris for two years. In 1913 he tried to sell it to an art dealer in Florence, saying he wanted to return it to Italy, and he was arrested. The painting came back far more famous than it left.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to hear about the theft.
items: A short Witness History episode tells how it happened, and how the hunt made the painting famous.
And Vanished Smile is a brisk, funny book about the two years it was missing.

chapters.heading: The Woman in Gold
chapters.text: Some thefts were carried out by governments. In Vienna in 1907, Gustav Klimt finished a portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer, the wife of a rich Jewish sugar industrialist, in oil and real gold leaf. When Germany took over Austria in 1938, the Nazis seized the family’s property, including the painting. After the war it hung in the Belvedere, Austria’s national gallery, where it was known simply as the Woman in Gold. Austria said Adele had left it to the state. In the 1990s her niece, Maria Altmann, who had escaped to America, challenged that. After a long legal fight that reached the United States Supreme Court, an arbitration panel in Austria awarded the painting to her in 2006.

mediaNote.lead: This story has two good tellings, a podcast and a book.
items: A podcast episode follows the painting from Klimt’s studio to the courtroom.
And The Lady in Gold, by Anne-Marie O’Connor, tells the whole story of the painting and the family that lost it.

chapters.heading: Göring’s shopping
chapters.text: In occupied Paris, the theft was organized on a huge scale. From 1940 the Nazis seized art from Jewish families across France, and they used the Jeu de Paume, a small museum in the Tuileries Garden, as a sorting house. Hermann Göring, the head of the German air force, came again and again to pick out pieces for his own collection. He visited about twenty times. A French curator, Rose Valland, kept working at the museum throughout. The Germans did not know she understood German, and she secretly recorded what came in and where it was sent. After the liberation, her notes helped find and return thousands of works.
chapters.image: Jeu de Paume, Jardin des Tuileries, Paris 25 May 2017.jpg

items: For more, there is a video about Göring’s visits, and the curator who kept track of everything.

chapters.heading: The Scream
chapters.text: Some thieves just wanted attention. On February 12, 1994, the morning the Winter Olympics opened in Lillehammer, two men leaned a ladder against the National Gallery in Oslo, broke a window, and took Edvard Munch’s The Scream. It took them less than a minute. They left a note that said thanks for the poor security. The painting was found three months later in a hotel south of the city, in a sting run by Norwegian and British police. In 2004 armed men took another version of The Scream from the Munch Museum in broad daylight. That one was recovered two years later.
chapters.image: Edvard Munch, The Scream, 1893, National Gallery, Oslo (1) (35658212823).jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here is the theft, and the painting itself.
items: A short podcast episode tells how the thieves did it in under a minute.
And Great Art Explained looks at the painting, and why Munch made several versions.

chapters.heading: The Bührle robbery
chapters.text: The biggest art robbery in Swiss history took place on a Sunday afternoon in February 2008. Three armed men in ski masks walked into the Bührle Collection, a private museum in a villa in Zurich, and made the staff lie on the floor. They left with four paintings, by Cézanne, Degas, Van Gogh, and Monet, worth well over a hundred million dollars. Two of them were found days later in a car parked outside a hospital. The Cézanne, a portrait of a boy in a red vest, turned up in Serbia in 2012. The collection has since moved to a new wing of the Kunsthaus, the city’s art museum.

items: To follow the getaway, there is a true-crime walking tour that starts at the art museum and covers the city’s heists and robberies.

chapters.heading: The Spider-Man
chapters.text: In Paris in 2010, one burglar worked alone. Vjeran Tomic, known as the Spider-Man for his climbing, cut through a padlock and a window of the Museum of Modern Art one night in May. The alarm system was partly broken, and the guards saw nothing. He came out with five paintings, by Picasso, Matisse, Braque, Modigliani, and Léger, worth about a hundred million dollars. He was caught the next year. One of the men who had hidden the paintings for him told police that he had panicked and thrown them in the trash. They have never been found.

items: For the whole story, there is a podcast episode from The New Yorker about how he robbed the museum.

chapters.heading: Hatton Garden
chapters.text: The last stop is in Hatton Garden, London’s jewelry quarter. Over the Easter weekend of 2015, a gang of men, most of them in their sixties and seventies, got into the building of a safe-deposit company. They climbed down an elevator shaft to the basement and used a heavy drill to bore through a concrete wall into the vault. They emptied dozens of boxes of jewels, gold, and cash. The newspapers called it the biggest burglary in English history. The police caught most of them within weeks, partly by bugging their cars, where they talked openly about the job. Much of the loot has never been found.

items: To see the street, there is a walking tour of the jewelry quarter that passes the scene of the heist.

image: Visitors of Louvre in front of Mona Lisa.jpg

title: Organized crime
intro: Port cities and poor housing projects have bred gangs everywhere, but some have shaped how their cities are seen: Marseille and heroin, Naples and the Camorra, Belgrade and its gangster celebrities of the 1990s.
Most of the stories here are told by journalists who paid a price for telling them, or by films that the cities have mixed feelings about.

chapters.heading: Carbone and Spirito
chapters.text: Marseille, France’s great Mediterranean port, has had a reputation for crime for a century. In the 1930s two gangsters, Paul Carbone and François Spirito, ran protection, gambling, and prostitution in the city, from the bars around the Opéra quarter. They had friends in city politics, and they supplied men to break strikes and fix elections. During the war, both worked with the German occupiers. Carbone was killed in 1943 when the Resistance blew up a train he was on. In 1970 the film Borsalino, with Alain Delon and Jean-Paul Belmondo, turned a version of their story into a stylish caper.

items: To see the legend, there is Borsalino, with Delon and Belmondo as rival dandies who become partners.

chapters.heading: The French Connection
chapters.text: After the war, Corsican gangs in Marseille built a trade in heroin. They brought morphine base from Turkey, refined it in secret laboratories around the city, and smuggled it to New York. For two decades this pipeline, which Americans called the French Connection, supplied most of the heroin in the United States. French and American police broke it up in the early 1970s. In 1981 Pierre Michel, a judge who had pursued the gangs, was shot dead in the street by a gunman on a motorcycle. Today the drug trade belongs to young street gangs, who fight over dealing spots in the housing projects of the northern districts.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the story, past and present.
items: La French, with Jean Dujardin, tells the story of the judge’s duel with the mob boss behind the heroin pipeline.
And a podcast episode explains how the old trade gave way to the teenage gang wars of today.

chapters.heading: The Special Unit
chapters.text: Glasgow had a reputation for gang violence through much of the 20th century. Jimmy Boyle grew up in the Gorbals, a poor district south of the river, and became a feared gangster. In 1967 he was sentenced to life for murder, and in prison he fought the guards constantly. In 1973 Barlinnie Prison, in the east of the city, opened a Special Unit for its most violent long-term prisoners. It gave them art materials, let them wear their own clothes, and gave them a say in how the unit was run. Boyle began to sculpt and write. He was released in 1982 and became an artist and author. The unit was controversial, and it closed in 1994.

items: For the story, there is a Witness History episode about the experiment.

chapters.heading: The Magliana gang
chapters.text: In Rome in the 1970s and 1980s, a gang from Magliana, a working-class district in the south of the city, took over much of the drug trade and illegal gambling. The Banda della Magliana was unusual because of the company it kept. Investigators linked it to neo-fascist terrorists, to parts of the Italian secret services, and to the Vatican bank scandal of the early 1980s. Its leaders were killed one by one, by rivals and by each other. The story was told in a novel, Romanzo Criminale, by a judge, Giancarlo De Cataldo, and then in a film and a television series.

items: For the story, there is Romanzo Criminale, a long, gripping film about the rise and fall of the gang.

chapters.heading: The Long Good Friday
chapters.text: In London, the docks of the East End had once been among the busiest in the world, but by the 1970s they were almost all closed. In the film The Long Good Friday, released in 1980, Bob Hoskins plays Harold Shand, a gangster who plans to redevelop the derelict docks with American money. Over one Easter weekend, his empire starts to fall apart, as someone attacks his businesses and he cannot work out who. Within a few years the docks really were redeveloped, into the offices and apartments of Docklands and Canary Wharf. St. Katharine Docks, by Tower Bridge, is now a marina.
chapters.image: East Dock. St Katharine Docks, London 02.jpg

items: To see it, The Long Good Friday is a classic British gangster film, with Bob Hoskins at his best.

chapters.heading: The Camorra
chapters.text: In Naples, the local mafia is called the Camorra. It is not one organization but many clans, fighting over drugs, construction, garbage collection, and the trade in fakes. In 1985 the Camorra shot dead Giancarlo Siani, a young reporter who had written about the clans and the politicians who helped them. He was 26. In 2006 Roberto Saviano published Gomorrah, a book that named the clans and showed how far their business reached, from fake designer clothes to the illegal dumping of toxic waste. He has lived under police protection ever since. The Vele, giant sail-shaped housing blocks in the northern suburb of Scampia, became a symbol of the clan wars. Several of them have now been demolished.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into the story of the Camorra.
items: Gomorrah, Roberto Saviano’s book, is an insider’s report on the clans and their business.
Gomorrah, Matteo Garrone’s film from the book, shows the Camorra without any glamour.
Fortapàsc tells the true story of Giancarlo Siani.
And a report from France 24 visits the people of the Vele as one of the blocks comes down.

chapters.heading: A bomb at the Uffizi
chapters.text: In 1992 the Sicilian Mafia murdered the two judges who had led the fight against it, Giovanni Falcone and Paolo Borsellino. The next year it brought its war against the state to the mainland, with bombs in Rome, Milan, and Florence. On the night of May 27, 1993, a car bomb exploded in Via dei Georgofili, the narrow street behind the Uffizi gallery. Five people were killed, among them two young girls. The blast damaged the gallery and several of its paintings, and it destroyed a medieval tower on the street.

items: For the whole story, there is a podcast episode about the bomb and the hunt for those who planted it.

chapters.heading: Belgrade’s lost decade
chapters.text: In Serbia in the 1990s, the wars of Yugoslavia’s breakup and international sanctions brought runaway inflation and shortages. Smugglers, gangsters, and the leaders of paramilitary units grew rich, and in Belgrade they became celebrities. They appeared in magazines, ran football clubs, and married pop stars. The most famous of them, Željko Ražnatović, known as Arkan, led a paramilitary group accused of war crimes and married the folk singer Ceca. He was shot dead in a hotel lobby in 2000. The film The Wounds, from 1998, follows two boys from the tower blocks of New Belgrade who want to be like the gangsters they see on television.

items: To see it, there is The Wounds, the defining film of Serbia’s lost decade, which is brutal and not gentle.

chapters.heading: Veronica Guerin
chapters.text: In Dublin in the 1990s, heroin spread through the poorer parts of the city, and drug gangs grew rich. Veronica Guerin, a reporter for the Sunday Independent, wrote about the gang leaders, giving them nicknames to get around the libel laws. She was threatened, beaten, and shot in the leg, and she kept writing. On June 26, 1996, as she sat in her car at a red light on the Naas Road, a man on a motorcycle shot her dead. Her killing shocked Ireland. Within months the government set up the Criminal Assets Bureau, with the power to seize money and property from criminals.

items: For her story, there is Veronica Guerin, a film with Cate Blanchett as the reporter.

title: Scientists
intro: Many of the ideas that changed how we see the world were worked out in a few European rooms, often by people who had to move to find them.
This thread follows science from the student years of Copernicus in the 1490s to a famous meeting in occupied Copenhagen in 1941.

chapters.heading: Copernicus
chapters.text: Nicolaus Copernicus was born in 1473 in Toruń, a trading town on the Vistula River in Poland. From 1491 he studied at the university in Kraków, which was known for its teaching of astronomy. He went on to study law and medicine in Italy, and he spent most of his life as a church official in a small town on the Baltic coast. All the while, he was working on an idea: that the Earth and the other planets travel around the sun, not the sun around the Earth. His book setting it out was published in 1543, the year he died. The university’s oldest building, the Collegium Maius, has astronomical instruments from his time.

items: For his story, there is a podcast episode about the merchant’s son who upended the universe.

chapters.heading: Tycho and Kepler
chapters.text: Half a century later, the best observations of the sky were being made by a Danish nobleman, Tycho Brahe. As a student he had lost part of his nose in a duel, and he wore a replacement made of metal. On an island off the Danish coast, he built an observatory and measured the positions of the stars and planets more accurately than anyone before him. In 1599 he moved to Prague, to the court of the emperor Rudolf II, who loved science, magic, and curiosities. There he hired a young German mathematician, Johannes Kepler. Tycho died in 1601. Kepler used his observations to work out that the planets move in ellipses, not circles. Tycho is buried in the Týn Church on the Old Town Square.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Rudolf’s Prague.
items: A podcast episode tells the story of the astronomer with the metal nose.
And The Mercurial Emperor, by Peter Marshall, describes Rudolf’s court of astronomers, alchemists, and painters.

chapters.heading: Galileo’s telescopes
chapters.text: In Italy, Galileo Galilei heard about a new Dutch invention, the telescope, and in 1609 he built his own. When he turned it on the night sky, he saw mountains on the moon and four small moons circling Jupiter. He named the moons after the Medici, the ruling family of Florence, and the next year they made him their court mathematician. His support for Copernicus brought him into conflict with the Church. In 1633 he was tried by the Inquisition in Rome, forced to take back his views, and kept under house arrest for the rest of his life. Two of his telescopes are in the Museo Galileo in Florence. So is the middle finger of his right hand, taken from his body when it was moved to a new tomb in 1737.
chapters.image: Galilei telescopes, Museo Galileo, Florence, Inv. 242, 2428, 224088.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Galileo’s Florence.
items: A short video shows the finger in its glass case in the museum.
And Galileo’s Daughter, by Dava Sobel, tells his story through the letters of his daughter, a nun.

chapters.heading: Longitude
chapters.text: Sailors at sea could find their latitude from the sun, but not their longitude, their position east or west. Errors wrecked ships and cost lives. In 1675 King Charles II founded the Royal Observatory on a hill at Greenwich, east of London, to map the stars accurately enough to solve the problem. It was designed by Christopher Wren, who was an astronomer before he became an architect. The answer, in the end, was an accurate clock. From 1833 a red ball on the roof dropped every day at one o’clock, so that ships on the Thames could set their clocks by it. It still drops every day. In 1884 an international conference agreed to measure longitude from Greenwich.
chapters.image: View of the Royal Observatory Greenwich from One Tree Hill in Greenwich Park, London, 20260719 0940 4508.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the story of Greenwich.
items: A short video explains the time ball on the roof.
And a podcast episode follows Christopher Wren from astronomy to architecture.

chapters.place: Vinterviken and the Nobel Prize Museum, Stockholm
chapters.heading: Nobel
chapters.text: In Sweden, the story of science led to prizes. Alfred Nobel was a chemist working with nitroglycerin, a powerful explosive that was dangerously unstable. In 1864 an explosion at the family’s workshop in Stockholm killed his younger brother, Emil, and several others, and the city banned the experiments. Nobel moved them to a barge on a lake, and then to Vinterviken, a quiet bay on the edge of the city. There he found a way to make nitroglycerin safe to handle, and he called it dynamite. It made him one of the richest men in Europe. When he died in 1896, his will left most of his fortune to fund prizes for physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and peace, first given in 1901.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the story of the prizes.
items: A podcast episode tells how Nobel moved his explosives out of the city.
A book explains where the prizes came from, how the winners are chosen, and who has been missed.
And a short video visits Stockholm City Hall, where the winners dine every December.

chapters.heading: Maria Skłodowska
chapters.text: One of the most famous winners was born in Warsaw. Maria Skłodowska was born in 1867 on Freta Street, in the New Town, when Warsaw was ruled by the Russian Empire. Women could not study at the university, so she attended the Flying University, a secret school that moved from house to house. In 1891 she went to Paris to study physics. There she married Pierre Curie, and together they discovered two new elements, radium and polonium, which she named after Poland. In 1903 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics, and in 1911 she won the prize in chemistry. She was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes. The house where she was born is now a small museum.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to get to know her.
items: A podcast episode follows her from Freta Street to her two Nobel Prizes.
And Obsessive Genius, by Barbara Goldsmith, is a short, clear biography.

chapters.heading: Freud
chapters.text: In Vienna, Sigmund Freud lived and worked in the same apartment, at Berggasse 19, for 47 years. A doctor trained in the study of the nervous system, he began to treat patients by having them lie on a couch and talk freely about whatever came into their minds. From this he developed psychoanalysis, the idea that our behavior is shaped by wishes and memories we are not aware of. The Interpretation of Dreams came out in 1899. After Germany annexed Austria in 1938, the Nazis persecuted Vienna’s Jews, and Freud, at 82, left for London with his family. He took his famous couch with him. The Vienna apartment is a museum, and the couch is in his last home in London, also a museum.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Freud’s Vienna.
items: A podcast episode revisits Freud and the couch where he reinvented the mind.
Becoming Freud, by Adam Phillips, is a short book by a psychoanalyst about how Freud became Freud.
And A Dangerous Method, a film by David Cronenberg, follows Freud, his student Carl Jung, and a patient who came between them.

chapters.heading: Einstein
chapters.text: In 1896 a teenage Albert Einstein, who had left school in Germany, enrolled at the Polytechnic in Zurich, now called ETH, to train as a teacher of physics and mathematics. He was not a model student, and when he graduated, no university would hire him. He took a job at the Swiss patent office in Bern. In 1905, in his spare time, he published four papers, including the special theory of relativity, which changed physics. Zurich then took him back. He became a professor at the university in 1909 and at the Polytechnic in 1912, before leaving for Berlin in 1914.

items: For his early years, there is a podcast episode about how a middling student learned his physics in Zurich.

chapters.heading: The nucleus
chapters.text: In Manchester, a New Zealander named Ernest Rutherford ran the physics laboratory at the university from 1907 to 1919. With his students, he fired tiny particles at a sheet of gold foil. Most went straight through, but a few bounced back. In 1911 he explained why: almost all of an atom’s mass is packed into a tiny, dense center, which he called the nucleus. In 1917 he became the first person to turn one element into another, by splitting the nuclei of nitrogen atoms. Nearly a century later, in 2004, two scientists at the same university used sticky tape to peel graphene, a material one atom thick, off a block of graphite.
chapters.image: Front Entrance of the Rutherford building.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two discoveries made at the University of Manchester.
items: A podcast episode tells how Rutherford found the nucleus and split the atom.
And another tells how pencil lead and sticky tape led to a Nobel Prize for graphene.

chapters.heading: Bohr’s institute
chapters.text: The last stop is in Copenhagen. In 1921 the physicist Niels Bohr opened an institute on Blegdamsvej, a street by one of the city’s parks. It became the center of quantum physics, the strange science of the very small. Young physicists came from all over the world to work there. One of them was Werner Heisenberg, a German. In September 1941, when Denmark was under German occupation and Heisenberg was working on Germany’s nuclear program, he came to see Bohr. Nobody knows exactly what they said, and the two men later remembered it differently. In 1943, warned that he was about to be arrested, Bohr escaped by boat to Sweden, and from there he went to Britain and the United States.

items: For the mystery of that meeting, there is Copenhagen, a short play by Michael Frayn that imagines it from both sides.

image: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump.jpg

title: Writers’ cities
intro: Some books are hard to separate from the city they were written in. You can stand where Leopold Bloom bought his soap in Dublin, or where Kafka filed his reports in Prague.
This thread runs in date order, from Cervantes in a Seville jail in 1597 to a Nobel Prize for a Kraków poet in 1996. Each stop is one writer and the building or street most tied to them.

chapters.heading: Cervantes in jail
chapters.text: Miguel de Cervantes had a hard life before he became famous. He was wounded in a sea battle against the Ottomans, lost the use of his left hand, and spent five years as a captive in Algiers. Back in Spain, he took a job collecting supplies and taxes for the navy, and he spent years in Seville, then the richest city in Spain. In 1597 a bank where he had deposited tax money failed, and he was jailed in the Royal Prison on Calle Sierpes. In the prologue to Don Quixote, he says the book was conceived in a prison. The thieves and card sharps of his Exemplary Stories, published later, work the same streets of Seville.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Cervantes’s Seville.
items: A podcast episode tells how a tax collector in a city jail dreamed up Don Quixote.
And the Exemplary Stories include “Rinconete and Cortadillo,” about two boy thieves in the Seville underworld.

chapters.heading: Shakespeare’s Bankside
chapters.text: A few years later, in London, William Shakespeare was writing for a new theater. The Globe opened in 1599 on Bankside, on the south bank of the Thames. The area lay outside the control of the City of London, so it was full of things the City did not allow: bear-baiting pits, taverns, and brothels. The Globe was a round wooden building, open to the sky, where the cheapest tickets were for standing room in the yard. Shakespeare wrote many of his greatest plays for it, among them Hamlet, King Lear, and Macbeth. In 1613 a cannon fired during a performance of Henry VIII set the thatched roof alight, and the theater burned down. A reconstruction opened nearby in 1997.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two short videos about the Globe.
items: In one, the scholar Stephen Greenblatt describes the rough neighborhood around the theater in Shakespeare’s day.
And in the other, thousands of schoolchildren see Romeo and Juliet at the rebuilt Globe.

chapters.heading: Burns comes to town
chapters.text: In 1786 a young farmer from Ayrshire, in the southwest of Scotland, published a book of poems, many of them written in Scots, the language of Lowland Scotland. Robert Burns became famous almost overnight, and that winter he came to Edinburgh. The city was at the height of the Scottish Enlightenment, full of philosophers, scientists, and lawyers, and its salons took him up as a natural genius. He stayed for some months and then went back to farming. The Writers’ Museum, in a 17th-century house in a close off the Royal Mile, has his writing desk. It also keeps relics of two later Edinburgh writers, Walter Scott and Robert Louis Stevenson.
chapters.image: Edinburgh - Edinburgh, Lawnmarket, Lady Stair's Close, Lady Stair's House - 20140421142708.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into literary Edinburgh.
items: A podcast episode tells how a farmer’s son conquered Edinburgh society.
And a short video visits the Writers’ Museum and the pubs where writers and drinkers share tables.

chapters.heading: Andersen
chapters.text: Hans Christian Andersen was the son of a poor shoemaker in Odense, a town on the Danish island of Funen. In 1819, at fourteen, he went to Copenhagen alone, hoping to become an actor or a singer. He failed at both, but wealthy patrons paid for his schooling. He went on to write novels, plays, and travel books, but he is remembered for his fairy tales: The Little Mermaid, The Ugly Duckling, The Snow Queen, and more than 150 others. Many of them are sadder than their cartoon versions. He lived for years in three different houses on Nyhavn, the harbor street lined with colorful houses.

items: For the man behind the tales, there is a biography of Andersen, the shoemaker’s son who never felt he belonged.

chapters.heading: Ibsen comes home
chapters.text: Henrik Ibsen left Norway in 1864, frustrated by its small, narrow theater world, and lived abroad for 27 years, in Italy and Germany. There he wrote the plays that made him famous across Europe. In A Doll’s House, from 1879, a wife named Nora walks out on her husband and children, and audiences were shocked. In 1891 he came home to Kristiania, as Oslo was then called, and he was treated as a great man. He spent his last years in an apartment on Arbins gate, near the royal palace, and he walked to the Grand Café every day. The apartment is now a museum, with his study as he left it.

items: For more on the play that made him notorious, there is a podcast episode about A Doll’s House and how it shocked Europe.

chapters.heading: One day in Dublin
chapters.text: James Joyce left Dublin in 1904, at 22, and never lived there again. But he spent the rest of his life writing about it. His novel Ulysses, published in 1922, follows a few Dubliners through a single ordinary day, June 16, 1904, street by street and almost minute by minute. It opens in a Martello tower, an old coastal fort at Sandycove, south of the city. Its hero, Leopold Bloom, an advertising salesman, stops at Sweny’s pharmacy to buy a bar of lemon soap. The shop is now run by volunteers, and it still sells the soap. Every year on June 16, which is known as Bloomsday, people dress in Edwardian clothes and follow Bloom’s route around the city.
chapters.image: Sweny's pharmacy, Lincoln Place, Dublin, Ireland 11.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Joyce’s Dublin.
items: A podcast goes through Ulysses chapter by chapter, starting with that day in June.
Ulysses itself is hard, but you can read it in pieces.
And The Dead, John Huston’s last film, is based on Joyce’s story about a winter dinner party in Dublin in 1904.

chapters.heading: Kafka at the office
chapters.text: Franz Kafka was born in Prague in 1883 into a German-speaking Jewish family. He trained as a lawyer, and from 1908 he worked for the Workers’ Accident Insurance Institute, a semi-public agency that handled injury claims from factories. He was good at the job, and he wrote reports on safety in quarries and on machines that cut off workers’ fingers. His working day ended at two in the afternoon, and he wrote in the evenings and at night. In The Metamorphosis a salesman wakes up as a giant insect, and in The Trial a man is arrested and never told why. Before he died, in 1924, he asked his friend Max Brod to burn his unpublished manuscripts. Brod published them instead.
chapters.image: Na poříčí, Na Florenci, od Těšnova.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to meet Kafka.
items: A podcast episode looks at how a bureaucrat wrote nightmares about bureaucracy.
And Kafka, a black-and-white thriller by Steven Soderbergh, imagines an insurance clerk drawn into a conspiracy in Prague.

chapters.heading: Pessoa’s many names
chapters.text: In Lisbon, Fernando Pessoa worked as a freelance translator of business letters, moving from office to office in the lower town. He wrote poetry and prose under dozens of invented names, which he called heteronyms. Each had its own biography, its own style, and its own views, and some of them even reviewed each other’s work. Very little of it was published in his lifetime. When he died in 1935, a trunk with more than 25,000 pages was found in his room. His last apartment, in the district of Campo de Ourique, is now a museum and library called Casa Fernando Pessoa.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into his many voices.
items: A BBC discussion explores the many voices of Fernando Pessoa.
And José Saramago’s novel The Year of the Death of Ricardo Reis brings one of those invented poets back to Lisbon in 1936.

chapters.heading: Hemingway’s Paris
chapters.text: In the 1920s, Paris drew writers from all over the world, among them many Americans, because it was cheap and free. Ernest Hemingway arrived in 1921 as a young newspaper correspondent, with his first wife, Hadley. They lived in small apartments near the Latin Quarter. He borrowed books from Shakespeare and Company, an English-language bookshop and lending library run by Sylvia Beach, an American who also published Ulysses. He wrote in cafés and worked out his spare style. Many years later he wrote A Moveable Feast, a memoir of those years, published after his death. The present Shakespeare and Company, by Notre-Dame, opened in 1951 and took the name in 1964.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Hemingway’s Paris.
items: A Moveable Feast is his short memoir of being young, broke, and happy in the city.
And a short video visits the bar at the Ritz that is now named after him.

chapters.heading: Szymborska
chapters.text: The last stop is in Kraków. Wisława Szymborska moved there as a child and lived in the city for the rest of her life. After the war she lived for some years in the Writers’ House on Krupnicza Street, a building where the state housed writers. She published only a few hundred poems in all, short, dry, and funny, about ordinary things. In 1996 she won the Nobel Prize in Literature. She found the fame that followed hard to bear.
chapters.image: Krupnicza street, view to W, Kraków, Poland.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to meet her.
items: In a podcast episode, the comedian Frank Skinner reads two of her poems and talks about them.
And a rare film portrait shows the poet who avoided cameras, at home among her friends.

image: The interior of Sweny's pharmacy, Lincoln Place, Dublin, Ireland 02.jpg

title: The Enlightenment
intro: In the century after 1700, a loose network of writers and thinkers across Europe argued that reason, evidence, and open debate should decide things, rather than tradition, kings, or the church.

They called their age the Enlightenment. This thread follows the idea from a banned philosopher in Amsterdam to the salons of Paris, a Scottish city that briefly led the world in thinking, and one philosopher who left his body on display in London.
image: Anicet-Charles-Gabriel Lemonnier - In the Salon of Madame Geoffrin in 1755 - WGA12652.jpg

chapters.heading: A philosopher thrown out at 23
chapters.text: The story starts before the century did, in Amsterdam. In the 1600s the Dutch Republic, as the Netherlands was then called, was one of the few places in Europe where unusual ideas could be printed. Baruch Spinoza grew up there in a family of Portuguese Jews who had fled persecution in Iberia. In 1656, when he was 23, his community expelled him for his views, and it never took him back. He earned a modest living grinding lenses and kept writing. He argued that God and nature are the same thing, and that a state should let people think and speak freely. Most of his work was published only after his death in 1677, and it was banned across Europe. It was read anyway.

mediaNote.lead: Spinoza is hard to read, so here are two easier ways in.
items: A radio discussion among academics explains what he argued and why it frightened people.
A short, personal book by a modern philosopher tells the story of his expulsion.

chapters.heading: A book of all knowledge
chapters.text: By the middle of the 1700s the center of the argument had moved to Paris. There, the writer Denis Diderot and the mathematician Jean d’Alembert set out to gather everything known about the world into one work, the Encyclopédie. It covered science and philosophy, but also trades like weaving and printing, as if a craftsman’s knowledge mattered as much as a priest’s. The French crown banned it in 1759, and the volumes kept coming out anyway. Its ideas were argued over in salons, the regular gatherings that wealthy women held in their drawing rooms. Voltaire, the most famous writer of the age, spent years in exile for mocking the church and the state. In 1791, during the Revolution, his remains were moved to the Panthéon, a church turned into a burial place for the nation’s great figures.

mediaNote.lead: Two pieces take you to Enlightenment Paris.
items: A walking tour of the Latin Quarter passes the Panthéon, where Voltaire is buried.
A short video looks at The Oath of the Horatii, a painting by Jacques-Louis David that caught the mood of Paris a few years before the Revolution.

chapters.heading: A king who wanted to be a philosopher
chapters.text: Some rulers liked the new ideas, or liked being seen to. Frederick the Great, king of Prussia, the powerful German state centered on Berlin, wrote poetry, played the flute, and corresponded with Voltaire. Soon after taking the throne in 1740 he largely abolished torture, and he allowed religions that other states persecuted. In Potsdam, just outside Berlin, he built a small summer palace and named it Sanssouci, French for “without worries.” Voltaire came to live at his court in 1750. Within three years the two men had quarreled, and Voltaire left. Frederick also spent much of his reign at war, and he showed that a ruler could talk like a philosopher and still act like a king.

items: For the whole contradictory man, there is a radio discussion about his wars, his writing, and his court at Sanssouci.

chapters.heading: An earthquake tests the age
chapters.text: On the morning of November 1, 1755, a great earthquake struck Lisbon, followed by a tsunami and fires that burned for days. Tens of thousands of people died. Across Europe, writers asked how a loving God could allow it. Voltaire wrote a long poem about the disaster, and later Candide, a comic novel that mocks the idea that we live in the best of all possible worlds. In Lisbon itself, the king’s chief minister, the man later known as the Marquis of Pombal, answered with planning. He had the old center rebuilt on a straight grid of streets, with buildings framed in wood so they would sway rather than fall in the next quake.

items: To see what Pombal built, there is a short video about how he rebuilt the city after the earthquake.

chapters.place: Dr. Johnson’s House, Gough Square, London
chapters.heading: Knowledge for the public
chapters.text: In London the new spirit was less about philosophy and more about information. In a narrow house off Fleet Street, the writer Samuel Johnson spent nine years compiling the first great dictionary of English, published in 1755. Science was becoming public too. Traveling lecturers carried instruments from town to town and performed experiments for paying audiences. In 1768 the painter Joseph Wright of Derby showed one of them at work, pumping the air out of a glass bowl while a family watches a bird inside it struggle to breathe.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into that London.
items: A lively book describes the London Johnson lived in, from the gin to the wigs.
A short episode takes a slow look at Wright’s painting, which hangs in the National Gallery.

chapters.image: Dr Johnsons House - 17 Gough Square, City of London (4043340189).jpg

chapters.heading: Edinburgh’s great half-century
chapters.text: For a few decades, the boldest thinking in Europe came from Edinburgh, then a crowded, poor city. The philosopher David Hume argued that we can never prove that one thing causes another, and that much of what we believe rests on habit. His friend Adam Smith studied how trade and markets work, and in 1776 he published The Wealth of Nations, one of the founding books of economics. Smith spent his last years in a house on the Canongate, at the bottom of the Royal Mile, where he gathered friends for supper on Sundays. A statue of Hume now stands on the Royal Mile, and visitors rub its toe for luck, which Hume would have found funny.

mediaNote.lead: Four pieces go further into Edinburgh’s thinkers.
items: A short episode starts at Hume’s statue and explains his ideas.
An economics podcast asks what Adam Smith can still teach us.
A history book tells how this small city came to lead the world in thinking.
A walking tour follows the thinkers through the Old Town.

chapters.image: 6. Bronze statue of philosopher David Hume (1711-1776 CE), by Alexander Stoddart. Royal Mile, Edinburgh, Scotland, UK.jpg

chapters.heading: Reform from the top, for sixteen months
chapters.text: The new ideas could also be imposed from above. In 1770 Johann Struensee, a German doctor treating the mentally ill king of Denmark, became the real power at court. In sixteen months he issued hundreds of decrees in the king’s name. He ended censorship of the press, one of the first rulers in Europe to do so, and abolished torture. He also had an affair with the queen. In January 1772 a group of nobles arrested him after a masked ball, and three months later he was executed.

mediaNote.lead: Struensee’s story is told two ways.
items: A history podcast tells the story from the masked ball to the scaffold.
A Danish film dramatizes the affair and the reforms.

chapters.heading: A philosopher on display
chapters.text: The age ended with a joke that was also an argument. Jeremy Bentham, a London philosopher, believed that laws should aim at the greatest happiness for the greatest number of people, and that old customs had no special authority. He thought dead bodies should be useful, not just buried. When he died in 1832, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes and seated in a wooden cabinet, as he had asked. It still sits at University College London, with a wax head. The real one is kept in storage.

items: For the whole strange story, there is a short video about how his body ended up on display.

title: Film cities
intro: After the Second World War, European filmmakers took their cameras out of the studios and into the streets. Wave after wave followed, each in a different city, each reacting against the films that came before.
