This thread follows those movements from Rome to Bucharest, with a film or two to watch at every stop.

chapters.heading: Neorealism
chapters.text: In 1937, Mussolini opened Cinecittà, a huge film studio outside Rome, to make Italian films for the Fascist state. After the war, it was being used as a refugee camp. Italian directors had little money and no studio, so they filmed in the ruined streets, often with people who had never acted. The style became known as neorealism. In Bicycle Thieves, from 1948, Vittorio De Sica follows a poor man and his son as they search Rome for his stolen bicycle, which he needs for his job. The lead was played by a factory worker.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three neorealist films to watch.
items: Bicycle Thieves follows a father and son through postwar Rome.
Paisà, by Roberto Rossellini, tells the story of Italy’s liberation in six episodes, including one in Florence.
And Miracle in Milan, also by De Sica, is a gentler fable about a shantytown on the edge of the city.

chapters.heading: Bergman
chapters.text: In Sweden, one director took film in a more personal direction. Ingmar Bergman worked in the theater as much as in film, directing plays in Stockholm, and later ran the Royal Dramatic Theatre. In between, he made films about love, faith, and death. In Summer with Monika, from 1953, two working-class teenagers from Stockholm run away to the islands for a summer. Young French critics loved it. In The Seventh Seal, from 1957, a knight back from the Crusades plays chess with Death, and the image became one of the most famous in cinema.
chapters.image: The Royal Dramatic Theatre in Stockholm.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Bergman.
items: Summer with Monika is Bergman’s early film about two runaway teenagers.
And a BBC discussion looks at The Seventh Seal and its game of chess with Death.

chapters.heading: La Dolce Vita
chapters.text: Meanwhile, Rome was becoming glamorous. Cinecittà was cheap, and Hollywood studios began making films there, so many that the press called Rome “Hollywood on the Tiber.” In Roman Holiday, from 1953, Audrey Hepburn plays a runaway princess touring the city on a scooter. Seven years later, Federico Fellini made La Dolce Vita, following a gossip journalist through the night life of Rome. In its best-known scene, the actress Anita Ekberg wades into the Trevi Fountain. A photographer in the film is called Paparazzo, and his name gave us the word for celebrity photographers.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Rome on film.
items: Roman Holiday made the city’s monuments romantic for a generation.
La Dolce Vita is Fellini’s portrait of Rome’s high life in 1960.
A walking tour visits the locations of both films.
And The Great Beauty, by Paolo Sorrentino, is a modern heir to La Dolce Vita.

chapters.heading: The New Wave
chapters.text: In Paris, a group of young film critics at a magazine called Cahiers du cinéma decided they could make better films themselves. They used light cameras, real streets, and small budgets. In 1959, François Truffaut, aged twenty-seven, made The 400 Blows, about a neglected Paris boy drifting into trouble, and won the prize for best director at Cannes. A year later, Jean-Luc Godard made Breathless, about a small-time crook and an American student who sells newspapers on the Champs-Élysées. Its jumpy editing broke all the rules. The movement became known as the New Wave.
chapters.image: Auto's op de Champs-Elysées, met op de achtergrond de verlichte showroom van Cit, Bestanddeelnr 191-0378.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two films that started the New Wave.
items: The 400 Blows is Truffaut’s semi-autobiographical film about a boy adrift in Paris.
And Breathless is Godard’s jump-cut story of a crook and a student on the Champs-Élysées.

chapters.heading: The Czech New Wave
chapters.text: In the 1960s, Czechoslovakia’s communist government loosened its control, and a new generation of filmmakers took advantage. Many had trained at the Prague film school and worked at Barrandov, a big studio on the edge of the city. Their films were funny, absurd, and quietly critical of the regime. In 1966, Věra Chytilová made Daisies, about two young women who decide that since the world is spoiled, they will be too. Another film from Barrandov, Closely Watched Trains, won an Oscar. After the Soviet invasion of 1968, many of the films were banned, and the director Miloš Forman left for Hollywood.

items: To see the Czech New Wave at its wildest, there is Daisies, Věra Chytilová’s anarchic comedy, which the authorities banned.

chapters.heading: Almodóvar
chapters.text: In Spain, the change came with democracy. After the dictator Francisco Franco died in 1975, Madrid exploded with music, art, and night life, a scene known as the Movida. Its filmmaker was Pedro Almodóvar, who had come to the city from a village and worked for years as a clerk at the telephone company. His films were colorful, funny, and full of the people Franco’s Spain had hidden: women at the end of their rope, gay men, and drag queens. By 1988, with Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown, he was famous around the world.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Almodóvar’s Madrid.
items: Almodóvar on Almodóvar is a long, funny interview in which he talks through his films and his Madrid.
And What Have I Done to Deserve This? is his breakthrough film, about an exhausted cleaner in a Madrid tower block.

chapters.heading: Wings of Desire
chapters.text: Berlin had been a great film city once. In the 1920s, the Babelsberg studios outside the city made Fritz Lang’s Metropolis and Marlene Dietrich’s The Blue Angel. The Nazis and the war ended that. In 1987, the director Wim Wenders returned to the divided city to make Wings of Desire. In it, angels in long coats drift over Berlin, sitting on top of the Victory Column and listening to people’s thoughts. One of them falls in love with a trapeze artist and decides to become human. Two years later, the Wall came down.
chapters.image: Berliner Siegessäule - Berlin Victory Column photo1.jpg

items: To see the divided city through an angel’s eyes, there is Wings of Desire, Wim Wenders’s film about longing and the Berlin Wall.

chapters.heading: Dogme 95
chapters.text: In 1995, two Danish directors, Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg, published a manifesto called Dogme 95. It set out ten rules: films had to be shot on location, with a handheld camera, no added music, and no special lighting. They called it a vow of chastity. It was half a joke and half serious, and it worked. Vinterberg’s The Celebration, in 1998, was the first Dogme film, and it was a hit around the world. Others followed, including Italian for Beginners, a gentle comedy about lonely people in a Copenhagen suburb.
chapters.image: Hvidovre from highrise "Store Hus" in Avedøre.jpg

items: For a Dogme film that is more charming than harsh, there is Italian for Beginners, about grieving Copenhageners who meet at a night-school class.

chapters.heading: The Romanian New Wave
chapters.text: The last wave came from Bucharest. Romania’s filmmakers had grown up under the dictatorship of Nicolae Ceaușescu, and after 1989 they had almost no money. They made long, plain films about ordinary people and the leftovers of communism. In The Death of Mr. Lazarescu, from 2005, a sick old man is driven all night from one Bucharest hospital to another. In 2007, Cristian Mungiu won the top prize at Cannes for 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days, about a student arranging an illegal abortion in the 1980s.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the Romanian New Wave.
items: The Death of Mr. Lazarescu is the film that started the Romanian New Wave.
And in a podcast interview, Cristian Mungiu talks about his career, which began just as communism fell.

title: Cathedrals
intro: A great cathedral could take centuries to build. It often outlived the people who started it, and it could end up in a style they would not have recognized.
This thread visits ten of them, from Istanbul in the 500s to Barcelona, where the building is still going on. Each stop is one church and how it got built.

chapters.heading: Hagia Sophia
chapters.text: The story starts in Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire, now Istanbul. In 532, riots burned the city’s main church. The emperor Justinian had it rebuilt in under six years by two mathematicians, Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus. Their church, Hagia Sophia, has a huge dome resting on a ring of forty windows, so it seems to float on light. It was the largest church in the world for nearly a thousand years. When the Ottomans took the city in 1453, it became a mosque. It became a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two short films on Hagia Sophia.
items: One shows how the forty windows at the base of the dome make it seem to float.
And the other looks at what changed when it became a mosque again in 2020.

chapters.heading: St. Mark’s
chapters.text: Venice looked east to Constantinople, and its great church shows it. In 828, two Venetian merchants smuggled the body of St. Mark the Evangelist out of Alexandria, in Egypt, reportedly hidden under pork to keep Muslim customs officers away. The city built a church to hold it, modeled on a church in Constantinople, with five domes and gold mosaics. Then, in 1204, a crusade led by Venice sacked Constantinople itself. The Venetians shipped home marble, columns, and treasure, including four bronze horses, and covered St. Mark’s with them.
chapters.image: (Venice) St. Mark's Basilica, lunette - The body of St. Mark is received in Venice, ca. 1660 by Pietro Vecchia.jpg

items: For a quick look, there is a short video about the basilica that glitters with loot from Constantinople.

chapters.heading: The first Gothic
chapters.text: The next great change in church building began just north of Paris. In the 1140s, Abbot Suger rebuilt the choir of the abbey of Saint-Denis, where the kings of France were buried. He used pointed arches and ribbed vaults, which let the walls become thinner and filled with stained glass. This was the beginning of Gothic. Twenty years later, Paris began Notre-Dame, on the island in the Seine, in the new style. In April 2019, fire destroyed its roof and spire. Carpenters and masons rebuilt them, largely with medieval methods, and the cathedral reopened in December 2024.
chapters.image: Basilica of Saint Denis, Saint Denis, France 02.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways to look at the first Gothic churches.
items: A short video shows how Abbot Suger’s choir at Saint-Denis began Gothic architecture.
Another tours Notre-Dame, filmed before the fire.
And a third follows the craftspeople who rebuilt the cathedral’s roof and spire.

chapters.heading: Built on a mosque
chapters.text: Gothic spread across Europe, and in Spain it was built over the past. Seville had been a Muslim city until 1248, when it was conquered by the kingdom of Castile. For more than a century its Christians worshipped in the old Almohad mosque. Then, in 1401, the cathedral chapter decided to build a church so big that people would think them mad. They kept the mosque’s minaret as the bell tower, now called the Giralda, and its courtyard of orange trees. The result is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world. It holds a tomb said to contain Christopher Columbus.
chapters.image: Plaza Virgen de los Reyes, Seville, Spain - Sep 2009.jpg

items: For more, there is a podcast episode about how the minaret survived as the cathedral’s bell tower.

chapters.heading: Brunelleschi’s dome
chapters.text: In Florence, the cathedral had a different problem. It had been designed with a dome wider than any built since ancient Rome, and nobody knew how to build it. For decades the church stood with a hole in its roof. In 1418, the city held a competition, and Filippo Brunelleschi, a goldsmith, won. Starting in 1420, he built the dome without a wooden frame to hold it up. He used two shells, one inside the other, and laid the bricks in a herringbone pattern so each ring supported itself. It was finished in 1436, and it is still the largest brick dome in the world.
chapters.tip: You can climb between the two shells of the dome to the lantern. Book a time slot ahead.
chapters.image: Florence, Italy, Brunelleschi's Dome of Florence Cathedral.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the dome.
items: A short video explains how Brunelleschi built the dome without a frame.
And a podcast episode argues that his ideas came from Persian domes, not genius alone.

chapters.heading: Six centuries
chapters.text: Milan began its cathedral in 1386, and it took almost six hundred years to finish. It was built of white and pink marble from Candoglia, a quarry in the Alps, brought most of the way by water. Work went on slowly for centuries. Napoleon had the façade finished so he could be crowned King of Italy there in 1805. The last bronze door was put in only in 1965. In Milanese dialect, a job that never ends is still called a fabbrica del Duomo, a cathedral works.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Milan’s cathedral.
items: A short video climbs onto the marble roof to walk among the spires.
And a food podcast tells the legend of a glassmaker’s apprentice on the cathedral’s windows, who is said to have invented saffron risotto.

chapters.heading: St. Peter’s
chapters.text: In Rome, the greatest building project of the age destroyed one of the oldest churches in Christendom. In 1506, Pope Julius II had the old basilica of St. Peter, more than a thousand years old, pulled down. He hired the architect Donato Bramante to build a new one. Over the next 120 years the job passed from one architect to the next, among them Michelangelo, who designed the dome. To pay for it, the church sold indulgences, which promised to shorten time in purgatory. Martin Luther’s protest against them helped set off the Reformation. The basilica’s interior was finished by Gian Lorenzo Bernini, who built the bronze canopy over the altar.
chapters.image: Basilica di San Pietro in Vaticano September 2015-1a.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two short films on St. Peter’s.
items: One follows the basilica from Bramante to Bernini.
And the other looks at Bernini’s bronze canopy over the tomb of St. Peter.

chapters.heading: Wren’s St. Paul’s
chapters.text: In London, a catastrophe made room for a new cathedral. The Great Fire of 1666 ruined old St. Paul’s, along with most of the medieval city. Christopher Wren, an astronomer turned architect, designed its replacement, with a great dome inspired by St. Peter’s. It was built from 1675 to 1710, and Wren lived to see it finished. On the night of December 29, 1940, German bombs set the City around it on fire. A photograph of its dome rising through the smoke became the defining image of the Blitz.
chapters.image: St Paul's Cathedra Millennium Bridge JBU04.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into St. Paul’s.
items: A podcast episode tells the story of Wren, the scientist who rebuilt London.
And another tours the bomb damage of 1940 and tells the story behind the famous photograph.

chapters.heading: Gaudí’s basilica
chapters.text: Barcelona is still building its great church. The Sagrada Família was begun in 1882, and the next year the young architect Antoni Gaudí took it over. He threw out the plain Gothic design and spent the rest of his life on something stranger, with towers like honeycombs and columns that branch like trees. In 1926, he was hit by a tram, and he died with less than a quarter of it built. Work has gone on ever since, paid for by visitors’ tickets, with architects trying to work out what he intended.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the Sagrada Família.
items: A 99% Invisible episode looks at how architects are piecing together a church its designer never finished.
Another podcast episode looks at how it became a lifelong obsession for Gaudí.
And a short video reads its façades, from the side Gaudí lived to see to the side added after his death.

chapters.heading: Two cathedrals
chapters.text: The last stop is Liverpool, which built two cathedrals in the 20th century, one at each end of Hope Street. In 1903, Giles Gilbert Scott, aged only 22, won the competition for the Anglican one. Building began in 1904 and went on until 1978, long after his death, and the result is the largest cathedral in Britain. The Catholics hired Edwin Lutyens, who designed a cathedral with a dome larger than St. Peter’s. Work stopped in the Second World War with only the crypt built. In the 1960s, Frederick Gibberd built a round concrete cathedral on top of it, nicknamed Paddy’s Wigwam.
chapters.image: Liverpool Metropolitan Cathedral at dusk (reduced grain), corrected perspective.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Liverpool’s two cathedrals.
items: A short video tells the story of the young architect and his 74 years of building.
A podcast episode tours the art inside the round Catholic cathedral.
And another video tells the story of the cathedral that would have outdomed St. Peter’s.

image: Dome of Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore (Florence).jpg

title: Fashion
intro: For two centuries, European cities have competed to set the way the world dresses. London gave men the suit, Paris made fashion an art, and Milan turned it into a global business.
This thread follows fashion from a dandy in Regency London to the designer boutiques of Milan.
image: Via Montenapoleone during the Christmas period, Milan, Italy.jpg

chapters.heading: The dandy
chapters.text: Modern menswear began with one man in London. George Bryan Brummell, known as Beau Brummell, was a friend of the Prince of Wales in the years around 1800. While other rich men wore silk, lace, and bright colors, Brummell wore a plain dark coat, tight pale trousers, and a crisp white cravat, all perfectly cut and spotlessly clean. He was said to spend hours dressing each morning. The tailors who made his clothes worked around Mayfair, where Savile Row later became the center of the trade. Brummell ran up huge debts and fled to France in 1816. A statue of him now stands on Jermyn Street.
chapters.image: View up Savile Row from Burlington Gardens - geograph.org.uk - 4435615.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Brummell’s London.
items: An episode of Articles of Interest explains how Brummell’s plain style changed men’s clothes.
And a walking tour of Mayfair passes the tailors of Savile Row.

chapters.heading: The craftsmen
chapters.text: In 19th-century Paris, luxury started with skilled craftsmen. In 1837, Thierry Hermès opened a workshop making harnesses for horse-drawn carriages. In 1880 his family moved the business to 24 rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré, where it still is, and later turned to bags, silk scarves, and leather goods. Small makers of fans, gloves, and hats served the same rich customers. In 1858, an Englishman, Charles Frederick Worth, opened a dress shop in Paris and began showing his own designs on live models, instead of simply making what clients asked for. He is often called the first couturier.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the craftsmen of Paris.
items: A CBS report goes upstairs at the Hermès flagship, where saddles are still made by hand.
And a one-minute video visits Duvelleroy, a Paris fan maker since 1827.

chapters.heading: Chanel
chapters.text: In the early 20th century, women’s clothes were still built around corsets. Gabrielle “Coco” Chanel changed that. She opened a hat shop on the rue Cambon in 1910, and soon moved into clothes. She made simple, comfortable dresses from jersey, a fabric then used for men’s underwear. In 1921 she launched a perfume, Chanel No. 5, and in 1926 Vogue praised her short black dress as a kind of uniform for modern women. For more than thirty years she lived at the Ritz, around the corner from her shop, and she died there in 1971.

items: For a walk through her world, there is a tour of Chanel’s Paris, from the Ritz to her shop on the rue Cambon.

chapters.heading: Ferragamo
chapters.text: Italy’s fashion story starts with a shoemaker. Salvatore Ferragamo, from a poor village near Naples, made his first pair of shoes at nine. He emigrated to the United States and made shoes for Hollywood stars. In 1927 he came back and settled in Florence, the old center of Italian craft. When leather and steel were scarce in the 1930s, he invented the wedge heel, made of cork. In 1951, a Florentine businessman held the first show of Italian fashion for American buyers, and Florence became the capital of Italian style.

items: For his story, there is a podcast from the Ferragamo Museum about the barefoot boy who became shoemaker to Hollywood.

chapters.heading: The New Look
chapters.text: The war nearly finished Paris fashion. Fabric was rationed, and many fashion houses had closed. In 1945, to raise money and show the world they were still there, the couturiers dressed more than two hundred small dolls in miniature outfits and showed them at the Louvre. Then, in February 1947, a designer called Christian Dior showed his first collection, at 30 avenue Montaigne. His dresses had tiny waists and huge, long skirts that used yards of fabric. An American editor, Carmel Snow, called it a “New Look,” and Paris was back on top.

items: To hear how a show of dolls saved Paris fashion, there is an episode of Articles of Interest on the Théâtre de la Mode.

chapters.heading: Marimekko
chapters.text: Not all fashion came from couture. In 1951, in Helsinki, Armi Ratia started a company called Marimekko to sell bold printed cotton. Its loose, simple dresses were far from Dior’s tight waists. In 1960, Jacqueline Kennedy wore Marimekko dresses during her husband’s presidential campaign, and American sales took off. Ratia had told her designers she did not want flower prints. In 1964 one of them, Maija Isola, ignored her and made Unikko, a print of big red poppies. It became the company’s best-known design, and it is still printed at its factory in east Helsinki.
chapters.image: Marimekko facility in Herttoniemi, Helsinki, Finland, 2020.jpg

items: For a look at the factory, there is a CBS report on how Marimekko prints Finland’s bright self-image.

chapters.heading: Swinging London
chapters.text: In the 1960s, young people in London began dressing for themselves, not like their parents. In 1955, Mary Quant had opened a boutique called Bazaar on the King’s Road in Chelsea, and she made short skirts famous. On Carnaby Street, in Soho, boutiques sold bright, cheap clothes for young men. In 1966, Time magazine put “London: The Swinging City” on its cover. That same year, Michelangelo Antonioni filmed Blow-Up, about a fashion photographer in Swinging London who thinks he has photographed a murder.

items: To see Swinging London on film, there is Blow-Up, Antonioni’s mystery about a fashion photographer.

chapters.heading: Underground Berlin
chapters.text: Divided Berlin had no fashion industry to speak of, and that left room for something stranger. In the 1970s, the designer Claudia Skoda began making knitwear in Kreuzberg, in a factory loft she shared with artists and musicians. She called it Fabrikneu. Her fashion shows were more like performances, with music and dancing. West Berlin was cheap, and it was full of people who did not want to fit in. That spirit lasted after the Wall came down. Berliners still dress more for themselves than for the catwalk.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Berlin style.
items: In a short Vice video, Claudia Skoda tells the story of Berlin’s underground fashion scene.
And a short film from The New York Times asks Berliners about the way they dress.

chapters.heading: Milan
chapters.text: The last stop is Milan, which took Italian fashion from Florence and made it a global business. In the 1970s, designers began showing ready-to-wear collections in Milan, close to its textile factories. Giorgio Armani founded his company in 1975, and Gianni Versace showed his first collection in 1978. Their shops filled a few streets near Via Montenapoleone, now called the Quadrilatero della Moda, the fashion quadrangle. The business had a dark side too. In 1995, Maurizio Gucci, heir to the Florentine fashion house, was shot dead outside his office in Milan. His former wife was convicted of arranging the killing.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into fashion in Milan.
items: An audio tour walks through the Quadrilatero and explains how Milan became a fashion capital.
A Milan podcast episode hears from Carla Sozzani, the editor who opened the concept store 10 Corso Como.
A BBC episode tells the story of the murder of Maurizio Gucci.
And The House of Gucci, by Sara Gay Forden, tells how a leather firm became a global brand and a family war.

title: World’s fairs
intro: For a century, cities staged world’s fairs to show off new technology, new architecture, and themselves. Many of the buildings were meant to be temporary, and some of the best known are still standing.
The stops run in date order, from Barcelona in 1888 to Milan in 2015.

chapters.heading: Barcelona’s first fair
chapters.text: The first great world’s fair was held in London in 1851, in the Crystal Palace, and other cities soon wanted their own. Barcelona held its Universal Exhibition in 1888, on the site of the Ciutadella, a fortress built by the Spanish king to control the city after he conquered it in 1714. The citadel was hated, and when it was torn down, its grounds became a park. The fair left behind a brick triumphal arch, the Arc de Triomf, and a park full of buildings that still stand. The novelist Eduardo Mendoza set his City of Marvels in the booming city between this fair and the next one, in 1929.

items: If you want to read it, City of Marvels is a great comic novel about a poor boy who rises with the city.

chapters.heading: Paris three times
chapters.text: Paris held five world’s fairs, and each left something behind. For the fair of 1889, a hundred years after the French Revolution, the engineer Gustave Eiffel’s company built an iron tower three hundred meters tall as its entrance. Many artists protested that it was ugly. It was meant to come down after twenty years, but it was kept, partly because it was useful as a radio antenna. The fair of 1900 brought the first Métro line and the Grand Palais. At the fair of 1937, the pavilions of Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union faced each other across the Trocadéro, and Picasso’s Guernica hung in the pavilion of the Spanish Republic.
chapters.image: Eiffel tower at Exposition Universelle, Paris, 1889.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the Paris fairs.
items: A video explains how the Eiffel Tower was built, and why it was meant to be temporary.
Paris 1900, a documentary made from archive film, shows the city from the 1900 fair to the war.
And a short newsreel shows the 1937 fair at the Trocadéro.

chapters.heading: The Ibero-American Exposition
chapters.text: In 1929 Seville held the Ibero-American Exposition, to celebrate Spain’s ties with its former colonies in the Americas. The architect Aníbal González built its centerpiece, the Plaza de España, a huge semicircle of brick buildings around a canal crossed by tiled bridges. Along its base runs a bench with an alcove for each of Spain’s provinces, decorated with tiles showing its map and a scene from its history. The fair itself was a financial failure, overtaken by the Wall Street crash, but the plaza is now one of the best-known sights in the city.

items: For a closer look, there is a tour that circles the plaza bench by bench, reading the tiled panels.

chapters.heading: Mies’s pavilion
chapters.text: That same year, Barcelona held its second world’s fair, on the hill of Montjuïc. Most of the buildings were grand and old-fashioned. The German pavilion, designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, was the opposite: a low, flat roof floating over walls of marble, onyx, and glass. There was almost nothing inside except a pair of chairs he designed for the king and queen of Spain. It was taken down after the fair. But photographs of it made it one of the most influential buildings of the century, and in 1986 it was rebuilt on the same site.

items: For more, there is a video about how a temporary pavilion was torn down and then rebuilt as a legend.

chapters.heading: The Empire Exhibition
chapters.text: In 1938, Glasgow held the Empire Exhibition in Bellahouston Park, on the south side of the city, to lift spirits after the Depression and show off Scotland’s industry. It was a showcase of modern architecture, with white pavilions and a 90-meter tower on a hill, designed by the architect Thomas Tait. Nearly thirteen million people came, despite one of the wettest summers on record. A year later the Second World War began, and almost all of it was taken down. Only a few buildings survive.
chapters.image: 1938 Empire Exhibition view west along Scottish Avenue.jpg

items: For a short history, there is a podcast episode about the modernist world’s fair in a south side park.

chapters.heading: The fair that never opened
chapters.text: Mussolini planned a world’s fair in Rome for 1942, to mark twenty years of Fascist rule. He began a whole new district for it on open land south of the city, with wide avenues and monumental buildings of white marble and travertine. Its best-known building is the Palace of Italian Civilization, a cube of stacked arches nicknamed the Square Colosseum. The Second World War stopped the fair, and it never opened. After the war, the district was finished as a business and government quarter. It is called EUR, after the initials of the exposition.
chapters.image: Palazzo della civiltà del lavoro (EUR, Rome) (5904657870).jpg

items: For the bigger story, there is Mussolini’s Rome, by Borden Painter, about how the dictator rebuilt the city to look like an empire.

chapters.heading: The Atomium
chapters.text: In 1958, Brussels held the first world’s fair after the Second World War. Its theme was the peaceful use of science, especially atomic energy. Its symbol was the Atomium, a model of an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times. Its nine steel spheres, joined by tubes with escalators inside, stand 102 meters high on the Heysel plateau, north of the center. It was meant to stand for six months. It became the most famous landmark in Belgium, and it is still there.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Expo 58.
items: A newsreel shows the fair and its promise of a bright atomic future.
A podcast episode tells how the Atomium was built, and why it never left.
And Expo 58, by Jonathan Coe, is a gentle, funny spy novel set at the fair.

chapters.heading: Feeding the planet
chapters.text: The last stop is in Milan. In 2015 it held a world’s fair on the theme Feeding the Planet, Energy for Life, about food, farming, and hunger. It was built on a new site at Rho, on the city’s northwest edge, and more than twenty million people visited its national pavilions. After it closed, most of the pavilions were taken down, and the site is being turned into a district for science, research, and a university campus.

items: For a tour, there is a video from the fair about feeding the planet.

title: Art Nouveau
intro: Around 1900, architects and designers in a dozen cities turned against the old historical styles and tried something new: curving iron, plant forms, tiles, glass, and furniture designed to match the building. It had a different name nearly everywhere it went: Art Nouveau, Modernisme, Secession, Jugendstil, Liberty.
This thread starts in Brussels, where it began, and ends in Prague. The style lasted only about twenty years, until the First World War, but much of it is still standing.

chapters.heading: Where it began
chapters.text: Art Nouveau began in Brussels, in a townhouse for a professor. In 1893 the architect Victor Horta designed the Hôtel Tassel, on a quiet street south of the center. Inside, iron columns branch at the top like plant stems, and curving lines painted on the walls and set into the mosaic floors carry the shapes around the rooms. It is usually called the first Art Nouveau building. Horta went on to design houses for wealthy clients across the city, each one different, and he designed every detail, down to the door handles. His own house and studio, a few streets away, is now the Horta Museum.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Horta’s Brussels.
items: A short film explains how his town houses launched Art Nouveau architecture.
In another, an art historian talks with the director of the Horta Museum about the architect and his city.
And a walking tour passes the Hôtel Tassel and other treasures of the district.

chapters.place: Glasgow School of Art and Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow
chapters.heading: Mackintosh’s Glasgow
chapters.text: In Glasgow, Charles Rennie Mackintosh developed his own version of the style, lighter and more geometric. He worked closely with his wife, the artist Margaret Macdonald, who designed panels and decoration for their interiors. His great building was the Glasgow School of Art, built between 1897 and 1909. For Kate Cranston, a businesswoman who ran a chain of tea rooms, he and Macdonald designed the Willow Tea Rooms on Sauchiehall Street, down to the chairs, menus, and cutlery. The art school was gutted by fire in 2014 and again in 2018. The tea rooms have been restored, and they serve tea again.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Mackintosh’s Glasgow.
items: A short film shows how the Willow Tea Rooms were restored.
A podcast episode tells the story of the art school, and how it burned twice.
Another tells the story of Margaret Macdonald, whom Mackintosh called three-quarters of his work.
And Charles Rennie Mackintosh, by Alan Crawford, is a compact illustrated life.

chapters.heading: The Métro entrances
chapters.text: In Paris, the style’s best-known champion was Hector Guimard. In the late 1890s he built Castel Béranger, an apartment building in the 16th arrondissement, full of twisting ironwork. When the city built its first Métro line in 1900, Guimard designed its entrances: green cast-iron frames that grow out of the sidewalk like plants, with lamps like buds. Some Parisians found them strange, and the whole style was nicknamed style Métro. A few entrances, such as Porte Dauphine and Abbesses, keep his rare glass canopies.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Guimard’s Paris.
items: A short video looks at the Métro entrance at Porte Dauphine.
And a walking tour of the 16th arrondissement starts at Castel Béranger, the birthplace of Parisian Art Nouveau.

chapters.heading: Modernisme
chapters.text: In Barcelona, the style was called Modernisme, and it became a statement of Catalan pride. The city was growing fast into the Eixample, a new grid of streets, and rich families competed to build the most striking houses on its main avenue, the Passeig de Gràcia. On one block, three rival architects built side by side, among them Antoni Gaudí, whose Casa Batlló has a roof like a dragon’s back and balconies like masks. Another of them, Lluís Domènech i Montaner, built the Palau de la Música Catalana, a concert hall of glass and mosaic under a great stained-glass skylight, which opened in 1908.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Modernisme.
items: A short video walks the block where rival architects lined up their showpieces.
A podcast episode looks at Domènech i Montaner and his concert hall.
Another follows Gaudí from his childhood to his first major commission.
And an architecture historian’s walk traces the city’s Modernista golden age.

chapters.heading: Liberty
chapters.text: In Italy, the style was called stile Liberty, after Liberty & Co., the London shop that sold the new designs. In Milan, the richest examples are in the streets around Porta Venezia, the old eastern gate. The grandest is Palazzo Castiglioni, finished in 1904 on Corso Venezia for a wealthy engineer. Its entrance was flanked by two large stone nudes, and the neighbors were so offended that the statues were moved to another building. The Milanese still joke about it.
chapters.image: 9028 - Milano, C.so Venezia - Giuseppe Sommaruga, Pal. Castiglioni (1904) - Foto Giovanni Dall'Orto 22-Apr-2007.jpg

items: For more, there is a podcast episode from Milan’s house museums about Liberty in the Porta Venezia district.

chapters.heading: The Secession
chapters.text: In Vienna, in 1897, a group of young artists led by the painter Gustav Klimt broke away from the city’s official artists’ association, which they found stuffy and conservative. They called themselves the Secession. A year later they built their own exhibition hall, with a dome of gilded bronze laurel leaves and, over the door, the motto “To every age its art, to art its freedom.” For an exhibition in honor of Beethoven in 1902, Klimt painted a long frieze about humanity’s search for happiness. It is still in the building’s basement. His painting The Kiss, from 1908, covered in gold leaf, hangs in the Belvedere.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Klimt’s Vienna.
items: A BBC discussion explains how the Secession broke away to reinvent art.
A short video looks at the Beethoven Frieze.
And Great Art Explained looks at The Kiss.

chapters.heading: Mucha comes home
chapters.text: Alphonse Mucha, a Czech artist, made his name in Paris in the 1890s with posters for the actress Sarah Bernhardt. Full of flowing hair and flowers, they became defining images of Art Nouveau. In 1910 he came home to Prague, wanting his art to serve the Czech nation. He decorated the Lord Mayor’s Hall in the Municipal House, the city’s new concert hall and civic center, which opened in 1912. Two years later, the First World War ended the style almost everywhere. After the war, Mucha designed the first banknotes and stamps of independent Czechoslovakia.
chapters.image: Casa municipal, Praga, República Checa, 2022-07-02, DD 09.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Art Nouveau Prague.
items: A short video visits the Mucha Museum.
And a walk through the New Town takes in Art Nouveau buildings and elegant cafés.

title: Modern architecture
intro: In the early 20th century, architects began to reject ornament and historical styles. They wanted buildings shaped by their use, built with new materials, and full of light and air.
This thread follows modern architecture from a scandalous Vienna shopfront to the inside-out towers of London, by way of workers’ housing, concert halls, and a concrete apartment block in Marseille.

chapters.heading: Ornament and crime
chapters.text: The story starts in Vienna, with an architect who hated decoration. In 1910, Adolf Loos gave a lecture called “Ornament and Crime,” arguing that modern people should live without ornament. That same year he was finishing a building on the Michaelerplatz, right across from the emperor’s palace. Its upper floors were plain white walls with bare windows. The Viennese were outraged and called it “the house without eyebrows.” In the 1920s, the philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein, working with one of Loos’s students, designed a house for his sister in the same severe spirit, down to the door handles.

items: For a building designed by a philosopher, there is an episode of Philosophize This! on Wittgenstein and the house he built for his sister.

chapters.heading: The Amsterdam School
chapters.text: Not every modern architect wanted bare walls. In Amsterdam, a group of young architects built in brick, with curves, towers, and carved details. Their style became known as the Amsterdam School. Its first great building was the Scheepvaarthuis, the offices of six shipping companies, finished in 1916, covered with sculptures of sea gods and seafarers. A national housing law had made it possible for cities to build homes for workers. So the same architects also built whole streets of public housing. The best known, Het Schip, finished in 1920, is shaped like a ship, and part of it is now a museum.

items: For a look inside the Scheepvaarthuis, now a hotel, there is a short video by a local filmmaker.

chapters.heading: The Bauhaus
chapters.text: In Germany, modern design became a school. In 1919, the architect Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar, to bring together art, craft, and industry. Its teachers designed furniture, lamps, typefaces, and buildings for mass production. The school moved to Dessau and then to Berlin, and in 1933 it closed under pressure from the Nazis, who saw it as un-German. In Berlin, meanwhile, the city was building housing for workers. The Horseshoe Estate, designed by Bruno Taut, curves around a pond, with bright colors, balconies, and gardens.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into modern Berlin.
items: A short video from Quartz explains the ideas and politics behind the Bauhaus.
And a short film from UNESCO looks at Berlin’s 1920s housing estates, including the Horseshoe.

chapters.heading: Alvar Aalto
chapters.text: In Finland, modern architecture took a gentler, more natural form. Its master was Alvar Aalto. In the 1930s he designed a tuberculosis sanatorium full of light. With his wife, the architect Aino Aalto, and two friends, he also founded Artek, a company to make and sell their bent birch furniture, which is still made today. In 1936 they built a house and studio in Munkkiniemi, a leafy suburb of Helsinki. His last great building in the city was Finlandia Hall, a concert hall of white marble beside the bay, opened in 1971. In 1975 it hosted a summit of leaders from East and West, who signed the Helsinki Accords.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Aalto’s Helsinki.
items: A short film goes inside Studio Aalto, where he drew his late buildings.
A Monocle podcast episode tells how Finlandia Hall became a Cold War summit stage.
Alvar Aalto: Architect, by John Stewart, is a frank life of the man and his work.
And an audio tour walks through two hundred years of Helsinki architecture, ending with Aalto.

chapters.heading: A machine for living
chapters.text: After the Second World War, France needed housing quickly, and the government turned to Le Corbusier, the most famous modern architect in the world. He had long called a house “a machine for living in.” In Marseille, he built the Unité d’Habitation, a huge concrete block on stilts, finished in 1952. It held 337 apartments, a shopping street halfway up, and a school and running track on the roof. Locals called it “the madman’s house.” Its rough concrete, left as it came from the molds, inspired the style later called brutalism.
chapters.image: View from the Cité radieuse towards the sea with Îles du Frioul, Marseille.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the Unité.
items: A video explains how the Unité became Le Corbusier’s model of modern living.
And Marseille Mix, by the architect William Firebrace, is a fragmentary tour of the city that lingers here.

chapters.heading: Milan’s towers
chapters.text: In Milan, modern architecture became a symbol of the postwar economic boom. In 1958, a firm of architects called BBPR finished the Torre Velasca, on a bomb-damaged site near the cathedral. Its upper floors jut out like a medieval castle keep, and critics were divided. At the same time, the architect Gio Ponti and the engineer Pier Luigi Nervi were building the Pirelli Tower, a slim glass skyscraper for the tire company, beside the central station. When it was finished, it was the tallest building in Italy. In 1961, the director Michelangelo Antonioni opened his film La Notte with a long shot sliding down its glass face.
chapters.image: Milano - via Vitruvio e grattacielo Pirelli.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Milan’s towers.
items: A short video tells the story of the Torre Velasca.
And La Notte, by Michelangelo Antonioni, opens on the Pirelli Tower and follows a marriage through one day.

chapters.heading: Room 606
chapters.text: In Denmark, modern design reached into every object. In 1956, the airline SAS hired the architect Arne Jacobsen to design a hotel by Copenhagen’s central station. He designed the building, Copenhagen’s first skyscraper, and everything inside it: the lamps, the door handles, the cutlery, and two new chairs, the Egg and the Swan. The hotel opened in 1960. Most of its rooms have since been redone, but one, Room 606, has been kept almost exactly as he designed it. Jacobsen’s cutlery later appeared in Stanley Kubrick’s film 2001: A Space Odyssey.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Danish modern design.
items: Room 606, by Michael Sheridan, is a book about the hotel and everything Jacobsen designed for it.
And an audio tour starts at the hotel and walks through a century of Danish design.

chapters.heading: The Barbican and Lloyd’s
chapters.text: The last stop is London, on ground cleared by the Blitz. The German bombing of 1940 flattened Cripplegate, a district at the northern edge of the City. On that site, the city built the Barbican, a complex of concrete towers and terraces around a lake, with homes for thousands of people, a school, and an arts center. It took until 1982 to finish. Many people hated it, and many now love it. A few streets away, in 1986, Richard Rogers finished the Lloyd’s building for the insurance market. It puts its stairs, lifts, and pipes on the outside, as if the building had been turned inside out.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into modern London.
items: A short film from the Architecture Foundation shows how the Barbican works, inside and out.
And a video from Dezeen tells how Richard Rogers turned the Lloyd’s building inside out.

title: Socialist cities
intro: Socialist governments wanted to build new kinds of cities: workers’ housing with courtyards and kindergartens, wide avenues for parades, and towers to show who was in charge. Red Vienna did it by vote in the 1920s. After 1945, the communist states of Eastern Europe did it on a much bigger scale.
This thread follows the buildings, from Vienna’s public housing to Ceaușescu’s palace in Bucharest.

chapters.heading: Red Vienna
chapters.text: After the First World War, Vienna was a city of terrible housing, with families crowded into damp rooms. In 1919 the Social Democrats won control of the city government, and they set out to change it. Paid for by new taxes on luxuries such as servants, cars, and horses, they built more than 60,000 public apartments in fifteen years. The buildings had light and running water, and shared courtyards, laundries, baths, and kindergartens. The most famous is the Karl-Marx-Hof, finished in 1930, which stretches for more than a kilometer. In 1934 the experiment ended in a short civil war, when the army shelled the building. The city still owns its housing, and about half of the Viennese live in subsidized homes.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two reports from Monocle on Red Vienna.
items: One tells how workers moved into the palaces a socialist city built for them.
And the other shows how Vienna’s public housing still shapes the city a century later.

chapters.heading: A steel town for Kraków
chapters.text: After the Second World War, Poland came under communist rule, and in 1949 the government began building Nowa Huta, New Steelworks, on farmland east of Kraków. It was a vast steel mill with a planned town for its workers, laid out with avenues radiating from a central square, in the grand style called socialist realism. The regime also hoped that a new working class would outweigh old Kraków, with its university, its churches, and its conservative professors. The town was planned without a church. Its residents fought for years to build one, and the Ark of the Lord church finally opened in 1977. Andrzej Wajda’s film Man of Marble tells the story of a bricklayer who became a model worker there.
chapters.image: Nowa Huta - Plac Centralny z lotu ptaka.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Nowa Huta.
items: A short video walks its broad avenues from the central square.
Man of Marble, Andrzej Wajda’s landmark film, digs up the buried story of one of its model workers.
Toward Nowa Huta, a documentary, wanders through the town decades later.
And “HUTA,” by the rapper Szaran, is about growing up there now.

chapters.place: Palace of Culture and Science, Warsaw
chapters.heading: Stalin’s gift
chapters.text: Warsaw was almost completely destroyed in the war, and the communist government rebuilt much of it in socialist realism, a Soviet style of grand classical buildings decorated with heroic workers. The MDM district, built in the early 1950s around Constitution Square, has arcades, giant lampposts, and reliefs of model workers. Then came a gift from the Soviet Union: the Palace of Culture and Science, built by Soviet workers between 1952 and 1955. At 237 meters, it was for decades the tallest building in Poland. Many Varsovians disliked it as a symbol of Soviet control. But it was also where, in 1967, the Rolling Stones played one of the first concerts by a Western rock band behind the Iron Curtain.
chapters.image: Palace of Culture and Science, Warsaw (by Pudelek).jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into socialist Warsaw.
items: A video from an engineering history channel tells the story of the tower Stalin gave Warsaw.
Another explains the MDM district and its socialist realism.
A podcast episode tells the story of the Rolling Stones concert of 1967.
And A Minor Apocalypse, by Tadeusz Konwicki, is a dark comedy about a writer wandering Warsaw on what may be his last day.

chapters.heading: Stalinallee to Plattenbau
chapters.text: In East Berlin, the government built its showpiece boulevard in the early 1950s: the Stalinallee, nearly two kilometers of grand apartment blocks faced with tiles, with shops on the ground floor. The building workers who constructed it started the uprising of June 1953. After Stalin fell from favor in the Soviet Union, the street was renamed Karl-Marx-Allee in 1961. By then East Germany had switched to a cheaper method: concrete slabs made in factories and bolted together on site. These buildings, called Plattenbau, went up by the hundreds of thousands across the country, and many still stand.
chapters.image: Berlin-Friedrichshain, zicht op de Karl Marx Allee bij de Friedrichs Strasse Dm09085173 IMG 5358 2024-09-05 09.28.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into East Berlin’s housing.
items: Good Bye, Lenin! is set in an apartment on Karl-Marx-Allee as East Germany ends.
A walking tour explores Alexanderplatz and its communist-era buildings.
And a short report looks at the Plattenbau blocks built on both sides of divided Berlin.

chapters.heading: New Belgrade
chapters.text: Yugoslavia broke with Stalin in 1948, and its architects were free to follow Western modernism instead of Soviet socialist realism. That same year, the government began building a new capital on marshland across the Sava River from old Belgrade. New Belgrade grew into a city of wide boulevards, government buildings, and huge housing blocks, many of them in raw concrete. Its best-known landmark is the Western City Gate, finished in 1977. It is two concrete towers joined by a bridge at the top, with a revolving restaurant, built for a state trading company. People from across Yugoslavia moved into its apartments, among them the musicians of the city’s new-wave scene in the 1980s.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into New Belgrade.
items: A podcast episode tells how a showcase of socialist modernism was built on farmland.
A short report looks at the Western City Gate, the tower that greets everyone arriving from the airport.
An architect’s video makes the case for Belgrade as a concrete capital.
And “Par godina za nas,” by the band Ekatarina Velika, is one of the best-loved songs of the former Yugoslavia.

chapters.heading: A tower over Žižkov
chapters.text: In Prague, the communist government began a television tower in 1985 in Žižkov, an old working-class district east of the center. It is 216 meters tall, a cluster of three concrete columns holding pods, and it looks like a rocket. Many people believed it was also meant to jam Western radio broadcasts. It was not finished until after the regime fell in 1989, and Praguers often voted it the ugliest building in the city. In 2000 the artist David Černý added ten giant crawling babies to its sides, and the tower became a landmark. Žižkov is now one of the city’s liveliest neighborhoods.

items: To hear today’s Prague, there is a recording of “Kokalero,” trap in Prague slang by the rapper Yzomandias.

chapters.heading: Ceaușescu’s palace
chapters.text: The last and largest project was in Bucharest. After the earthquake of 1977, Nicolae Ceaușescu had about a fifth of the old city demolished, including churches, monasteries, and whole neighborhoods, and around 40,000 people were moved. In their place he built the House of the People, a palace for his government, and a boulevard leading to it that is longer than the Champs-Élysées. Thousands of workers built it around the clock through the 1980s, using marble, timber, and crystal from across Romania, while ordinary Romanians lived with shortages of food, heat, and electricity. It was still unfinished when he was overthrown in 1989. It is now the Palace of the Parliament, one of the largest buildings in the world.
chapters.image: Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest (51878975552).jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Ceaușescu’s Bucharest.
items: A short video explains how the palace swallowed a fifth of the old city.
The Last Hundred Days, by Patrick McGuinness, is a novel set in Bucharest in the regime’s final months.
And a podcast episode hears from a British diplomat who watched Romania go hungry to pay off its debts.

title: Markets
intro: A city’s markets show you what it eats, what it sells, and who lives there.

They also last. Some of the markets in this thread have traded on the same spot for hundreds of years. The stops run in order of age, from the market halls of ancient Rome to a quay in Marseille where fishermen still sell their catch every morning.

chapters.heading: Rome’s ancient shopping street
chapters.text: The oldest stop is in Rome, and it is nearly two thousand years old. Around the year 100 the emperor Trajan had a new forum built, a public square for the city’s business. Beside it his architect, Apollodorus of Damascus, cut into the Quirinal hill and built a curving complex of brick halls and vaulted rooms on several levels. It is usually called Trajan’s Markets. Some of the rooms were probably offices, so the name may flatter it. Even so, it is the best-preserved shopping street of the ancient world.

items: To see how it was put together, there is a short video about how Trajan’s Markets were built and what they held.

chapters.heading: A square laid out for trade
chapters.text: Long after Rome’s empire was gone, the towns of Europe traded in the open, on a market square. One of the biggest is in Kraków, in southern Poland. Mongol armies burned the city in 1241. In 1257 it was laid out again around a square of about four hectares, one of the largest in medieval Europe. The long building in the middle, the Cloth Hall, was its trading floor. The ground has risen since then, and the medieval market now lies about four meters below the paving. Archaeologists dug out its stalls and roads, and you can walk among them in a museum under the square. Just north of the old town, farmers still sell produce at Stary Kleparz, which has been a market since the 1300s.
chapters.image: Kraków Cloth Hall, Café Noworolski, 3 Main Market square, Old Town, Kraków, Poland.jpg

mediaNote.lead: There are three ways to explore Kraków’s markets further.
items: A podcast episode tells how the city grew rich on trade and survived the Mongols.
One short video goes down into the museum under the square.
Another visits the farmers’ stalls at Stary Kleparz.

chapters.heading: Four thousand shops under one roof
chapters.text: Two centuries later, another city put its market under a roof. In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed the Second, known as the Conqueror, took Constantinople, the city now called Istanbul. Soon afterward he built a domed warehouse where merchants could lock up their valuables. Streets of shops grew around it, and over time those streets were roofed in too. The result is the Grand Bazaar. It now holds about 4,000 shops on some sixty lanes.

mediaNote.lead: Two things here take you inside the bazaar.
items: A podcast episode tells its history, including its darker stories.
A short video walks through the lanes.

chapters.heading: When a tulip cost a house
chapters.text: Markets do not only sell things you can carry home. In the 1630s traders in the Dutch Republic, as the Netherlands was then called, bought and sold tulip bulbs that were still in the ground. In the winter of 1636 and 1637 the price of rare bulbs kept rising, until a single bulb could cost as much as a house on an Amsterdam canal. In February the prices collapsed. The story is often told as the first financial bubble. Historians now think the damage was smaller than the legend. Amsterdam still sells bulbs at the Bloemenmarkt, a flower market on the Singel canal, where traders have worked from boats since 1862.
chapters.image: Amsterdam - Singel - Bloemenmarkt - Flowermarket - View WNW I.jpg

items: If you want to understand the bubble, there is a short podcast episode in which an economist explains how the tulip trade worked.

chapters.heading: Madrid’s Sunday flea market
chapters.text: A different kind of market sells what people no longer want. In Madrid it happens every Sunday, in the streets that run downhill from La Latina, an old neighborhood in the center. The flea market there is called El Rastro, and it has been going since about 1740. It grew up in the tanners’ district, near the slaughterhouse. Rastro means trail, and the name is said to come from the blood left behind when carcasses were dragged down the hill. For food, Madrid has the Mercado de San Miguel, an iron-and-glass hall that opened nearby in 1916.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two things worth a look before a Sunday in Madrid.
items: A podcast episode recorded at El Rastro describes what is for sale and gives tips for a visit.
A short video picks out things to eat at the Mercado de San Miguel.

chapters.heading: Florence’s iron-and-glass food hall
chapters.text: Iron-and-glass halls like San Miguel were an invention of the 1800s. They let cities build big, bright buildings and move their food sellers indoors. Florence built its central market this way in 1874, in the San Lorenzo district. The architect was Giuseppe Mengoni, who also designed the Galleria, the glass-roofed shopping arcade in Milan. The ground floor still sells meat, cheese, and vegetables. It is also the place to try lampredotto, a sandwich made from the fourth stomach of a cow. Florentines line up for it.

items: If you are curious about that sandwich, there is a video about lampredotto, and the people who line up for it.

chapters.heading: The ragpickers’ market outside Paris
chapters.text: While Florence was moving its food sellers indoors, Paris was pushing its poorest traders out. In the 1880s the city’s ragpickers, people who made a living sorting through trash for things to sell, were moved outside the city walls. They set up just beyond the northern gate, at Saint-Ouen. The market became known as les puces, the fleas. It grew into one of the largest antiques markets in the world. Today it is a dozen separate markets with about 1,700 dealers.

items: To see what it looks like today, there is a short video that explores the stalls at Les Puces and stops for lunch.

chapters.heading: Budapest’s hall beside the Danube
chapters.text: In the 1890s Budapest built a market hall of its own, and built it big. The Great Market Hall opened in 1897 beside the Liberty Bridge, on the bank of the Danube. It is a long steel hall under a roof of colored tiles made by Zsolnay, a Hungarian ceramics firm. Barges once brought goods straight inside, through a tunnel from the river. The ground floor is still full of paprika, sausages, and pickles.

mediaNote.lead: Two videos here go further into the hall and its food.
items: One looks around the market hall.
The other tells the story of goulash, the paprika stew that became Hungary’s national dish.

chapters.heading: The Barras, built from barrows
chapters.text: Glasgow’s best-known market started with one woman and some handcarts. Maggie McIver rented out barrows to street traders in the East End of the city. In the 1920s she built a covered market for them on the Gallowgate, one of the main streets there. It was called the Barras, the local word for barrows. Her traders wanted somewhere to go in the evening. So in 1934 she built a dance hall above the market, the Barrowland Ballroom. It later became one of Britain’s best-loved rock venues.

mediaNote.lead: There are two ways to hear more about Maggie McIver’s market.
items: A video marks a hundred years of the Barras.
A podcast episode tells the story of the Barrowland Ballroom.

chapters.heading: Fish off the boat in Marseille
chapters.text: The last stop is the simplest market of all. Every morning, fishermen tie up at the Quai des Belges, the quay at the head of Marseille’s Old Port, and sell their catch straight off the boats. They have done it for generations. This is where bouillabaisse starts, the fish stew the city is known for. The American cook Julia Child lived in Marseille in the 1950s, and years later she made the stew on television. Trajan’s Markets are a ruin now. On this quay the oldest kind of market carries on: someone with something to sell, and a place to stand.
chapters.tip: Get there by 8; most of the fish is gone by mid-morning.

mediaNote.lead: Two things here follow the fish from the quay to the pot.
items: A podcast episode uses bouillabaisse to tell the story of who came to Marseille.
The other is the Julia Child episode, in which she makes the stew.

title: Bridges
intro: A bridge decides how a city grows, and holding a bridge has often decided who holds the city.

This thread starts with a bridge built by a Roman emperor and ends with one printed by robots. In between are bridges that carried shops, saints, and severed heads, and one that carries a canal full of water.

chapters.heading: The emperor’s bridge
chapters.text: In 134 the emperor Hadrian built a bridge across the Tiber in Rome to reach the huge round tomb he was building for himself. The tomb later became a fortress for the popes, the Castel Sant’Angelo, and the bridge became the main way for pilgrims to cross the river to St. Peter’s. It was also a place of execution. In 1599 Beatrice Cenci, a young noblewoman, was beheaded at the end of the bridge for the murder of her father, who had abused her for years. Many Romans thought she should have been spared, and she became a popular heroine. Around 1670, the sculptor Gian Lorenzo Bernini and his workshop added the ten marble angels that line the bridge today.

items: For her story, there is a podcast episode about Beatrice Cenci’s crime, her execution, and her legend.

chapters.place: London Bridge and Tower Bridge, London
chapters.heading: London’s bridges
chapters.text: For most of its history, London had only one bridge across the Thames. Norse sagas say that in 1014 the Viking prince Olaf Haraldsson helped the English king take back the city by tying ropes to the wooden bridge and rowing until it fell. The stone bridge that replaced it, finished in 1209, carried houses and shops. The heads of executed traitors were stuck on spikes over its southern gate. Everyone else crossed the river by boat, rowed by watermen who fought hard against any new bridge. The second central bridge, at Westminster, opened only in 1750. Tower Bridge, whose roadway lifts to let ships pass, opened in 1894.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three short videos about London’s river crossings.
items: One tells the story of the Norse ships that pulled down the wooden bridge.
Another explains how Londoners crossed by ferry before 1750.
And a third climbs Tower Bridge to raise the roadway.

chapters.heading: The bridge they spared
chapters.text: In Florence, the Ponte Vecchio, the Old Bridge, was rebuilt in stone after a flood in 1345, with shops along both sides. In 1565 Cosimo I de’ Medici, the ruler of Florence, had the architect Giorgio Vasari build a private corridor across the roofs of the shops. It let him walk from his offices in the Uffizi to his palace on the other side of the river without going out among his subjects. The bridge was then full of butchers, and in 1593 his son replaced them with goldsmiths, whose shops are still there. In August 1944, as the German army retreated from Florence, it blew up every bridge in the city except this one. Nobody knows for certain why it was spared.
chapters.image: Ponte Vecchio from Ponte Santa Trinita Blue hour.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the bridge’s story.
items: A short podcast episode asks why the retreating army spared it.
A video follows the private corridor the Medici built across it.
And another visits the goldsmiths who still keep shop on it.

chapters.heading: Charles Bridge
chapters.text: In Prague, the emperor Charles IV laid the first stone of a new stone bridge over the Vltava in 1357. For more than four centuries it was the only bridge across the river in the city. In 1393 a priest, John of Nepomuk, was tortured and thrown from it into the river on the orders of King Wenceslas IV. Legend says he died because he refused to tell the king what the queen had said in confession. He was made a saint, and in 1683 his statue became the first of the thirty Baroque statues of saints that now line the bridge. Most of the others were added in the decades around 1700.
chapters.tip: Go before 8 in the morning, when it is almost empty.
chapters.image: Prague 07-2016 View from Petrinska Tower img2.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to look at the bridge more closely.
items: A guide’s video walks along the bridge and its gallery of saints.
And a podcast episode tells the story of the priest thrown into the river.

chapters.heading: The Rialto
chapters.text: Venice needed a bridge over the Grand Canal at the Rialto, its market and banking district. For centuries the crossing was a wooden bridge, and it kept failing. One burned during a revolt in 1310, and another collapsed in 1444 under a crowd watching a wedding procession go by on the water. In 1588 the city finally began a bridge of stone. The commission went to Antonio da Ponte, whose surname means bridge. Famous architects, among them Michelangelo and Palladio, had sent in designs years before. Da Ponte’s single arch, with two rows of shops on top, was finished in 1591. It was the only way to cross the Grand Canal on foot until 1854.

items: If you want the bigger picture, there is a podcast episode that walks through the whole history of Venice, from island huts to mass tourism.

chapters.place: South Bridge and the Forth Bridge, Edinburgh
chapters.heading: Over valleys and firths
chapters.text: In Edinburgh, bridges were built over valleys, not water. The old town stands on a narrow ridge, and in the 1700s the city wanted to expand. South Bridge, finished in 1788, carries a street across the deep valley of the Cowgate on a row of nineteen arches. Most of the arches were closed in by buildings, and the dark vaults inside them were rented out as workshops, taverns, and storerooms. Later the poorest people in the city lived in them, until they were sealed up. A century later, engineers faced a much bigger gap. The red steel Forth Bridge, opened in 1890 west of the city, carries the railway across the Firth of Forth, a wide estuary of the sea.

mediaNote.lead: Here are the two bridges, one hidden and one famous.
items: A video explores the forgotten rooms sealed inside South Bridge.
And another compares the three bridges, from three centuries, that now cross the Firth of Forth side by side.

chapters.heading: Joining Buda and Pest
chapters.text: Buda and Pest, on opposite banks of the Danube, were separate towns with no permanent bridge between them. In winter, when ice floated on the river, people could be cut off for days. Count István Széchenyi, a reforming Hungarian nobleman, was once stuck on the wrong side for a week and missed his father’s funeral. He raised the money for a suspension bridge and hired two British engineers. William Tierney Clark designed it, and a Scotsman, Adam Clark, no relation, built it. The Chain Bridge opened in 1849, and Buda and Pest were united as one city in 1873. In January 1945 the retreating German army blew up the bridge. It was rebuilt by 1949, exactly a hundred years after it opened.
chapters.image: Széchenyi Chain Bridge in Budapest at night.jpg

items: For a quick look, there is a short video about the bridge and the castle hill above it.

chapters.heading: A bridge full of water
chapters.text: Manchester’s most surprising bridge carries water. In the 1890s the city built the Manchester Ship Canal, thirty-six miles long, so that ocean ships could sail inland and Manchester could become a port. But the new canal had to cross an older one, the Bridgewater Canal, which ran over the same spot on a stone aqueduct. The engineers replaced it with a steel trough on a pivot. When a ship comes along the new canal, gates close at each end of the trough, and the whole thing swings aside with the water still in it. It opened in 1894, and it still works.

items: To see it move, there is an archive film of the bridge swinging aside for a ship.

chapters.heading: Between two continents
chapters.text: In Istanbul, a bridge joins two continents. The Bosphorus is the narrow strait that divides the European and Asian sides of the city, and for centuries the only way across was by boat. The Bosphorus Bridge, a suspension bridge, opened in 1973, the first to join the two shores. On the night of July 15, 2016, a group of soldiers trying to overthrow the government blocked the bridge with tanks. Crowds of civilians came out to face them, and dozens of people were killed there before the coup failed. The bridge has been called the 15 July Martyrs Bridge since.
chapters.image: Bosphorus Bridge(15 July Martyrs Bridge), Istanbul, Turkey (Ank Kumar) 12.jpg

items: To hear from people who were there, there is a short Witness History episode about the night tanks and civilians faced off on the bridge.

chapters.heading: A printed bridge
chapters.text: The last stop is in Amsterdam, a city of canals with more than 1,500 bridges. In 2021 one of the newest was installed over the Oudezijds Achterburgwal, a canal in the oldest part of the city. It is a stainless-steel footbridge made by robots. The Dutch company MX3D used robotic arms to build it up layer by layer from molten metal, like a 3D printer. Engineers fitted it with sensors to measure how people walked across it, and how the steel held up. It was installed as an experiment, with a permit for two years.
chapters.image: World first 3D printed steel bridge in Amsterdam.jpg

items: To see how it was made, there is a short video about printing a bridge.

image: Prague morning - View towards Charles Bridge - Flickr - A Peach.jpg

title: Ships and harbors
intro: For most of history, the richest cities were the ones with the best harbors. Ships brought settlers, trade, and emigrants, and building them employed whole districts.
This thread runs from a Greek harbor founded around 600 BC to the Cod Wars of the 1970s. Most of the old shipyards have closed, and several have been turned into museums, hotels, or apartments.

chapters.heading: A Greek harbor
chapters.text: Around 600 BC, Greek sailors from Phocaea, a city on the coast of what is now Turkey, found a deep natural harbor on the south coast of Gaul. A legend says that a local king’s daughter chose one of them as her husband at her own wedding feast, and her father gave the couple land by the water. The colony they founded, Massalia, became Marseille, the oldest city in France. The harbor, now the Vieux-Port, has been the city’s heart ever since. Every morning, fishermen still sell their catch straight off the boats on the quay.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the old harbor.
items: A podcast episode tells the legend of the Greek bride and the founding of the city.
And another visits the fish market on the quay, and the immigrant story behind bouillabaisse.

chapters.heading: The Arsenale
chapters.text: Venice built its power on ships, and from the 1100s it built them in the Arsenale, a walled state shipyard in the east of the city. At its height it employed thousands of workers, the arsenalotti, and it was the largest industrial site in Europe. Ships were fitted out as they moved past a line of workshops, a little like an assembly line. In 1574 the Arsenale is said to have built a whole galley in a single day, while the king of France sat at a banquet. Its great gate, guarded by stone lions brought from Greece, still stands, and part of the yard is now used for the Venice Biennale.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two walks that end at the Arsenale.
items: One follows the politics of the old Republic from the Doge’s Palace to the shipyard.
And another explores Castello, the working-class neighborhood of sailors and shipbuilders around it.

chapters.heading: Setting out
chapters.text: In the 1400s, Portugal led Europe into the open ocean. Its sailors worked their way down the coast of Africa, and in July 1497 Vasco da Gama sailed from Belém, on the Tagus just west of Lisbon, with four ships. He rounded the Cape of Good Hope, and in 1498 he reached Calicut, in India, the first European to get there by sea. The spice trade that followed made Lisbon rich. With the profits, King Manuel I built the Jerónimos Monastery at Belém, in an ornate style full of carved ropes, shells, and sea creatures. Vasco da Gama is buried there.
chapters.image: Monument of the Discoveries in Belém, Lisbon, 20250604 1030 9078.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two walks around Belém.
items: One covers Lisbon’s age of discovery, and the 20th-century regime that romanticized it.
The other goes inside the Jerónimos Monastery, past the navigators’ tombs.

chapters.heading: Gateway to the Americas
chapters.text: After Columbus reached the Americas in 1492, Spain decided that all trade with its new empire would go through one port, so it could be controlled and taxed. It chose Seville, eighty kilometers up the Guadalquivir River from the sea. From 1503 every legal ship to and from the Americas had to sail from there, and silver from Mexico and Peru poured into the city. The Torre del Oro, the Tower of Gold, a twelve-sided tower built by the city’s earlier Muslim rulers, guarded the river port. As ships grew larger, the river became too shallow for them, and in 1717 the trade officially moved to Cádiz, on the coast.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Seville’s golden age.
items: A travel podcast tells the story of the river tower that once chained the harbor shut.
And a long walking tour follows the trade from the archive of the Indies down to the river.

chapters.heading: Famine ships
chapters.text: Ships also carried people away. During the Great Famine of 1845 to 1852, when the potato crop failed year after year, about a million people in Ireland died and more than a million emigrated. Hundreds of thousands left from Dublin’s quays, most of them first to Liverpool and then on to America. Many sailed on crowded, unsafe ships that became known as coffin ships. A replica of one emigrant ship, the Jeanie Johnston, is moored on the Liffey. The original made sixteen crossings to North America without losing a single passenger. Nearby, a group of thin bronze figures on Custom House Quay remembers the famine.

items: For a walk along the river, there is a docklands tour that runs from the famine ships to the tech offices of today.

chapters.heading: The Pier Head
chapters.text: Liverpool was the great emigrant port of Europe. Millions of people from Britain, Ireland, Scandinavia, and Eastern Europe sailed from it to America. In 1839 a young American sailor, Herman Melville, came to Liverpool on a merchant ship and found the docks crowded with emigrants and beggars. He later wrote about it in his novel Redburn. By 1900 the great passenger liners of the Cunard and White Star lines sailed from the Pier Head. In May 1915 the Cunard liner Lusitania was on her way home to Liverpool from New York when a German submarine torpedoed her off the coast of Ireland. Nearly 1,200 people died.
chapters.image: "The Three Graces", Liverpool Pier Head - geograph.org.uk - 4866613.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Liverpool’s waterfront.
items: Redburn, by Herman Melville, describes the docks he saw as a young sailor in 1839.
Dead Wake, by Erik Larson, tells the story of the Lusitania’s last voyage.
And “Ferry Cross the Mersey,” by Gerry and the Pacemakers, is about the ferries that still leave from the Pier Head.

chapters.heading: Titanic
chapters.text: In Belfast, the shipyard of Harland and Wolff was one of the largest in the world, employing thousands of men on Queen’s Island, on the east bank of the river Lagan. Between 1909 and 1911 it built the Titanic, then the largest ship ever made, for the White Star Line. Her chief designer was Thomas Andrews, a nephew of the company’s chairman. On her first voyage, in April 1912, she hit an iceberg in the North Atlantic and sank, and more than 1,500 people died. Andrews was among them. The shipyard’s drawing offices, where the ship was designed, are now a hotel, and the slipways where she was built lie beside the Titanic Belfast museum.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the Titanic’s birthplace.
items: A podcast episode begins the story of the Titanic, from the slipways on the Lagan.
A short biography of Thomas Andrews was written the same year he died.
And a walking tour explores the old shipyard district.

chapters.heading: Clydebuilt
chapters.text: On the River Clyde in Glasgow, shipbuilding was the great industry. Around 1900 the Clyde built about a fifth of all the world’s ships, and “Clydebuilt” meant quality. It was dangerous work. In July 1883 a small steamer, the Daphne, rolled over moments after her launch, with about two hundred workers still on board, and 124 of them drowned. The last great liner built on the river was the Queen Elizabeth 2, launched at Clydebank in 1967. By then the industry was in decline. In 1971 the government let Upper Clyde Shipbuilders go bankrupt. The workers, led by Jimmy Reid, did not strike. Instead they occupied the yards and kept working, and they forced the government to back down.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three stories from the Clyde.
items: A podcast episode tells the story of the Daphne disaster.
BBC footage from 1967 shows the workers building the QE2.
And a Witness History episode tells how the shipyard workers refused to let their yards close.

chapters.heading: The Cod Wars
chapters.text: The last stop is in Iceland, a country that lives from the sea. Fish were its main export, and British trawlers had long fished in Icelandic waters. Between 1958 and 1976, Iceland pushed its fishing limits out from four miles to twelve, then fifty, then two hundred. Each time, British trawlers kept fishing, and Icelandic coastguard ships cut their nets with special cutters. The Royal Navy sent warships to protect the trawlers, and there were collisions at sea. These were the Cod Wars. In the end Britain gave in, and two hundred miles became the international norm.
chapters.image: Elding Whale Watching boats Reykjavik harbour (25381979881).jpg
