items: For the story, there is a podcast episode about the tiny navy that won a war without firing a shot.

image: Finnieston Crane ^ Clyde Arc Bridge - geograph.org.uk - 3851383.jpg

title: Parks and gardens
intro: Gardens began as private paradises for emperors and kings. Over time most of them were opened to the public, and cities began making parks for everyone.
The stops run from a painted Roman garden to a park in Istanbul that people protested to save.

chapters.heading: A painted garden
chapters.text: Our first garden is painted. Around 30 BC, Livia, the wife of the emperor Augustus, had an underground dining room at her villa north of Rome painted floor to ceiling as a garden. The walls show fruit trees, flowers, and birds, as if the room opened onto an orchard. It would have stayed cool in the summer heat. In the 1950s the frescoes were cut from the walls to save them. They are now in the Palazzo Massimo, a museum near Rome’s main train station, where the room has been rebuilt.

items: For a closer look, there is a short video on the garden room, now rebuilt in the museum.

chapters.heading: A garden of medicines
chapters.text: Later gardens were practical as well as beautiful. Amsterdam founded the Hortus Botanicus in 1638, during an outbreak of plague, as a garden of medicinal herbs for doctors and apothecaries. Ships of the Dutch East India Company brought back plants from Asia, Africa, and the Americas. Some of them went on from here to plantations around the world. A single coffee plant grown here is said to be the ancestor of much of the coffee of Latin America.

items: For a visit, there is a short video tour of the 400-year-old garden.

chapters.heading: Le Nôtre’s Versailles
chapters.text: In France, gardens became a show of royal power. From 1661, the gardener André Le Nôtre laid out the gardens of Versailles for Louis XIV, outside Paris. He used terraces, clipped hedges, fountains, and a canal more than a mile and a half long, where the king kept gondolas. Everything was arranged in straight lines and long views, to show that the king controlled even nature. Courts all over Europe copied it. Le Nôtre also redesigned the Tuileries Garden in central Paris.

items: For more, there is a short video about the gardens and other sights beyond the palace walls.

chapters.heading: Kew
chapters.text: In England, a royal garden became a center of science. In 1759, Princess Augusta, the mother of George III, started a botanic garden at Kew, west of London. The architect William Chambers filled it with follies, including a ten-story Great Pagoda in 1762. In the 1840s, Kew built the Palm House, a huge greenhouse of iron and glass, to hold tropical plants collected across the British Empire. Kew is still a major research institution.
chapters.image: Kew Gardens Palm House, London - July 2009.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Kew.
items: A cheerful video starts at the Great Pagoda and tours the gardens.
And another tells the story of a lonely tree in the Palm House, the last male of its kind.

chapters.heading: The last king’s park
chapters.text: Poland’s last king made his garden a refuge. Stanisław August Poniatowski, elected king in 1764, bought a park south of Warsaw with an old bathhouse in it. He turned the bathhouse into a small palace standing in a lake, the Palace on the Isle, and filled the park with pavilions and a theater. He lost his throne in 1795, when Russia, Prussia, and Austria divided Poland between them. The park is now Warsaw’s favorite. On summer Sundays, pianists play Chopin by his monument there.

items: For a tour, there is a video from Polish television about the park and its bathhouse palace.

chapters.heading: Skansen
chapters.text: In Stockholm, a park was built to save a vanishing country. In the 1880s, Artur Hazelius, a teacher and collector, worried that industry was wiping out the old rural Sweden. He bought farmhouses, churches, and workshops from around the country, and he rebuilt them on a hill on Djurgården, an island park in the city. Skansen opened in 1891, the world’s first open-air museum. Its idea was copied across Europe.

items: For a quick look, there is a short video about the farmhouses rebuilt on the hill.

chapters.heading: Allotments
chapters.text: In Copenhagen, gardens were made for ordinary families. In the late 1800s, many workers lived in crowded apartments with no outdoor space. Allotment gardens, called kolonihaver, gave them a small plot of land outside the city, often with a tiny house. Vennelyst, on the island of Amager, was founded in 1892. The gardens were meant to give working families fresh vegetables and air. Today the waiting lists for a plot can run for years.

items: For more, there is a short episode of Monocle’s urbanism podcast from one of the allotments.

chapters.heading: Vigeland
chapters.text: In Oslo, one man filled a park with his life’s work. In 1921, the sculptor Gustav Vigeland made a deal with the city. He would give it all his future work, and it would give him a studio. He spent the rest of his life filling part of Frogner Park with more than two hundred granite and bronze figures, from babies to the very old. At the top of the park stands a granite column of 121 human bodies, carved over fourteen years.
chapters.image: Vigeland Sculpture Park - Granite sculptures on the staircase, Oslo, Norway.jpg

items: For a stroll through it, there is a short video about the park and its two hundred naked figures.

chapters.heading: Needle Park
chapters.text: Parks can also become places where cities hide their problems. From 1987, the police in Zurich let heroin users gather in the Platzspitz, a park on the river behind the Swiss National Museum. They hoped to keep drugs out of the rest of the city. Thousands of people came, from across Switzerland and beyond, and it became known as Needle Park. It was closed in 1992. Switzerland then began prescribing heroin to addicts under medical supervision, a policy that was later copied elsewhere. The park reopened in 1993.

items: For the story, there is a short video about the years when the park was Europe’s largest open drug scene.

chapters.heading: Gezi Park
chapters.text: The last park was saved by protest. Gezi Park is a small green space beside Taksim Square, in the center of Istanbul. In May 2013, a few dozen people camped there to stop its trees from being cut down for a shopping center. The police burned their tents. Within days, protests against the government had spread to cities across Turkey. The shopping center was never built, and the park is still there.
chapters.image: İstanbul - Taksim Gezi Parkı - Mart 2013 - r7.JPG

items: For a first-hand account, there is a BBC episode in which an actor tells how one social media post changed his life.

image: Versailles view from the Parterre d'eau.jpg

title: Going underground
intro: London opened the world’s first underground railway in 1863, with steam engines in shallow tunnels. Budapest and Glasgow followed, then Paris, and by the end of the 20th century almost every big European city had one.
This thread rides through some of the oldest and strangest of them, and ends in a city that is still waiting for its first line.

chapters.heading: The first
chapters.text: By the 1850s, London’s streets were jammed with horses, carts, and omnibuses, and the main railway stations stood on the edges of the city. A lawyer named Charles Pearson pushed for a railway under the streets to link them. The Metropolitan Railway opened in January 1863, running between Paddington and Farringdon by way of Baker Street. It was built by digging a deep trench along the road, laying the tracks, and roofing it over. The trains were pulled by steam engines, so the tunnels filled with smoke, but passengers came in huge numbers. The network grew into the Tube. Some stations later closed, and a few, such as Aldwych, are now used for filming.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the oldest underground railway.
items: Underground, Overground, by Andrew Martin, is a funny, nerdy history of the Tube.
A short video meets a signal operator who has worked at Edgware Road since 1963.
And another tours Aldwych, a station that closed in 1994.

chapters.heading: The first on the Continent
chapters.text: The first underground railway on the European continent opened in Budapest in 1896. The city was celebrating a thousand years since the Magyars arrived in Hungary. It wanted to carry visitors along Andrássy Avenue, its grand new boulevard, out to the City Park, without spoiling the street with tracks. The line was dug just under the road surface. Its stations are so shallow that you step down a few stairs from the sidewalk. Its little yellow trains still run, as Line 1, to Heroes’ Square.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the Budapest metro.
items: A walking tour starts outside a metro station at Heroes’ Square and ends at a thermal bath.
And Kontroll, a dark comedy thriller shot entirely in the real Budapest metro, follows a crew of ticket inspectors.

chapters.heading: The Clockwork Orange
chapters.text: Glasgow opened its subway at the end of 1896, the third underground railway in the world. It is a single loop of fifteen stations, running under both banks of the River Clyde. At first the trains were pulled by a steel cable that ran constantly around the loop, powered by a steam engine, and it was electrified only in 1935. The tunnels are narrow, so the trains are unusually small. Since they were painted orange in the 1970s, Glaswegians have called the system the Clockwork Orange. Its two lines run in opposite directions, and they are called simply the Inner Circle and the Outer Circle.
chapters.image: Subway train at Buchanan Street, Glasgow - DSC06203.JPG

items: For a ride around the loop, there is a video by a transport filmmaker about the world’s third-oldest underground.

chapters.heading: The Métro
chapters.text: Paris argued for decades about its railway. Some wanted it to run on viaducts above the streets, and there was outrage over a plan to run an elevated line past the opera house. In the end it went underground. The first Métro line opened in July 1900, in time for the World’s Fair, running from Porte de Vincennes to Porte Maillot. Hector Guimard, an Art Nouveau architect, designed its entrances, green cast-iron frames that look like plants growing out of the sidewalk. Dozens of them survive. The Métro grew quickly, and in 1967 Jean-Pierre Melville used its tunnels for the long chase in his crime film Le Samouraï.
chapters.image: Travaux du métro. Station gare de Lyon, vue prise en bas, 12ème arrondissement, Paris. 6 avril 1900. PH16949.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the Paris Métro.
items: A video tells the story of the debate over whether the railway should run above or below the streets.
Le Samouraï, with Alain Delon as a hitman, has a long chase through the Métro.
And a short video looks at Guimard’s entrance at Porte Dauphine.

chapters.heading: Spain goes underground
chapters.text: Spain’s first metro opened in Madrid in 1919, with a line under the center from Sol, the city’s main square, to Cuatro Caminos. One of its stations, Chamberí, closed in 1966, because its platforms were too short and too curved for longer trains. It was left as it was, with its tiled advertisements, and it is now a small museum. From Line 1 you can still see it flash past the window. Barcelona followed in 1924, with a line from Plaça de Catalunya up to Lesseps.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Spain’s first metros.
items: A short video tours Chamberí, the ghost station of the Madrid metro.
And a podcast episode covers the history of Barcelona’s tunnels, a century after the first line opened.

chapters.heading: Painted caves
chapters.text: Stockholm opened its tunnelbana in 1950. The city is built on hard granite, and many of its later stations were blasted out of the bedrock and left rough, like caves. From the 1950s the city invited artists to decorate them, and today more than ninety stations have paintings, sculptures, or installations. It is sometimes called the world’s longest art gallery. During the Cold War, parts of the system, like many basements in the city, were also built to serve as shelters in a nuclear war.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Stockholm underground.
items: A short video points out the small jokes and details built into the metro.
And a podcast episode follows the hosts’ discovery of a Cold War shelter in their own basement, and why the city built so many.

chapters.heading: Digging through history
chapters.text: Building a new metro in an old city is slow, because every tunnel turns into an archaeological dig. In Istanbul, digging for the Marmaray rail tunnel at Yenikapı uncovered the Harbor of Theodosius, a Byzantine port that had silted up. In its mud lay the wrecks of dozens of ships from the 400s to the 1000s. It held up the project for years, and it changed what historians know about Byzantine shipbuilding. In Rome, the new Metro C line passes under the historic center. Its new stations display what was found on the way down, from Roman walls to a soldiers’ barracks.
chapters.image: Roma Colosseo Metro C Fori Imperiali.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two digs under modern cities.
items: An archaeologist tours Rome’s new Metro C stations and the finds displayed in them.
And nautical archaeologists explain the Byzantine harbor and ships found under Istanbul.

chapters.heading: No metro yet
chapters.text: The last stop has no metro at all. Belgrade, a city of well over a million people, has been planning one since the 1920s, and it is one of the largest cities in Europe without one. Plans were drawn up again and again, and then shelved by wars, crises, and changes of government. The closest thing the city has is Vukov Spomenik, a deep underground station on the commuter railway, which opened in 1995. Work on a real metro began in the 2020s.

items: For the whole story, there is a video about the capital still waiting for its metro.

image: Kungsträdgården T-bana Metro station in Stockholm Sweden.png

title: Fire, flood, and earthquake
intro: Cities burn, flood, and shake, and some of the ones we visit were shaped by disaster as much as by any architect. London’s skyline after 1666 and Lisbon’s grid of streets after 1755 were both built on ruins.
This thread runs in date order, from Rome in AD 64 to the steel gates that now rise from the seabed to protect Venice.

chapters.heading: Rome burns
chapters.text: In July of AD 64, a fire broke out in the shops around the Circus Maximus, the great racetrack in the valley below the Palatine Hill. It spread through the crowded wooden houses for six days, and much of the city burned. The emperor Nero was out of Rome when it started. The story that he played the fiddle while the city burned is a later invention, not least because the fiddle had not been invented. But he did use the cleared land in the center for a vast new palace, the Golden House, and many Romans suspected him. Nero blamed the city’s small Christian community, and many of them were executed.

items: For the real story, there is a podcast episode about the fire and the myth of the fiddle.

chapters.heading: Vesuvius
chapters.text: Fifteen years later came another disaster. In AD 79 Mount Vesuvius, on the Bay of Naples, erupted. A column of ash and pumice rose miles into the sky and rained down on Pompeii. The next morning, avalanches of superheated gas and ash swept down the mountain and killed everyone left in Pompeii and in Herculaneum, a smaller town on the coast. The towns lay buried until excavations began in the 1700s. So much was preserved that bakers’ loaves were found still in their ovens, scored into slices. Some of them are in the archaeological museum in Naples.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the eruption.
items: A podcast episode describes the day the volcano froze a city.
An archaeologist’s audio guide walks through Pompeii, from the Forum to the houses.
And a food historian looks at one of the loaves baked that day.

chapters.place: Pudding Lane and the Monument, London
chapters.heading: The Great Fire
chapters.text: In London, the great disaster was fire. Early on September 2, 1666, a fire started in a baker’s house on Pudding Lane, near London Bridge. A strong east wind drove it through the narrow streets of wooden houses for four days. It destroyed most of the medieval City, including more than 13,000 houses, 87 churches, and old St. Paul’s Cathedral. Surprisingly few deaths were recorded. Christopher Wren rebuilt St. Paul’s, with its great dome, and dozens of the churches. With the scientist Robert Hooke, he also designed the Monument, a tall stone column near where the fire began. Its height, 202 feet, is the distance from its base to the bakery.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways to follow the fire.
items: A walking tour with the historian Dan Snow traces the fire’s path from Pudding Lane.
A one-minute video explains the Monument.
And Rick Steves’s audio tour of St. Paul’s Cathedral explains the church that rose from the ashes.

chapters.heading: All Saints’ Day
chapters.text: On the morning of November 1, 1755, All Saints’ Day, a huge earthquake struck Lisbon while much of the city was at Mass. Churches collapsed on their congregations. Survivors fled to the open ground by the river, and a tsunami swept in from the sea. Fires then burned for days. Tens of thousands of people died. The king’s chief minister, later the Marquis of Pombal, took charge. He had the lower town rebuilt on a grid of straight streets, with buildings framed inside by wooden cages designed to flex in an earthquake. The roofless Carmo Convent, on the hill above, was left as a ruin.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the earthquake and what came after.
items: A short video tells how Pombal rebuilt the city.
This Gulf of Fire, by Mark Molesky, tells the story of the disaster and how Europe argued about God afterward.
And a short Witness History episode tells the story through the people who survived.

chapters.heading: The Seine floods
chapters.text: In Paris, the danger was the river. In January 1910, after weeks of heavy rain, the Seine rose more than eight meters above its normal level. It flooded streets, cellars, and the new tunnels of the Métro for weeks, and people moved around the city in boats and on wooden walkways. Parisians still judge how high the river is by the Zouave, a stone statue of a French soldier on a pier of the Pont de l’Alma. In 1910 the water reached his shoulders.
chapters.image: Crue de la Seine. Rue Surcouf, 7ème arrondissement, Paris, le 28 janvier 1910. PH3201.jpg

items: For more, there is a podcast episode about the flood of 1910 and the soldier on the bridge.

chapters.heading: Vesuvius again
chapters.text: Vesuvius did not go quiet. In March 1944, during the Second World War, with Allied troops already holding Naples, it erupted again, for eleven days. Lava flowed down its slopes and swallowed most of San Sebastiano al Vesuvio, a village on the mountain. Falling ash and rock wrecked dozens of American bombers parked at an airfield nearby. It was the last eruption of Vesuvius so far.

items: To hear from witnesses, there is a short Witness History episode about the wartime eruption.

chapters.heading: The Arno floods
chapters.text: On November 4, 1966, after days of rain, the Arno burst its banks in Florence. Water, mud, and heating oil filled the streets to a depth of several meters, flooding churches, libraries, and museums. Dozens of people died. Young volunteers came from all over the world to help, and they became known as the mud angels. They dug books, archives, and paintings out of the mud. One of the worst losses was the great painted crucifix by Cimabue, from the 1200s, in the church of Santa Croce, which lost much of its paint.
chapters.image: National Library manuscripts being washed in Florence after the 1966 flood of the Arno - UNESCO - PHOTO 0000001407 0001 - Restoration.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to see what happened.
items: Dark Water, by Robert Clark, tells the story of the flood and the people who saved the city’s art.
And British Pathé newsreel footage shows the city buried in mud.

chapters.heading: The 1977 earthquake
chapters.text: On the evening of March 4, 1977, an earthquake struck Romania. About 1,500 people died, most of them in Bucharest, where apartment blocks built between the wars along the main boulevards collapsed. The dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu used the damage as an excuse. In the 1980s he demolished a large part of the old city, including churches and whole neighborhoods, to build his vast new civic center and the Palace of the Parliament.

items: To see what happened, there is archive footage of the earthquake and the collapsed blocks.

chapters.heading: High water
chapters.text: On November 4, 1966, the same day the Arno flooded Florence, the highest tide ever recorded flooded Venice. The city has always lived with acqua alta, high water, but the floods have grown more frequent as the sea rises and the city slowly sinks. After decades of delay and a corruption scandal, a system of 78 steel gates called MOSE was installed on the seabed at the three openings of the lagoon. When a high tide is forecast, air is pumped in, and the gates rise to hold back the sea. They were first used in 2020. St. Mark’s Square, the lowest part of the city, still floods most often.
chapters.image: San Marco, Acqua Alta - Venice, Italy - panoramio.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two short videos about the water.
items: One explains why St. Mark’s Square floods first.
And the other shows how the gates rise from the seabed.

title: Plague cities
intro: The Black Death killed about a third of Europe’s people in the late 1340s, and plague kept coming back for nearly four hundred years. Cities learned to live with it. They invented quarantine, built churches to give thanks when it passed, and left monuments that are still there.
The stops run in date order, from Florence in 1348 to the last great outbreak, in Marseille in 1720.

chapters.heading: The Decameron
chapters.text: Plague arrived in Italy in 1347 on ships from the Black Sea, and in the spring of 1348 it reached Florence. It killed perhaps half of the city’s people within months. The writer Giovanni Boccaccio lived through it, and he opened his book the Decameron with a description of the city in the grip of the disease. Then the stories begin. Seven young women meet three young men in the church of Santa Maria Novella, and they agree to leave the city for a villa in the hills. To pass the time while the plague burns itself out, they take turns telling stories.

items: If you want to know what it was like, there is a podcast episode that uses the Decameron to show how Florentines lived through the Black Death.

chapters.heading: Quarantine
chapters.text: Plague kept coming back, and Venice, a trading city full of ships from the east, worked out how to defend itself. In 1423 it opened the first permanent plague hospital, a lazaretto, on an island in the lagoon, where the sick were sent away from the city. Later it added a second island, where ships, crews, and goods from infected ports had to wait for forty days before they could land. The word quarantine comes from the Italian for forty days, quaranta giorni. Even so, the plague of 1630 killed about a third of the city. During the outbreak, the government vowed to build a church if the city was saved. The result was Santa Maria della Salute, Our Lady of Health, the great domed church at the mouth of the Grand Canal.
chapters.image: (Venice) - Santa Maria della Salute - Le due cupole e i due campanili.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to see how Venice fought the plague.
items: A walking tour from the Rialto covers Venetian ideas, from banking to quarantine.
And a short video tells the story of the church the city built to give thanks.

chapters.heading: The Betrothed
chapters.text: The same epidemic hit Milan even harder. It arrived in 1629 with German soldiers fighting a war in northern Italy, and in 1630 it killed about half of the city. Frightened people looked for someone to blame, and rumors spread of “anointers” who smeared walls and doors with poison. Several men were tortured and executed on that charge. Two hundred years later, the writer Alessandro Manzoni set the end of The Betrothed, the best-known Italian novel, during this plague. Its climax takes place in the lazzaretto, the vast plague hospital outside the city walls, where thousands of the sick were crowded together.
chapters.image: Dal Re, Marc'Antonio (1697-1766) - Vedute di Milano - Il lazzaretto.jpg

items: If you have time for a long novel, The Betrothed follows two village lovers through bread riots and the plague.

chapters.heading: The Great Plague
chapters.text: In London, the last great outbreak came in 1665. It began in the spring, in the poor parishes outside the city walls. By the end of the year it had killed about a hundred thousand people, around a fifth of the population. The rich left town, including the king and his court. Houses with plague inside were shut up with the families still in them, and marked with a red cross. Samuel Pepys, a young official at the Navy Office, stayed and wrote about it in his diary. The next year he described something else: the Great Fire of 1666, which burned most of the old city.
chapters.image: Monument to the Great Fire of London EC3R 8AH.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to hear about London in 1665.
items: A historian explains how the plague spread, and how ordinary Londoners tried to cope.
And the diary of Samuel Pepys tells it day by day, along with everything else in his life.

chapters.heading: The skulls of Fontanelle
chapters.text: Naples suffered one of the worst outbreaks of all. In 1656 plague killed about half of its people, perhaps 150,000 in a few months. There was not room to bury them, and many bodies were carried to an old quarry in the Sanità district, at the foot of a hill. Later epidemics added more. In the 1870s a priest had the bones arranged in the caves, and it became the Fontanelle Cemetery. Local people began to adopt individual skulls. They cleaned them, built little shrines for them, and prayed for the souls of the dead, in return for help with their own lives. In 1969 the church banned the practice as superstition, but the cemetery is open to visitors.

items: To see inside, there is a short video about the cemetery and the people who cared for its skulls.

chapters.heading: The last great outbreak
chapters.text: The last great outbreak in Western Europe came in 1720. In May a merchant ship, the Grand Saint-Antoine, arrived in Marseille from the eastern Mediterranean with a valuable cargo of silk and cotton. Several people on board had already died. The ship should have stayed in strict quarantine, but the rules were bent, reportedly because merchants wanted the cargo in time for a big trade fair. Fleas in the cloth carried the plague into the city. Over the next two years, about half of Marseille’s people died. France built a wall across the hills of Provence to stop the disease spreading, and parts of it still stand.

items: For the whole story, there is a long podcast episode about the ship, the quarantine that was skipped, and what followed.

image: The Triumph of Death by Pieter Bruegel the Elder.jpg

title: Cemeteries
intro: Cemeteries are some of the most peaceful places in a city, and some of the most crowded with stories. Each one shows how a city thought about death, and who it wanted to remember.
The stops run from an ancient Greek burial ground to a forest cemetery in Stockholm, roughly in the order they were made.

chapters.heading: The Kerameikos
chapters.text: Ancient Athenians buried their dead outside the city walls, beside the roads leading out of town. Their main cemetery was the Kerameikos, named after the potters who worked nearby. Around 750 BC, families marked graves with huge painted pots. Later, they put up carved stone slabs showing the dead as they had been in life. In 431 BC, at the start of a long war with Sparta, the Athenian leader Pericles gave a famous speech here in honor of the war dead. The historian Thucydides wrote it down.
chapters.image: Wall street of the tombs sacred way Kerameikos Athens.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into the Kerameikos.
items: An audio tour walks through the Kerameikos, along the ancient Street of Tombs.
A short video looks at the Dipylon Amphora, a giant painted pot that once stood over a grave.
Another looks at the gravestone of Hegeso, a woman shown choosing jewelry from a box.
And a BBC discussion looks at Thucydides and the war that broke Athens.

chapters.heading: The catacombs
chapters.text: The Romans also banned burials inside the city. Their tombs lined the roads out of town, especially the Appian Way, which ran south toward Naples. Most Romans were cremated, but early Christians and Jews preferred to bury their dead. Beneath the fields beside the roads, they dug miles of tunnels in the soft volcanic rock, with shelves cut into the walls for bodies. These are the catacombs. Some walls are painted, and the Catacomb of Priscilla may hold one of the oldest known images of the Virgin Mary.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Rome’s catacombs.
items: A short video from Rick Steves goes down into the Catacombs of San Callisto, beside the Appian Way.
And another explores the Catacomb of Priscilla and its paintings.

chapters.heading: Layers of graves
chapters.text: In medieval Prague, the Jewish community lived in a walled quarter, and its cemetery could not grow. So for more than three hundred years, new graves were dug on top of old ones, with fresh soil added over the top. The old gravestones were raised to the new surface, and today about twelve thousand of them lean together in a small, crowded garden. Among those buried here is Rabbi Judah Loew, a scholar who died in 1609. Legend says he made the golem, a man of clay brought to life to protect the quarter. Burials stopped in 1787, when the emperor banned them inside the city.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the Old Jewish Cemetery.
items: A video tells the story of the cemetery and its layers of graves.
And Utz, a short novel by Bruce Chatwin, is about a porcelain collector in communist Prague whose windows look over it.

chapters.heading: Père Lachaise
chapters.text: By the 18th century, the old churchyards of Paris were overflowing, and the smell was unbearable. In 1780 the city closed its biggest cemetery, and from 1786 it moved millions of bones into old limestone quarries under the city. These became the Catacombs. For new burials, Napoleon’s government opened cemeteries on the edge of Paris, including Père Lachaise in 1804. At first nobody wanted to be buried so far out. So the city moved the remains of famous writers there, among them the playwright Molière, and it soon became the most fashionable place in Paris to be buried. Oscar Wilde, Édith Piaf, and Jim Morrison lie here.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Père Lachaise.
items: A podcast episode tells how Paris moved six million dead into its old quarries.
An audio tour by Rick Steves visits the famous graves of Père Lachaise.
“La Vie en rose” is the best-known song of Édith Piaf, who is buried here.
And a BBC discussion tells the story of the Paris Commune of 1871, whose last fighters were shot against a wall in the cemetery.

chapters.heading: Glasnevin
chapters.text: Paris started a fashion for big new cemeteries outside the city, and other cities soon followed. In Dublin, the reason was also political. Under British rule, Irish Catholics had faced limits on holding their own funeral services. Daniel O’Connell, the lawyer who led the campaign for Catholic rights, founded Glasnevin Cemetery in 1832, open to people of every religion. After his death, a tall round tower, like those of early Irish monasteries, was built over his grave. Many leaders of Irish independence lie here, including Michael Collins, killed in the civil war in 1922.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Glasnevin.
items: A short video looks at the round tower built over O’Connell’s grave.
And Michael Collins, by Tim Pat Coogan, is the life of the revolutionary leader buried here.

chapters.heading: The Necropolis
chapters.text: A year later, Glasgow opened its own grand cemetery, inspired by Père Lachaise. The Necropolis, or “city of the dead,” covers a hill beside the cathedral. Glasgow’s merchants, rich from trade and industry, competed to build the most impressive monuments, from Greek temples to Egyptian obelisks. On the south side of the river, a second cemetery, the Southern Necropolis, served the poorer districts. In 1954, hundreds of children from the Gorbals stormed it one night with stakes and knives, hunting a vampire they believed had killed two boys.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Glasgow’s cemeteries.
items: A short film by the Friends of Glasgow Necropolis tours the hill and its monuments.
A podcast episode tells the story of the Gorbals vampire hunt of 1954.
And Taggart, a long-running Glasgow detective series, often filmed among its monuments.

chapters.heading: Highgate
chapters.text: London’s churchyards were as crowded as those of Paris, and between 1833 and 1841 private companies opened seven large cemeteries around the edge of the city. Highgate, on a hillside in North London, opened in 1839. It had winding paths, an avenue of Egyptian tombs, and a circle of vaults around an old cedar tree. Karl Marx was buried there in 1883. Another company ran a railway from near Waterloo to a vast cemetery in Surrey, with separate carriages for coffins. By the 1960s, Highgate was overgrown, and in 1970 the newspapers filled with stories of a vampire haunting it.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into London’s Victorian cemeteries.
items: A short video from Atlas Obscura tells the story of the Highgate vampire panic.
And a podcast episode visits what is left of the London Necropolis Railway, the train for the dead.

chapters.heading: A beautiful corpse
chapters.text: Vienna went further than anyone. In 1874 it opened the Zentralfriedhof, or Central Cemetery, on open land far southeast of the city. It is one of the largest cemeteries in Europe. Like Père Lachaise, it was unpopular at first, so the city moved famous composers there, including Beethoven and Schubert, into a section of honorary graves. The Viennese are known for their fondness for a schöne Leich, a beautiful corpse, meaning a grand funeral. Today the cemetery has its own tram stops, and the pop star Falco lies among the composers.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the Zentralfriedhof.
items: A short film from Vienna’s tourist office tours the cemetery and the city’s love of a good funeral.
“Heite grob ma Tote aus” is a darkly funny song by Voodoo Jürgens, a former gravedigger.
And “Rock Me Amadeus” is the hit by Falco, who is buried here.

chapters.heading: The Woodland Cemetery
chapters.text: The last stop is a cemetery that feels like a forest. In 1915, two young Swedish architects, Gunnar Asplund and Sigurd Lewerentz, won a competition to design a new cemetery on an old gravel pit south of Stockholm. They kept the pine trees and placed the graves among them. Visitors walk up a long path past open grass toward a stone cross and a crematorium, finished in 1940. It is one of the few 20th-century buildings on the UNESCO World Heritage list, and it inspired cemetery designers around the world. Asplund died the year it was finished, and he is buried there. So is the actress Greta Garbo.

items: For a short look, there is a film from UNESCO about how two young architects turned a gravel pit into a forest of the dead.

title: Wine
intro: Europe has made wine for nearly three thousand years, and the trade in it has shaped cities, treaties, and tastes.

This thread follows wine from the Greek settlers who planted the first vines in France to a community vineyard on the edge of London. Along the way it stops at a sherry town in Spain, a wine tavern in Vienna, and a blind tasting in Paris that changed the business.

chapters.heading: Greeks plant the first vines
chapters.text: The story begins at the harbor that is now Marseille. Around 600 BC, Greek settlers from Phocaea, a city on the coast of what is now Turkey, founded a trading town there and called it Massalia. They brought vines and olive trees with them, and they planted the first vineyards in Gaul, the land that would become France. From the harbor, wine traveled up the river Rhône to peoples in the north who had never made it.

items: To hear more about the city’s Greek beginnings, there is a podcast episode about the settlers who founded it.

chapters.heading: Harvest scenes on a Christian tomb
chapters.text: The Romans spread vines across their empire, and wine was part of daily life for anyone who could afford it. When the empire became Christian, wine did not lose its place, because it was central to the Mass. You can see the old and new meet in a round building on the edge of Rome, built around 350 as a tomb for Constantina, a daughter of the emperor Constantine. Its ceiling mosaics show small winged figures picking grapes, carting them in, and treading them, the same scenes that had decorated pagan villas.

items: For a closer look at the mosaics, there is a short video about the building and the grape harvest on its ceiling.

chapters.place: Jerez de la Frontera, near Seville
chapters.heading: Sherry goes around the world
chapters.text: In the 1500s, wine from southern Spain sailed further than any wine before it. It came from Jerez, a town south of Seville that the Moors had called Sherish. English merchants turned that name into “sherry.” When Ferdinand Magellan set out in 1519 on the voyage that first sailed around the world, his ships are said to have carried more sherry than weapons. In England it became a fashion. Falstaff, the drinking knight in Shakespeare’s plays, gives a whole speech in praise of it.

mediaNote.lead: There are two good places to start with sherry.
items: A podcast episode tells how the town’s name became sherry.
In another, a sherry enthusiast explains the bodegas, the wineries where it ages, from La Venencia, an old sherry bar in Madrid.

chapters.image: Bodega Gonzalez- Byas Jerez de la Frontera.JPG

chapters.heading: The English and port
chapters.text: The English never made much wine, but they shaped how it was made elsewhere. When wars with France cut off French wine, English merchants turned to Portugal. A treaty in 1703 lowered the tax on Portuguese wine, and English and Scottish firms set up in Porto, at the mouth of the Douro river. To keep the wine sound on the voyage north, they added brandy to it, and port was born. Several of the big port houses still have British names.

items: To hear how that family trade continues, there is a podcast episode with the son of a port maker who now runs a Portuguese restaurant in London.

chapters.image: Boats of Port Wine in Vila Nova de Gaia, Porto in the background - panoramio.jpg

chapters.heading: A wine city with its own taverns
chapters.text: Vienna is one of the few capitals that still grows wine inside its city limits, on the hills to the north and west. In 1784 the emperor Joseph II allowed growers to sell their own wine, and simple food to go with it, without a license. That gave rise to the Heuriger, a wine tavern where you drink the new vintage. A grower who has wine to sell hangs a bundle of pine branches over the door, and villages like Grinzing, on the city’s edge, are full of them.

mediaNote.lead: Two pieces bring you to the table.
items: A short video visits the winemakers of Grinzing.
A food walk through the old center includes a glass of Viennese wine.

chapters.place: Site of Les Caves de la Madeleine, Paris
chapters.heading: The tasting that upset France
chapters.text: For two centuries, everyone agreed that the best wine came from France. Then, in May 1976, Steven Spurrier, an English wine merchant with a shop in Paris, held a blind tasting. French experts tasted top French wines alongside new ones from California, without knowing which was which. A Californian wine won in both the red and the white categories. A single journalist was there to report it, and the result changed what the world thought wine from outside Europe could be.

items: For the story from someone who was there, there is a short podcast episode about the tasting.

chapters.heading: A small glass in the shade
chapters.text: Most wine in Europe is still drunk in a simple way. In Venice, people stop at a bàcaro, a small wine bar, for an ombra, a small glass of house wine, and a few cicchetti, the snacks on the counter. Ombra means shade. One story says it comes from the wine sellers who once moved their stalls around St. Mark’s Square to stay in the shadow of the bell tower. The oldest bàcari are near the Rialto market, and some claim to have been pouring for five hundred years.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways to find the right bar.
items: A short video tours the bars around the Rialto.
A drinks writer talks about her guide to drinking in Venice.
A walking tour stops at five of the old bars.

chapters.image: " 05 - ITALY - un bacaro a Venezia Osteria appetizers restaurant in Venice wine enoteca.jpg

chapters.heading: Vines in north London
chapters.text: The thread ends where you might least expect wine. England was long too cold and damp for good grapes. As summers have warmed, vineyards have spread across the south of the country, and English sparkling wine now wins prizes. On the northern edge of London, in Enfield, volunteers tend Forty Hall Vineyard, the only commercial vineyard in the city, and make wine from its grapes.

items: To meet the people who work it, there is a short video about the vineyard and its volunteers.

title: Beer
intro: In northern Europe, beer was an everyday drink for centuries, often safer than the water. Its breweries grew into some of the biggest businesses in their countries, and some of them spent the money on museums, palaces, and art.

This thread starts in a Prague tavern that has brewed for more than five hundred years and ends with the brewery that gave the world its lager yeast. Along the way, beer halls are the setting for some darker history.

chapters.heading: U Fleků
chapters.text: The story starts in Prague, in a tavern called U Fleků, in the New Town. It has brewed beer on the same spot since at least 1499, and it still makes a single dark lager, served in its wood-paneled halls and garden. The Czech lands grow some of the best hops and barley in Europe, and today Czechs drink more beer per person than any other people. Prague’s pubs are at the heart of the country’s most famous comic novel, The Good Soldier Švejk, by Jaroslav Hašek, published in the 1920s. It opens in a real pub, U Kalicha, where Švejk chats about the archduke’s murder in Sarajevo and is arrested by a police spy. From there he stumbles cheerfully into the First World War.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two companions for a Prague pub.
items: A podcast episode tells how U Fleků survived five centuries of wars and communism.
And The Good Soldier Švejk is the great Czech comic novel, bawdy and endlessly funny.

chapters.heading: Purity and Oktoberfest
chapters.text: In Bavaria, beer became a matter of law. In 1516 the dukes of Bavaria ruled that beer could be made only from barley, hops, and water. Yeast was added to the list later, once people understood what it did. The rule is often called the purity law, and Bavarian brewers still follow it. In 1589 the duke opened the Hofbräuhaus as the court brewery, because he did not want to keep paying for expensive beer from the north. Its beer hall in the old town is now the most famous in the world. Munich’s other great beer institution started by accident. In 1810 the city held a horse race to celebrate a royal wedding, and the party was so popular that it was repeated every year. It became Oktoberfest.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Munich’s beer culture.
items: A walking tour led by a beer sommelier goes from the monks and the purity law to Oktoberfest.
A short video runs through the huge numbers behind Oktoberfest.
And in A Time of Gifts, Patrick Leigh Fermor, walking across Europe at eighteen, spends an evening in the Hofbräuhaus among huge drinkers and brownshirts.

chapters.heading: Guinness
chapters.text: In Ireland, the great beer was dark. In 1759 Arthur Guinness took over a small, run-down brewery at St. James’s Gate, on the western edge of Dublin, and signed a lease for nine thousand years at forty-five pounds a year. At first he brewed ale, but by the end of the century he had switched to porter, a dark beer from London. Guinness stout became Ireland’s best-known export, and by the late 1800s St. James’s Gate was the largest brewery in the world. The company also built housing, baths, and clinics for its workers. It is still brewing on the same site.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to look beyond the brewery tour.
items: In a podcast series, a historian digs through the company’s own archive for stories the tour skips.
And a walking tour of the Liberties, the old neighborhood around the brewery, covers its breweries and back alleys.

chapters.heading: The beer flood
chapters.text: In London, the porter breweries grew to an enormous size, and they competed to build the biggest vats. At the Meux brewery, off Tottenham Court Road, one vat held more than half a million liters. On October 17, 1814, one of its iron hoops gave way, and the vat burst. It broke open others, and a wave of more than a million liters of beer smashed through the brewery wall and into the crowded slum of St. Giles behind it. Eight people were killed, most of them women and children at a wake in a cellar. A court ruled that it was an act of God, and nobody was held responsible.

items: For the full story, there is a video about the flood and the dark porter that caused it.

chapters.heading: Beer halls and the Nazis
chapters.text: Munich’s beer halls were also where Adolf Hitler found his first audiences. In February 1920 he announced the program of the Nazi party at a meeting in the Hofbräuhaus. In November 1923 he burst into the Bürgerbräukeller, a large beer hall across the river, fired a pistol into the ceiling, and declared a national revolution. The coup collapsed the next day, and Hitler went to prison. After he came to power, he returned to the Bürgerbräukeller every year to speak on the anniversary. In 1939 a carpenter named Georg Elser spent weeks hiding a bomb inside a pillar behind the speaker’s platform. Hitler cut his speech short and left thirteen minutes before it went off.

mediaNote.lead: Two stories cover both nights at the Bürgerbräukeller.
items: A historian explains the failed coup of 1923, and how it became a Nazi myth.
And 13 Minutes, a German film, tells the story of Georg Elser and his bomb.

chapters.heading: Carlsberg
chapters.text: The last stop is in Copenhagen. In 1847 J. C. Jacobsen founded the Carlsberg brewery on a hill outside the city, and he named it after his son, Carl. Jacobsen cared about science, and he built a laboratory at the brewery. In 1883 a chemist there, Emil Christian Hansen, grew the first pure culture of lager yeast. Carlsberg gave it away to other brewers, and most of the lager in the world is still made with its descendants. Carl later ran his own brewery and spent much of his fortune on art. He founded the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, a museum of ancient and modern sculpture across from Tivoli Gardens. Today small breweries have spread across the city.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two sides of beer in Copenhagen today.
items: A short video tours the Glyptotek, the art museum the beer money built.
And another visits a small brewery whose owner built it from secondhand equipment.

title: The coffeehouse
intro: Coffee came to Europe from the Ottoman Empire, and the coffeehouse came with it: a public room where anyone who could pay for a cup could sit, read, and argue. Writers worked in them, spies met in them, and governments tried more than once to shut them down.
This thread starts in Istanbul and ends in Lisbon. Almost every stop is a café you can still sit in.

chapters.heading: Where it started
chapters.text: Coffee came from Yemen, across the Red Sea from Arabia, and in the 1550s it reached Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire. The city’s first coffeehouses opened in Tahtakale, the market district by the Golden Horn. They caught on fast. Men met there to talk, play games, and listen to storytellers, and the authorities did not like it. Sultans and religious leaders tried more than once to close them as places of gossip and rebellion, but the coffeehouses always came back. Three hundred years later, European and Levantine families built a different kind of café life across the water, in the district of Pera, along the street now called İstiklal Avenue.
chapters.tip: Turkish coffee is served with its grounds. Let them settle, and stop drinking before you reach them.

mediaNote.lead: Two podcast episodes cover each side of the story.
items: A comedy history podcast about the Ottoman court covers coffeehouse culture, along with law codes and festivals.
An episode of the Ottoman History Podcast follows the Vallaury family, who ran cafés on the main street of Pera.

chapters.heading: A seat for the afternoon
chapters.text: From Istanbul, coffee spread west to Venice, London, and Paris. But the city that made the coffeehouse its own was Vienna, which the Ottoman army besieged in 1683. Its first licensed coffeehouse opened two years later. By 1900 there were hundreds, and the coffeehouse had become the city’s shared living room, warmer and more comfortable than many people’s homes. For the price of one cup you could stay all afternoon, read the newspapers, and write letters. Café Central, opened in 1876 in a grand former bank on Herrengasse, drew writers, chess players, and political exiles. Leon Trotsky, the Russian revolutionary, played chess there before the First World War. In 2011 Vienna’s coffeehouse culture was listed as intangible heritage by Austria’s commission for UNESCO.
chapters.tip: One coffee buys a seat for as long as you like. It comes with a glass of water, and you can ask for the newspapers.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways to understand the Viennese café.
items: A podcast episode about the coffee trade explores the grand cafés where writers lingered for hours.
A short video shows what you get for the price of one coffee, from the marble tables to the newspapers.
And Stefan Zweig’s memoir The World of Yesterday remembers the café-going Vienna he grew up in, before the wars ended it.

chapters.place: Grand Café, Karl Johans gate, Oslo
chapters.heading: Ibsen’s lunch
chapters.text: In the late 1800s, the Viennese idea of the café spread north and east. In Kristiania, as Oslo was then called, the Grand Café on Karl Johans gate, the main street, became the meeting place of writers and artists. Its most famous regular was Henrik Ibsen, the playwright of A Doll’s House and Hedda Gabler. He came home in 1891 after nearly thirty years abroad. Each day he walked to the Grand Café at the same time and sat at the same table. People said you could set your watch by him, and visitors came to see him arrive. A large mural inside, painted in the 1920s, shows him among the city’s writers and artists.

items: If you want to know the man behind the routine, there is a biography of Ibsen, the prickly playwright who changed modern theater.

chapters.heading: Six hundred coffeehouses
chapters.text: Budapest took to coffeehouses with even more enthusiasm. Around 1900 it was one of the fastest-growing cities in Europe, and it had about six hundred cafés. Writers had their regular tables, magazines were edited from them, and some cafés never closed at all. Many were lost in the Second World War, and more under communism, when they were seen as bourgeois. Gerbeaud, a confectioner’s café that has stood on Vörösmarty Square since 1870, is one of the grand ones that survived.

mediaNote.lead: Two books bring that world back.
items: John Lukacs’s Budapest 1900 is a portrait of the city at its peak, full of coffeehouses, poets, and money.
In Between the Woods and the Water, Patrick Leigh Fermor, who walked across Europe at nineteen, falls in with Budapest’s café society in 1934.

chapters.heading: Art Nouveau rooms
chapters.text: Prague built its grand cafés in the same years, when the city was rich and growing fast. In the 1900s and 1910s, the writer Franz Kafka met his friends at the Café Louvre on Národní, the avenue that runs down to the river. Café Slavia, across the street from the National Theatre, was where actors and writers went after the show. Under communism it became a meeting place for dissidents, among them Václav Havel, the playwright who became president after the revolution of 1989. The café inside the Municipal House, an Art Nouveau concert hall opened in 1912, still has its original interior.
chapters.tip: The café inside the Municipal House keeps its original 1912 interior.

mediaNote.lead: Two walking tours cover this well.
items: A tour of the New Town takes in Art Nouveau buildings and elegant cafés, and ends on the avenue where the Velvet Revolution began.
Another follows Kafka through the old town, with readings from his work, and ends near a café he went to.

chapters.heading: Spies on Terazije
chapters.text: Farther south, Belgrade’s best-known café opened in 1908 on the ground floor of the Hotel Moskva, a grand building on Terazije, the city’s main square. Through two world wars and the Cold War, it was where diplomats, journalists, and agents watched each other over coffee. Yugoslavia belonged to neither the Soviet bloc nor the West, so both sides worked in Belgrade, and the café was one of their favorite places to meet. It still serves its own cake, the Moskva šnit, made with pineapple, cherries, and almonds.
chapters.image: Hotel Moskva and the fountain in Belgrade.jpg

items: For a spy’s view of it, there is a podcast episode in which a former CIA officer describes meeting a Yugoslav source in Belgrade’s cafés.

chapters.heading: The poets’ table
chapters.text: Between the two world wars, Warsaw had its own poets’ café. Mała Ziemiańska, on Mazowiecka Street, opened in 1918, the year Poland became independent again. Its upstairs room belonged to the Skamander group, young poets such as Julian Tuwim and Antoni Słonimski, who wrote about ordinary city life in everyday language. The other tables went to painters, actors, and journalists. In 1939 Germany invaded Poland, and in 1944, after the Warsaw Uprising, the German army destroyed most of the city center. The café was never rebuilt.

items: To see where it stood, there is a video from POLIN, the museum of Polish Jewish history, about the café and the poets who held court there.

chapters.heading: The existentialists’ café
chapters.text: Paris had cafés long before Vienna’s golden age. The Procope, which opened in 1686, is often called the oldest in the city. But it was in the 1940s that the Paris café became a symbol of intellectual life. During the German occupation, the philosophers Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir worked most days at the Café de Flore, on Boulevard Saint-Germain. One reason was that the café was heated and their rooms were not. After the war their ideas, known as existentialism, became famous around the world, and so did the cafés of Saint-Germain-des-Prés where they wrote.
chapters.tip: Coffee costs less standing at the counter than at a table, and more on the terrace.
chapters.image: Café de Flore, 172 boulevard Saint-Germain, Paris 6e.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Paris café life.
items: Sarah Bakewell’s At the Existentialist Café tells the story of Sartre, Beauvoir, and their friends, and makes their ideas easy to follow.
A very short video looks at the café life of the Latin Quarter, next door to Saint-Germain.

chapters.heading: Pessoa’s table
chapters.text: The thread ends in Lisbon, where coffee has a special link to Brazil, Portugal’s former colony and one of the world’s largest coffee growers. A Brasileira opened in the Chiado district in 1905 to sell Brazilian coffee, and it gave a free cup to everyone who bought a bag of beans. It became a meeting place for writers and artists. Its best-known customer was Fernando Pessoa, a poet who wrote under dozens of invented names. A bronze statue of him sits at a table outside. His other favorite, Martinho da Arcada, on the great riverside square called the Praça do Comércio, has been open since 1782.
chapters.tip: In Lisbon an espresso is “uma bica.”

mediaNote.lead: If you want to linger in Pessoa’s Lisbon, here are three places to start.
items: The Book of Disquiet, his strange, fragmentary diary of a Lisbon bookkeeper, is best read in short pieces.
A one-minute video at Martinho da Arcada explains five ways to order coffee like a local.
And a short photography walk starts at a café where poets and painters once met, and heads down to the river.

title: Football cities
intro: In most of Europe, a football club is more than a team. It can stand for a religion in Glasgow, a nation in Barcelona, or a country that no longer exists in Belgrade. Its ground is a place of pilgrimage and, more than once, of disaster.
Each stop is a stadium, with the story of what it means to its city.

chapters.heading: The Old Firm
chapters.text: We start in Glasgow, with one of the oldest rivalries in football. Celtic was founded in 1887 by Brother Walfrid, an Irish Marist brother, to raise money for the poor of the city’s East End. It became the club of Glasgow’s Irish Catholics, and Rangers, across the city, became the club of its Protestants. The two are known together as the Old Firm. In 1967 Celtic, managed by Jock Stein, became the first British team to win the European Cup. In 1971, 66 fans died in a crush on a stairway at Ibrox, the Rangers ground, after a New Year match.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the Old Firm.
items: A documentary explains the rivalry and its roots in Ireland.
A podcast episode tells the story of the Ibrox disaster of 1971.
And a biography of Jock Stein tells how a former miner built the team that won Europe.

chapters.heading: The Kop
chapters.text: In Liverpool, the club’s story is told through its fans. In 1959, Bill Shankly, a Scottish manager, took over Liverpool FC, then in the second division, and built it into a winning club. Its fans stood on the Kop, a huge terrace behind one goal. In 1963 they adopted “You’ll Never Walk Alone,” a song from a musical, as their anthem. In 1989, 97 Liverpool fans died in a crush at Hillsborough, a stadium in Sheffield, during a cup semifinal. The police blamed the fans. It took 27 years and a second inquest to establish that the victims had been unlawfully killed.
chapters.image: The Kop at Anfield Stadium, Liverpool - geograph.org.uk - 5885064.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Anfield.
items: A BBC film from 1974 shows the Kop swaying and singing.
“You’ll Never Walk Alone,” by Gerry and the Pacemakers, is the song the Kop adopted.
Red or Dead, a long novel by David Peace, retells Shankly’s years at the club.
And a podcast episode tells the story of Hillsborough and the families’ fight for the truth.

chapters.heading: After Munich
chapters.text: Manchester United’s story turns on a disaster too. In February 1958, the team was flying home from a European Cup match in Belgrade. After refueling in Munich, its plane crashed on its third attempt to take off from a snowy runway. Twenty-three people died, eight of them players from a famously young team. The manager, Matt Busby, survived and rebuilt the club, and ten years later United won the European Cup. Its ground, Old Trafford, is known as the Theatre of Dreams.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Old Trafford.
items: A podcast episode tells the story of the Munich air disaster.
Another recalls how Eric Cantona, a French maverick, ended the club’s 26-year wait for a league title.
The Class of ’92 is a documentary about six young players who grew up together at the club.
And a walking tour loops around the stadium, past the statues of its legends.

chapters.heading: More than a club
chapters.text: In Barcelona, the football club came to stand for a nation. Under Francisco Franco, the dictator who ruled Spain from 1939 to 1975, the use of the Catalan language in public was restricted. FC Barcelona’s ground was one of the few places where tens of thousands of people could shout in Catalan together. The club’s motto, “more than a club,” is spelled out in the seats of the Camp Nou, its stadium since 1957. The stadium is being rebuilt while the team keeps playing.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into Barça.
items: A podcast episode tells how the club became a symbol of Catalan identity.
Take the Ball, Pass the Ball is a documentary about Pep Guardiola’s great Barcelona team.
Fear and Loathing in La Liga, by Sid Lowe, is a funny history of the rivalry with Real Madrid.
And a short report visits the Camp Nou, the largest stadium in Europe.

chapters.heading: The other side of El Clásico
chapters.text: Barcelona’s great rival is Real Madrid, and the two clubs’ matches are called El Clásico. Real won the first five European Cups, from 1956 to 1960, and for many Catalans it became the club of Franco’s regime. Its stadium, the Santiago Bernabéu, is named after the president who built it. It opened in 1947, on Madrid’s main avenue, the Paseo de la Castellana. It has just been rebuilt with a steel skin and a roof that closes.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the Bernabéu.
items: A short video shows how the stadium got its steel skin and closing roof.
And Fear and Loathing in La Liga tells the same rivalry from the Madrid side.

chapters.heading: A city’s one club
chapters.text: Marseille is a different kind of football city. It has only one big club, Olympique de Marseille, and the whole city follows it. In 1993, it became the first French team to win the Champions League. A few weeks later, it was caught up in a match-fixing scandal and stripped of its French title. Its fans, organized in ultras groups, fill the two curved ends of the Stade Vélodrome with flares, flags, and chants.

items: To see the fans, there is a short film that follows Marseille’s ultras to a European final.

chapters.heading: Two clubs, one stadium
chapters.text: In Milan, two rival clubs share one stadium. AC Milan was founded in 1899. In 1908, members who wanted the club to sign foreign players broke away and founded Inter. Since 1947, both have played at San Siro, a stadium on the west side of the city. In the 1960s, Inter’s Argentine coach Helenio Herrera won two European Cups with a defensive style known as catenaccio, the door bolt. Today the two clubs plan to replace the old stadium with a new one.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into San Siro.
items: A podcast episode tells how Helenio Herrera taught Inter to defend.
A short BBC report looks at the clubs’ plans to replace the stadium.
“Luci a San Siro,” by the songwriter Roberto Vecchioni, is about courting in a car near the stadium.
And Calcio, by the historian John Foot, is a history of Italian football.

chapters.place: FC Bayern Museum, Allianz Arena, Munich
chapters.heading: The Jewish president
chapters.text: In Munich, Bayern’s history includes a story the club long kept quiet. Kurt Landauer, the son of a Jewish merchant family, was Bayern’s president when it won its first German championship in 1932. The next year, the Nazis came to power, and he was forced out. He was held for a time in Dachau concentration camp, then escaped to exile in Switzerland. After the war he came home and was elected president again. Bayern now honors him openly, and its museum tells his story.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into his story.
items: A short film from the club reads from Landauer’s letters.
And Bayern, by Uli Hesse, is a history of the club that includes his story.

chapters.place: Red Star and Partizan stadiums, Belgrade
chapters.heading: The Eternal Derby
chapters.text: The last stop is Belgrade, the capital of Serbia, once the capital of Yugoslavia. Its two big clubs, Red Star and Partizan, were both founded in 1945, and their grounds are a short walk apart. Their match is called the Eternal Derby. In May 1991, Red Star won the European Cup in Bari, in Italy, beating Marseille on penalties. Its players came from across Yugoslavia. Within weeks, Slovenia and Croatia declared independence, war followed, and the team was scattered.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Belgrade football.
items: A short film follows the Eternal Derby, which brings the city to a halt.
A podcast episode tells how Yugoslavia’s last great team won Europe.
And a short video tells the story of the penalty shootout in Bari.

title: Olympic cities
intro: The modern Olympics began in Athens in 1896. European cities have used them since to rebuild, to show off, and once to make propaganda. Most of the stadiums are still in use.
This thread follows the Games through seven cities, in date order.

chapters.heading: The first modern Games
chapters.text: The ancient Olympic Games ended in the 4th century AD. In the 1890s, a French educator, Pierre de Coubertin, set out to revive them. The first modern Games opened in Athens in April 1896, in the ancient Panathenaic Stadium. A wealthy Greek merchant, Georgios Averoff, paid to rebuild it in white marble. Only a few hundred athletes took part, almost all men. The most popular winner was Spyridon Louis, a Greek water carrier, who won the first marathon.

items: For the whole story, there is an episode of The Rest Is History that starts in this stadium and follows the Games up to the Second World War.

chapters.heading: Hitler’s Games
chapters.text: Forty years later, the Olympics became propaganda. Berlin had won the 1936 Games before the Nazis came to power, and Hitler used them to show the world a confident, orderly Germany. The regime built a huge new stadium and staged the first torch relay. Leni Riefenstahl filmed it all for her documentary Olympia. But the star of the Games was Jesse Owens, a Black American athlete, who won four gold medals. The Olympiastadion is still in use.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into the 1936 Games.
items: A short video from the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum explains how the Nazis used the Games.
And Race is a film about Jesse Owens and his four gold medals.

chapters.heading: The skater from Oslo
chapters.text: Winter sports had their own Games from 1924, and Norway’s first great Olympic star was a girl from Oslo. Sonja Henie trained on the ice at Frogner Stadium. She competed in her first Winter Olympics at eleven, and she won figure-skating gold at three in a row, in 1928, 1932, and 1936. She then moved to Hollywood and became one of its best-paid film stars. Her home city hosted the Winter Olympics in 1952, and a statue of her now stands at the stadium.
chapters.image: Holmenkollbakken - no-nb digifoto 20150625 00168 NB MIT FNR 11656 B.jpg

items: For her story, there is a podcast episode about the girl from Oslo who won three Olympics, then conquered Hollywood.

chapters.heading: Helsinki 1952
chapters.text: That same year, Helsinki hosted the Summer Games. The city had been chosen for 1940 and built a stadium with a tall white tower, but the war canceled the Games. In 1952 it finally hosted them. The Soviet Union competed for the first time, in the early years of the Cold War. The star of the Games was Emil Zátopek, a Czechoslovak army officer. In eight days he won the 5,000 meters, the 10,000 meters, and the marathon, which he had never run before.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into the Helsinki Games.
items: A short report looks at how the Soviet Union joined the Olympics in a small Nordic capital.
A podcast episode tells how Zátopek won three gold medals in eight days.
Olympia 52, Chris Marker’s first feature film, is a documentary about those Games.
And The Happiest Day in the Life of Olli Mäki, a gentle true story, ends with a 1962 title fight in the Olympic Stadium.

chapters.heading: The cheerful Games
chapters.text: In 1972, West Germany wanted its Games to be the opposite of 1936. In Munich, the designer Otl Aicher gave them soft blues and greens, and sport pictograms that are still copied. The stadium had a light, tent-like roof of acrylic panels. On September 5, eight Palestinian gunmen broke into the Israeli team’s apartments in the Olympic Village and took athletes hostage. All eleven Israeli hostages were killed, along with a German police officer. The Games went on after a day of mourning. Days later, the United States lost its first ever Olympic basketball game, to the Soviet Union, in a disputed final.

mediaNote.lead: Here are four ways into the Munich Games.
items: A short video explains Otl Aicher’s colors and pictograms.
A DW documentary shows how live television turned the hostage siege into a global broadcast.
One Day in September is the Oscar-winning documentary about the attack.
And a podcast episode tells how the last three seconds of the basketball final were replayed until the Americans lost.

chapters.heading: The city rebuilt
chapters.text: Barcelona used the 1992 Games to rebuild itself. For a century, the city had turned its back on the sea, behind railway lines and factories. For the Olympics, it cleared the old industrial waterfront and built beaches, a new Olympic Village, and a ring road. The main stadium was on Montjuïc, a hill above the port. The opening song was “Barcelona,” a duet by Freddie Mercury and the opera singer Montserrat Caballé. Mercury had died the year before. Other host cities still point to Barcelona as a model.
chapters.image: Aerial view of Somorrostro Beach and Port Olympic in Barcelona, Spain (51227006624).jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into the Barcelona Games.
items: A short video walks from the old town down to the beaches built for the Games.
Marathon, by the director Carlos Saura, is the official film of those Games.
And “Barcelona” is the duet by Freddie Mercury and Montserrat Caballé.

chapters.heading: East London
chapters.text: London hosted the Games for the third time in 2012, and like Barcelona it used them to rebuild. It put the Olympic Park in Stratford, in East London, on old industrial land along the River Lea. The architect Zaha Hadid designed the aquatics center, with a roof shaped like a wave, and it is now a public swimming pool. The main stadium was designed so it could be shrunk after the Games, and it is now home to West Ham United, a football club.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into London’s Olympic Park.
items: A short video looks at Zaha Hadid’s aquatics center.
And another shows how the stadium was designed to change after the Games.
